def store_performance_analysis(data):
    """
    Comprehensive analysis of store performance patterns

    Parameters:
    data (pandas.DataFrame): Original dataset

    Returns:
    dict: Store performance insights
    """
    print("\nSTORE PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS")
    print("=" * 40)

    # Store revenue analysis
    store_revenue = data.groupby('Store_Id').agg({
        'Product_Store_Sales_Total': ['sum', 'mean', 'count'],
        'Product_MRP': 'mean',
        'Product_Weight': 'mean'
    }).round(2)

    store_revenue.columns = ['Total_Revenue', 'Avg_Revenue_Per_Product', 'Product_Count', 'Avg_MRP', 'Avg_Weight']
    store_revenue = store_revenue.reset_index()

    # Add store characteristics
    store_info = data.groupby('Store_Id').agg({
        'Store_Size': lambda x: x.iloc[0],
        'Store_Location_City_Type': lambda x: x.iloc[0],
        'Store_Type': lambda x: x.iloc[0],
        'Store_Establishment_Year': lambda x: x.iloc[0]
    }).reset_index()

    # Merge information
    store_analysis = store_revenue.merge(store_info, on='Store_Id')
    store_analysis['Store_Age'] = 2022 - store_analysis['Store_Establishment_Year']
    store_analysis['Revenue_Per_Product'] = store_analysis['Total_Revenue'] / store_analysis['Product_Count']

    print("Store Performance Summary:")
    print(store_analysis.to_string(index=False))

    # Performance ranking
    store_analysis['Revenue_Rank'] = store_analysis['Total_Revenue'].rank(ascending=False)
    store_analysis['Efficiency_Rank'] = store_analysis['Revenue_Per_Product'].rank(ascending=False)

    # Best and worst performers
    best_performer = store_analysis.loc[store_analysis['Revenue_Rank'] == 1].iloc[0]
    worst_performer = store_analysis.loc[store_analysis['Revenue_Rank'] == store_analysis['Revenue_Rank'].max()].iloc[0]

    performance_insights = {
        'best_performer': {
            'store_id': best_performer['Store_Id'],
            'total_revenue': best_performer['Total_Revenue'],
            'characteristics': f"{best_performer['Store_Type']}, {best_performer['Store_Size']}, {best_performer['Store_Location_City_Type']}"
        },
        'worst_performer': {
            'store_id': worst_performer['Store_Id'],
            'total_revenue': worst_performer['Total_Revenue'],
            'characteristics': f"{worst_performer['Store_Type']}, {worst_performer['Store_Size']}, {worst_performer['Store_Location_City_Type']}"
        },
        'store_analysis': store_analysis
    }

    return performance_insights

def product_category_insights(data):
    """
    Analyze product category performance patterns

    Parameters:
    data (pandas.DataFrame): Original dataset

    Returns:
    dict: Product insights
    """
    print("\nPRODUCT CATEGORY ANALYSIS")
    print("=" * 35)

    # Category performance
    category_performance = data.groupby('Product_Type').agg({
        'Product_Store_Sales_Total': ['sum', 'mean', 'count'],
        'Product_MRP': 'mean',
        'Product_Weight': 'mean'
    }).round(2)

    category_performance.columns = ['Total_Revenue', 'Avg_Revenue', 'Transaction_Count', 'Avg_MRP', 'Avg_Weight']
    category_performance = category_performance.reset_index()
    category_performance['Revenue_Contribution_%'] = (category_performance['Total_Revenue'] / category_performance['Total_Revenue'].sum() * 100).round(2)

    # Sort by total revenue
    category_performance = category_performance.sort_values('Total_Revenue', ascending=False)

    print("Product Category Performance:")
    print(category_performance.to_string(index=False))

    # Top and bottom performers
    top_categories = category_performance.head(3)['Product_Type'].tolist()
    bottom_categories = category_performance.tail(3)['Product_Type'].tolist()

    category_insights = {
        'top_performers': top_categories,
        'bottom_performers': bottom_categories,
        'category_analysis': category_performance
    }

    return category_insights

# Generate business analysis
store_insights = store_performance_analysis(data)
category_insights = product_category_insights(data)

docs.title: Market Opportunity
docs.text:
The Indian used car market presents a compelling business opportunity with unique dynamics. In 2018-19, while new car sales recorded 3.6 million units, approximately 4 million second-hand cars were transacted, indicating a larger pre-owned market than the new car segment.

Cars4U, a emerging tech startup, aims to capitalize on this market shift where consumers increasingly prefer pre-owned vehicles over new purchases, particularly as economic factors drive preference for cost-effective alternatives.

docs.title: Core Business Challenge
docs.text: Unlike new car pricing—which is relatively deterministic and managed by Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs)—used cars present significant uncertainty in both pricing and supply dynamics. This complexity creates both risk and opportunity for market participants.

docs.title: Analytical Objectives
docs.text:
Primary Goal: Develop a robust predictive model for used car pricing to enable competitive positioning and profit optimization.

Secondary Goals:

  • Generate actionable market insights for inventory acquisition strategies

  • Identify key value drivers in the used car market

  • Provide data-driven recommendations for market expansion

Success Metrics: Model accuracy (R²), prediction error (RMSE), and business applicability of insights.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 1: Environment Setup and Data Loading]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Dataset Characteristics
docs.text:
The analysis encompasses 6,019 used car listings with 13 attributes covering vehicle specifications, condition indicators, and pricing information.

Target Variable: Price (used car selling price in INR 100,000 units)

Key Predictor Categories:

  • Vehicle Identity: Name, Brand, Model

  • Market Context: Location, Year of manufacture

  • Condition Indicators: Kilometers driven, Owner type

  • Technical Specifications: Engine displacement, Power, Mileage, Seats

  • Fuel and Transmission: Fuel type, Transmission type

  • Reference Pricing: New car price

docs.title: Data Quality Assessment
docs.text:
Missing Data Pattern: Significant missing values observed in technical specifications (Power: 175 missing, Engine: 46 missing) and reference pricing (New_Price: substantial missingness). The target variable Price contains 1,234 missing entries requiring removal from modeling dataset.

Data Type Issues: Several numerical columns stored as text format requiring preprocessing (Power: "bhp" suffix, Engine: "CC" suffix, Mileage: mixed units "kmpl"/"km/kg").

Outlier Presence: Extreme values identified in kilometers driven (maximum: 6,500,000 km for a 2017 vehicle) indicating data entry errors requiring correction.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 2: Data Loading and Initial Exploration]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Distribution Analysis Insights
docs.text:
Price Distribution: Highly right-skewed with mean ₹9.47 lakh and maximum ₹160 lakh. Log transformation successfully normalizes distribution, enabling more effective modeling of luxury and budget segments.

Kilometers Driven: Extreme right skewness with values ranging from 171 km to 6.5 million km. Log transformation essential for analysis, though extreme outliers require removal.

Technical Specifications:

  • Power distribution shows most vehicles (mode: 90-100 bhp) with luxury outliers above 250 bhp

  • Engine displacement follows similar pattern with concentration in mid-range values

  • Mileage appears normally distributed after handling zero values (treated as missing)

docs.title: Market Composition Analysis
docs.text:
Geographic Distribution: Mumbai (13.1%) and Hyderabad (12.1%) dominate listings, indicating mature used car markets in these metros.

Fuel Type Dominance: 99% gasoline/diesel split with minimal alternative fuel adoption (1% CNG/LPG/Electric), reflecting market maturity stage.

Transmission Preference: 71.8% manual transmission preference indicating price-conscious consumer base.

Ownership Pattern: 82.1% first-owner vehicles with 15.9% second-owner, suggesting rapid turnover in certain segments.

docs.title: Relationship Pattern Discovery
docs.text:
Price Drivers Identified:

  • Strong Positive Correlation: Year of manufacture (r=0.xx), Engine power, New car price

  • Weak/No Correlation: Kilometers driven (counterintuitive finding requiring investigation)

  • Segmentation Effects: Automatic transmission commands premium pricing; luxury 2-seaters and utility 8-10 seaters occupy distinct price brackets

Geographic Pricing Variations: Coimbatore and Bangalore show higher price variability (larger IQR), suggesting less mature market pricing.

docs.title: Critical Analysis Limitations
docs.text:
Correlation vs Causation: Strong correlations don't guarantee predictive power, particularly for kilometers driven relationship.

Market Segment Bias: Dataset may under-represent certain segments (electric vehicles, commercial vehicles) affecting generalizability.

Temporal Considerations: Analysis snapshot may not capture seasonal pricing variations or market cycle effects.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3: Exploratory Data Analysis]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Missing Value Treatment Strategy
docs.text:
Systematic Approach Applied:

  • Seats: Imputed using brand-model median, with domain knowledge fallback (Maruti Estilo: 5 seats)

  • Technical Specifications: Median imputation for Engine, Power after unit standardization

  • Mileage: Median imputation for electric vehicles (unavoidable missing by design)

  • New_Price: Median imputation considering right-skewed distribution

  • Price (Target): Complete case deletion (1,234 rows removed) to maintain prediction integrity

docs.title: Feature Engineering Innovations
docs.text:
Text Processing:

  • Brand Extraction: Systematic extraction from vehicle names revealing Maruti and Hyundai market dominance

  • Model Extraction: Secondary feature creation enabling granular analysis

  • Category Validation: Brand pricing hierarchy matches domain expectations (Lamborghini: ₹120L average)

Unit Standardization:

  • Mileage Harmonization: CNG efficiency conversion (km/kg → kmpl using 1.40 factor)

  • Price Normalization: Crore/Lakh standardization to consistent Lakh units

Transformation Engineering:

  • Log Transformations: Applied to Price and Kilometers_Driven for normality

  • Categorical Encoding: One-hot encoding with dummy trap avoidance (drop_first=True)

docs.title: Data Quality Validation
docs.text:
Final Dataset: 4,785 observations after quality control procedures

Completeness: Zero missing values post-imputation

Distribution Improvement: Log transformations successfully normalize skewed variables

Feature Count: 45 total features post-encoding (13 original + engineered + dummy variables)

docs.title: Preprocessing Limitations
docs.text:
Imputation Assumptions: Median imputation assumes missing-at-random mechanism, which may not hold for luxury vehicles.

Information Loss: Brand and model extraction may lose specific variant information affecting price discrimination.

Sample Bias: Complete case deletion may systematically exclude certain market segments.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 4: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering]

docs.title: Algorithmic Approach Rationale
docs.text:
Progressive Complexity: Implementation follows increasing model complexity to understand performance-interpretability trade-offs.

Baseline Establishment: Linear regression provides interpretable baseline with coefficient understanding.

Regularization Exploration: Ridge regression addresses potential multicollinearity in automotive features.

Non-parametric Methods: Tree-based models capture non-linear relationships and feature interactions.

docs.title: Train-Test Methodology
docs.text:
Split Ratio: 70-30 train-test split balancing model training needs with robust evaluation

Reproducibility: Fixed random_state=1 ensuring consistent results across experiments

Evaluation Framework: Dual metrics (R² and RMSE) providing complementary performance perspectives

docs.title: Model Implementation Results
docs.text:
Linear Regression Performance:

  • Training R²: ~0.88 indicating strong linear relationships

  • Test R²: ~0.87 demonstrating good generalization

  • Interpretation: Coefficient significance reveals key price drivers

Ridge Regression (Recommended):

  • Training R²: ~0.89 with improved generalization

  • Test R²: ~0.89 showing optimal bias-variance balance

  • Business Value: Robust predictions with reduced overfitting risk

Decision Tree Analysis:

  • Initial Performance: Severe overfitting (Train R²: ~0.98, Test R²: ~0.76)

  • Post-Tuning: Improved generalization (Train R²: ~0.85, Test R²: ~0.83)

  • Feature Importance: Power, Year, Engine emerge as critical predictors

Random Forest Performance:

  • Ensemble Benefit: Strong performance (Train R²: ~0.92, Test R²: ~0.88)

  • Feature Ranking: Consistent identification of key predictors

  • Computational Cost: Higher resource requirements for marginal improvement

docs.title: Model Selection Rationale
docs.text:
Ridge Regression Recommendation:

  • Performance: Optimal R²=0.89 with RMSE=3.62 on test data

  • Interpretability: Maintains coefficient interpretability unlike ensemble methods

  • Robustness: Regularization prevents overfitting on correlated automotive features

  • Business Applicability: Fast inference suitable for real-time pricing applications

Cross-Validation Needs: Single train-test split may not capture full model stability

Market Segment Performance: Aggregate metrics may mask poor performance in specific segments (luxury, commercial)

docs.text:
Geographic Opportunity Mapping:

  • Southern Market Premium: Markets like Coimbatore and Bangalore show higher price variability, suggesting premium positioning opportunities

  • Metro Market Maturity: Mumbai and Hyderabad demonstrate established markets with predictable pricing patterns

Inventory Acquisition Strategy:

Market Expansion Priorities:

docs.title: Introduction & Background
docs.text:
This tutorial examines one of the most significant case studies in statistical analysis and risk assessment: the Challenger Space Shuttle disaster. On January 28, 1986, the Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds into its flight, leading to the deaths of seven crew members. The disaster was caused by the failure of O-ring seals in the solid rocket boosters, which became brittle in the unusually cold weather conditions.

Tutorial Objectives:

  • Understand how logistic regression applies to binary classification problems

  • Learn to interpret relationships between continuous predictors and binary outcomes

  • Analyze the statistical evidence that could have prevented a tragedy

  • Develop critical thinking about statistical decision-making in high-stakes situations

Why This Case Matters: This analysis demonstrates how statistical methods can inform critical safety decisions. The data available before the launch showed a clear relationship between temperature and O-ring failure risk, yet this information wasn't effectively communicated to decision-makers.

Methodology Overview: We'll use logistic regression to model the probability of O-ring failure as a function of launch temperature. This approach is ideal for binary outcomes (failure/no failure) and provides interpretable coefficients for decision-making.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 1: Environment Setup]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Overview & Understanding
docs.text:
Dataset Characteristics:

  • Size: 120 observations from previous shuttle launches

  • Variables:

  • X: Launch temperature (°F)
  • Y: O-ring failure occurrence (0 = no failure, 1 = failure)
  • Observation: Sequential identifier

Data Quality Assessment: The dataset contains 120 complete observations with no missing values. All variables are numeric, with the outcome variable properly coded as binary (0/1).

Statistical Summary:

  • Temperature Range: 53°F to 81°F

  • Average Temperature: 70°F

  • Failure Rate: 8.3% (10 failures out of 120 observations)

  • Temperature Distribution: Normal distribution centered around 70°F

Business Context: Each observation represents a previous shuttle launch, providing historical evidence of the temperature-failure relationship. The relatively low failure rate (8.3%) is typical in reliability engineering but requires careful statistical modeling to detect patterns.

Data Limitations:

  • Small sample size for rare events analysis

  • Limited to temperature as single predictor

  • Historical data may not reflect all current engineering factors

  • No information about failure severity or type

[See Code Walkthrough Section 2: Data Loading and Inspection]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Exploratory Data Analysis
docs.text:
Key Findings from Data Exploration:

Temperature Distribution Analysis:

  • Mean: 70°F with standard deviation of 7.1°F

  • Range: 28°F spread from coldest (53°F) to warmest (81°F)

  • Quartiles: 25th percentile at 67°F, 75th percentile at 75.25°F

Failure Pattern Analysis:

  • Total Failures: 10 out of 120 launches (8.3% failure rate)

  • Failure Distribution: Concentrated at lower temperatures

  • Critical Observation: All failures occurred at or below 75°F

Statistical Significance Indicators: The exploratory analysis reveals a clear pattern suggesting temperature dependency, but formal statistical testing is required to quantify the relationship strength and significance.

Risk Assessment Implications: The failure rate appears inversely related to temperature, suggesting higher risk in colder conditions. This pattern, while observable in raw data, requires statistical modeling to provide reliable probability estimates for decision-making.

Data Quality Verification:

  • No outliers detected in temperature measurements

  • Binary outcome variable properly coded

  • Consistent data collection methodology across observations

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3: Exploratory Data Analysis]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Visualization
docs.text:
Visualization Strategy: The scatter plot visualization effectively reveals the temperature-failure relationship by plotting failure counts against temperature values. This approach separates failures (red points) from non-failures (blue points at zero level).

Key Visual Insights:

Temperature-Failure Pattern:

  • High Temperature Zone (75°F+): No failures observed

  • Moderate Temperature Zone (65-75°F): Scattered failures

  • Low Temperature Zone (<65°F): Higher failure concentration

Critical Visual Evidence:

  • 53°F Cluster: Multiple failures (3) and non-failures at the same temperature

  • Temperature Threshold: No failures above 75°F in the dataset

  • Risk Gradient: Clear visual trend of decreasing failures with increasing temperature

Interpretation Challenges: The visualization reveals both the relationship and its uncertainty. At 53°F, both failures and non-failures occurred, highlighting the probabilistic nature of the relationship rather than a deterministic threshold.

Decision-Making Implications: The visual evidence strongly suggests that launching at temperatures below historical norms (especially below 60°F) significantly increases failure risk. The Challenger launch temperature was 31°F, well below any previous launch temperature.

Visualization Limitations:

  • Overlapping points may hide some data patterns

  • Binary nature of outcomes limits statistical resolution

  • No confidence intervals or uncertainty estimates shown

[See Code Walkthrough Section 4: Data Visualization]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Logistic Regression Modeling
docs.text:
Model Specification: The logistic regression model estimates the probability of O-ring failure as a function of launch temperature using the logit link function:

Mathematical Framework: log(odds) = β₀ + β₁ × Temperature

Where odds = P(failure) / P(no failure)

Model Performance Metrics:

Goodness of Fit:

  • Log-Likelihood: -29.089

  • Pseudo R-squared: 0.1549 (moderate explanatory power)

  • Likelihood Ratio Test: p-value = 0.001094 (highly significant)

Statistical Significance:

  • Temperature Coefficient: -0.1466 (p = 0.002)

  • Intercept: 7.4049 (p = 0.015)

  • Both parameters statistically significant at α = 0.05

Model Validation Results: The model successfully converged in 7 iterations, indicating stable parameter estimation. The significant likelihood ratio test confirms that temperature significantly improves prediction over a null model.

Predictive Capability: The model provides probability estimates for any given temperature, enabling risk-based decision making. However, the moderate pseudo R-squared indicates substantial unexplained variance, suggesting additional factors influence O-ring reliability.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 5: Logistic Regression Implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Model Interpretation & Results
docs.text:
Coefficient Interpretation:

Temperature Effect (β₁ = -0.1466):

  • Risk Reduction: Each 1°F temperature increase reduces the log-odds of failure by 0.1466

  • Practical Impact: Each 1°F increase reduces failure odds by approximately 13.6%

  • Statistical Significance: p = 0.002 provides strong evidence against the null hypothesis

Intercept Interpretation (β₀ = 7.4049):

  • Theoretical Baseline: Log-odds of failure when temperature = 0°F

  • Practical Note: Not physically meaningful since 0°F is outside the observed range

Probability Calculations: At the Challenger launch temperature of 31°F: P(failure) = 1 / (1 + exp(-[7.4049 - 0.1466 × 31])) ≈ 0.82

This suggests an 82% probability of O-ring failure at 31°F, far exceeding acceptable risk levels.

Risk Assessment Framework:

  • Low Risk Zone: Temperatures above 70°F (P(failure) < 0.05)

  • Moderate Risk Zone: 60-70°F (P(failure) = 0.05-0.20)

  • High Risk Zone: Below 60°F (P(failure) > 0.20)

  • Extreme Risk Zone: Below 40°F (P(failure) > 0.60)

Business Decision Implications: The model provides quantitative risk estimates for launch decisions. A typical aerospace risk tolerance might accept failure probabilities below 1-5%, suggesting launches should be postponed when temperatures drop below 65-70°F.

Confidence Intervals: The coefficient confidence interval [-0.239, -0.054] indicates the temperature effect is robust, with the worst-case scenario still showing substantial risk reduction with increased temperature.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 6: Model Interpretation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Critical Analysis & Limitations
docs.text:
Model Strengths:

Statistical Robustness:

  • Highly significant temperature effect (p = 0.002)

  • Stable parameter estimation with reliable convergence

  • Clear monotonic relationship between temperature and failure risk

  • Appropriate statistical method for binary outcome data

Practical Utility:

  • Provides quantitative risk estimates for decision-making

  • Simple, interpretable model suitable for non-statisticians

  • Historical validation through observed disaster at extreme low temperature

Model Limitations:

Statistical Constraints:

  • Sample Size: Only 120 observations with 10 failures limits precision

  • Pseudo R-squared: 0.1549 indicates substantial unexplained variance

  • Single Predictor: Temperature alone may not capture all failure mechanisms

  • Extrapolation Risk: Model predictions below 53°F (observed minimum) are uncertain

Methodological Concerns:

  • Rare Events: 8.3% failure rate challenges statistical power

  • Temporal Independence: Assumes each launch is independent (may not hold for sequential launches)

  • Engineering Complexity: O-ring failure involves multiple mechanical and environmental factors

  • Model Assumptions: Linearity of log-odds relationship may not hold across entire temperature range

Real-World Implementation Challenges:

Decision-Making Context:

  • Economic Pressure: Launch delays carry substantial financial costs

  • Political Pressure: High-profile missions face external pressure to proceed

  • Communication Gaps: Statistical evidence must be translated for engineering and management audiences

  • Risk Tolerance: Acceptable failure rates vary by mission type and crew safety considerations

Alternative Approaches:

  • Multiple Logistic Regression: Include additional predictors (humidity, wind, mechanical factors)

  • Survival Analysis: Model time-to-failure for better reliability estimates

  • Bayesian Methods: Incorporate prior engineering knowledge and uncertainty

  • Machine Learning: Random forests or neural networks for non-linear pattern detection

Computational Requirements: The analysis requires minimal computational resources (< 1 second on standard hardware), making it suitable for real-time decision support.

Reproducibility Assessment: Results are highly reproducible given the stable dataset and well-established statistical methods. However, model interpretation requires domain expertise in aerospace engineering and risk management.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 7: Model Validation and Diagnostics]

↩ Back to Top

Purpose: Implements logistic regression to model the probability of O-ring failure as a function of launch temperature.

Flow: 1. Model Specification: SM.logit() creates a logistic regression model object 2. Formula Definition: 'Y~X' specifies Y as dependent variable, X as independent variable 3. Model Fitting: model.fit() performs maximum likelihood estimation 4. Results Display: result.summary() provides comprehensive statistical output

Impact: This is the core analytical step that quantifies the temperature-failure relationship and provides statistical evidence for decision-making.

docs.title: Mathematical Foundations
docs.text:
Logistic Regression Equation: 

logit(P) = log(P/(1-P)) = β₀ + β₁ × Temperature

Where: - P = Probability of O-ring failure - β₀ = Intercept parameter - β₁ = Temperature coefficient

Probability Transformation: 

P(Failure) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(β₀ + β₁ × Temperature)))

Maximum Likelihood Estimation: The fitting process maximizes the likelihood function: 

L(β₀, β₁) = ∏[P^yᵢ × (1-P)^(1-yᵢ)]

docs.title: Statistical Output Interpretation

Parameter Estimates: - Intercept: 7.4049 (SE = 3.041, p = 0.015) - Temperature coefficient: -0.1466 (SE = 0.047, p = 0.002)

Statistical Significance: Both parameters are statistically significant at α = 0.05, providing strong evidence for the temperature-failure relationship.

def failure_probability(temperature, intercept=7.4049, coef=-0.1466):

    log_odds = intercept + coef * temperature
    probability = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-log_odds))
    return probability

docs.title: Confidence Intervals and Uncertainty
docs.text:
Coefficient Confidence Interval: - Temperature coefficient: [-0.239, -0.054] - Interpretation: We are 95% confident the true coefficient lies in this range - Worst case (CI lower bound): exp(-0.054) = 0.947 (5.3% reduction per °F) - Best case (CI upper bound): exp(-0.239) = 0.787 (21.3% reduction per °F)

Probability Confidence Intervals: 

def probability_ci(temperature, intercept=7.4049, coef=-0.1466, 
                   coef_se=0.047, intercept_se=3.041):
    """Calculate 95% confidence interval for failure probability."""
    # Point estimate
    log_odds = intercept + coef * temperature

    # Standard error of log-odds using delta method
    se_log_odds = np.sqrt(intercept_se**2 + (temperature * coef_se)**2)

    # 95% CI for log-odds
    log_odds_lower = log_odds - 1.96 * se_log_odds
    log_odds_upper = log_odds + 1.96 * se_log_odds

    # Transform to probability scale
    prob_point = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-log_odds))
    prob_lower = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-log_odds_upper))
    prob_upper = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-log_odds_lower))

    return prob_point, prob_lower, prob_upper

docs.title: Section 7: Statistical Concepts and Mathematical Foundations
Logistic Regression Theory
docs.text:
Why Logistic Regression? 1. Binary Outcome: O-ring failure is inherently binary (fail/don't fail) 2. Probability Bounds: Ensures predictions stay between 0 and 1 3. Non-linear Relationship: Captures S-shaped relationship between predictors and probability 4. Interpretable Parameters: Coefficients have clear odds ratio interpretation

Linear vs. Logistic Regression: 

# Linear regression problems with binary outcomes:
# 1. Predictions can exceed [0,1] bounds
# 2. Assumes constant variance (violated with binary data)
# 3. Residuals not normally distributed

# Logistic regression advantages:
# 1. Uses logit link to ensure [0,1] bounds
# 2. Appropriate error distribution (binomial)
# 3. Maximum likelihood estimation

docs.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation Details
docs.text:
Likelihood Function Construction: For binary outcomes, the likelihood for observation i is: 

L_i = P^y_i × (1-P)^(1-y_i)

Where: - P = predicted probability - y_i = observed outcome (0 or 1)

Full Dataset Likelihood: 

L(β₀, β₁) = ∏(i=1 to n) [P_i^y_i × (1-P_i)^(1-y_i)]

Log-Likelihood (easier to optimize): 

ℓ(β₀, β₁) = Σ(i=1 to n) [y_i × log(P_i) + (1-y_i) × log(1-P_i)]

Optimization Process: 

# Conceptual implementation of MLE
def log_likelihood(params, X, y):
    beta0, beta1 = params
    log_odds = beta0 + beta1 * X
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-log_odds))

    # Avoid log(0) issues
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-15, 1 - 1e-15)

    ll = np.sum(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p))
    return -ll  # Minimize negative log-likelihood

# StatsModels handles this optimization automatically

docs.text:
Integrated Script Structure: 

# Complete analysis workflow
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as SM

def challenger_analysis(data_path='challenger-data.csv'):
    """Complete Challenger O-ring failure analysis."""

    # 1. Data loading and inspection
    data = pd.read_csv(data_path)
    print("Data Overview:")
    print(data.describe())

    # 2. Exploratory analysis
    failures = data.loc[data.Y == 1]
    no_failures = data.loc[data.Y == 0]

    # 3. Visualization
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    failures_freq = failures.X.value_counts()
    no_failures_freq = no_failures.X.value_counts()

    plt.scatter(failures_freq.index, failures_freq, c='red', s=40, label='Failures')
    plt.scatter(no_failures_freq.index, np.zeros(len(no_failures_freq)), 
                c='blue', s=40, label='No Failures')
    plt.xlabel('Temperature (°F)')
    plt.ylabel('Number of Failures')
    plt.legend()
    plt.title('O-Ring Failures vs. Launch Temperature')
    plt.show()

    # 4. Logistic regression
    model = SM.logit(formula='Y~X', data=data)
    result = model.fit()
    print("\nModel Results:")
    print(result.summary())

    # 5. Risk assessment for Challenger launch temperature
    challenger_temp = 31
    prob = failure_probability(challenger_temp, 
                               result.params['Intercept'], 
                               result.params['X'])
    print(f"\nRisk Assessment for {challenger_temp}°F:")
    print(f"Predicted failure probability: {prob:.1%}")

    return result

def failure_probability(temperature, intercept, coef):
    """Calculate failure probability at given temperature."""
    log_odds = intercept + coef * temperature
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-log_odds))

# Run complete analysis
if __name__ == "__main__":
    results = challenger_analysis()

Statistical Lessons:

  • Logistic regression effectively models binary outcomes with continuous predictors

  • Statistical significance doesn't guarantee practical significance in decision-making

  • Extrapolation beyond observed data ranges introduces substantial uncertainty

  • Model interpretation requires domain expertise alongside statistical knowledge

Risk Management Insights:

  • Communication of statistical findings to non-technical stakeholders is crucial

  • Historical data analysis can reveal patterns invisible in individual cases

  • Risk tolerance frameworks must be established before analysis, not after

Professional Practice:

  • Statistical models are tools for decision support, not decision replacement

  • Model limitations must be clearly communicated to stakeholders

  • Validation using independent data sources strengthens conclusions

  • Documentation and reproducibility are essential for critical applications

Income Analysis: - Mean monthly income: \(6,500 with high variance (\)1,000-$20,000) - Significant income inequality within organization - Critical Finding: Employees leaving earn 30% less than those staying

Experience Patterns: - Average company tenure: 7 years - Concerning Pattern: Employees leaving have 30% less total work experience - Promotion timing appears problematic (some employees 10+ years without promotion)

docs.title: Categorical Variable Insights
docs.text:
Department Analysis: - R&D: 65% of workforce, 14% attrition rate - Sales: 30% of workforce, 40% attrition rate (major concern) - HR: 5% of workforce, 25% attrition rate

Work-Life Balance Indicators: - Overtime Workers: 28% of employees, 30%+ attrition rate - Travel Requirements: Frequent travelers show 2x attrition rate - Distance from Home: Employees living farther attrite 16% more

docs.title: Statistical Significance
docs.text:
Strongest Predictors Identified: 1. Overtime status (odds ratio: 2.6x) 2. Monthly income (inverse relationship) 3. Job involvement levels 4. Work-life balance ratings 5. Years since last promotion

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3: Comprehensive EDA Implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Preprocessing Strategy
docs.text:
The preprocessing approach balances feature preservation with model requirements:

Variable Removal Decisions: - EmployeeNumber: Unique identifier with no predictive value - Over18: Single value variable (all employees over 18) - StandardHours: No variation across employees

docs.title: Feature Engineering Approach
docs.text:
Categorical Encoding: - One-Hot Encoding: Applied to multi-category variables (Department, JobRole, etc.) - Binary Mapping: Simple Yes/No variables converted to 1/0 - Ordinal Preservation: Satisfaction and involvement scales maintained as numerical

Feature Scaling Rationale: - Required for: Logistic Regression and SVM (distance-based algorithms) - Not Required for: Tree-based models (Decision Tree, Random Forest) - Method Used: StandardScaler (Z-score normalization)

docs.title: Train-Test Split Strategy
docs.text: 70-30 Split with Stratification: - Maintains 16% attrition rate in both training and test sets - Ensures model evaluation on representative data - Rationale: Prevents bias from uneven class distribution

docs.title: Preprocessing Limitations
docs.text:
Potential Issues: - Information Loss: One-hot encoding increases dimensionality - Multicollinearity: High correlations between experience-related variables - Feature Selection: No systematic feature selection applied

[See Code Walkthrough Section 4: Data Preprocessing Implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Algorithm Selection Rationale
docs.text:
Four algorithms were selected to cover different modeling approaches:

1. Logistic Regression - Strengths: Interpretable coefficients, probability outputs, baseline model - Use Case: Understanding feature relationships and establishing baseline performance

2. Support Vector Machine (SVM) - Linear Kernel: Tests linear separability assumption - RBF Kernel: Captures non-linear relationships - Use Case: Handling complex decision boundaries

3. Decision Tree - Strengths: Highly interpretable, handles non-linear relationships naturally - Weakness: Prone to overfitting - Use Case: Understanding decision pathways

4. Random Forest - Strengths: Reduces overfitting, feature importance, ensemble robustness - Use Case: Achieving best predictive performance

docs.title: Class Imbalance Handling
docs.text:
Challenge: 84% non-attrition vs 16% attrition creates bias toward majority class

Solution Applied: - Tree-based models: Class weights {0: 0.17, 1: 0.83} - Linear models: Threshold optimization using precision-recall curves

docs.title: Model Performance Summary
docs.text:
Logistic Regression (Optimized Threshold: 0.35): - Accuracy: 87% - Recall: 74% (significant improvement from 46% at default threshold) - Precision: 50% - Interpretation: Reasonable baseline with clear feature interpretation

SVM with RBF Kernel (Optimized Threshold: 0.35): - Accuracy: 88% - Recall: 82% (best among all models) - Precision: 52% - Interpretation: Best at identifying true attrition cases

Decision Tree (Default): - Training Performance: 100% (clear overfitting) - Test Recall: 80% - Test Precision: 73% - Interpretation: Overfits but provides interpretable rules

Random Forest (Default): - Training Performance: 100% (overfitting) - Test Recall: 80% - Test Precision: 75% - Interpretation: Best overall balance of metrics

docs.title: Critical Model Limitations
docs.text:
Overfitting Concerns: - Tree-based models show perfect training performance - Significant performance drop on test data - Risk: Models may not generalize to new employees

Precision-Recall Trade-off: - High recall comes at cost of precision - Business Impact: Many false positives means resources spent on employees not at risk

Feature Interpretation Challenges: - Random Forest feature importance may be unstable - Multicollinearity: Correlated features complicate interpretation

[See Code Walkthrough Section 5: Model Implementation & Training]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Evaluation Methodology
docs.text: Primary Metric: Recall for Attrition Class - Business Justification: Missing a departing employee is more costly than false alarms - Target: Maximize true positive identification while maintaining reasonable precision

docs.title: Threshold Optimization Process
docs.text: Precision-Recall Curve Analysis: - Optimal threshold identified at 0.35 for both Logistic Regression and SVM - Trade-off: Higher recall achieved by accepting lower precision - Business Context: Better to over-predict attrition than miss valuable departing employees

docs.title: Hyperparameter Tuning Results
docs.text:
Decision Tree Tuning: - Grid Search Parameters: max_depth, criterion, min_samples_leaf - Result: Tuned model reduces overfitting but sacrifices performance - Precision Drop: From 73% to 29% (concerning for business application)

Random Forest Tuning: - Grid Search Parameters: n_estimators, min_samples_leaf, max_features - Result: Slight improvement in recall with minimal precision loss - Best Performance: 82% recall, 76% precision on test data

docs.title: Feature Importance Analysis
docs.text:
Consistent Top Predictors Across Models: 1. OverTime: Strongest predictor across all models 2. MonthlyIncome: Inverse relationship with attrition 3. Age: Younger employees higher risk 4. TotalWorkingYears: Experience reduces attrition risk 5. DistanceFromHome: Longer commutes increase risk

Business Validation: - Feature rankings align with HR domain knowledge - Economic factors (income, overtime) dominate predictions - Work-life balance factors consistently important

docs.title: Model Selection Recommendation
docs.text:
For Production Use: Tuned Random Forest - Rationale: Best balance of recall (82%) and precision (76%) - Reliability: Ensemble method more robust than single models - Interpretability: Feature importance provides actionable insights

For Business Understanding: Logistic Regression - Rationale: Coefficient interpretation provides odds ratios - Transparency: Clear understanding of factor relationships - Baseline: Establishes performance floor for comparison

docs.title: Performance Limitations
docs.text:
Generalization Concerns: - Single organization data may not transfer to other companies - Industry-specific factors not captured - Temporal stability unknown (model may degrade over time)

Precision Challenges: - 24% false positive rate means significant resource waste - May cause employee morale issues if targeting becomes obvious - Cost-benefit analysis needed for implementation

[See Code Walkthrough Section 6: Model Evaluation & Tuning]

docs.title: Primary Attrition Drivers
docs.text:
1. Overtime Work Culture (Strongest Predictor) - Finding: Employees working overtime are 2.6x more likely to leave - Business Impact: 28% of workforce affected - Recommendation: Implement workload management and compensation for overtime

2. Compensation Inequity - Finding: Departing employees earn 30% less than retained employees - Business Impact: Losing talent due to uncompetitive compensation - Recommendation: Conduct comprehensive salary benchmarking

3. Department-Specific Risks - Sales Department: 40% attrition rate (critical concern) - HR Department: 25% attrition rate - Recommendation: Develop department-specific retention strategies

docs.text:

  • Overtime Policy Review: Implement strict overtime limits with adequate compensation

  • Compensation Audit: Review salaries for bottom quartile performers

  • Sales Team Intervention: Immediate focus on sales department retention

Medium-term Initiatives (3-12 months):

Long-term Strategic Changes (12+ months):

  • Career Development: Clear promotion pathways and timelines

Resource Allocation Optimization: - High-Risk Employees: Immediate manager intervention, retention bonuses - Medium-Risk Employees: Career development discussions, workload review - Low-Risk Employees: Standard engagement activities

docs.title: Evaluation Metrics Function
docs.text:
def metrics_score(actual, predicted):
    """
    Generate comprehensive classification report and confusion matrix.

    Parameters:
    actual: True labels
    predicted: Predicted labels

    Returns:
    Prints classification report and displays confusion matrix heatmap
    """
    print(classification_report(actual, predicted))

    cm = confusion_matrix(actual, predicted)
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))

    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='.2f', 
                xticklabels=['Not Attrite', 'Attrite'], 
                yticklabels=['Not Attrite', 'Attrite'])
    plt.ylabel('Actual')
    plt.xlabel('Predicted')
    plt.show()

Purpose: Create reusable function for consistent model evaluation across all algorithms.

Flow: 1. Generate detailed classification report with precision, recall, F1 2. Create confusion matrix visualization 3. Use meaningful labels for business interpretation

Impact: Standardizes evaluation process and ensures consistent reporting format across all models.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Precision-Recall Curve Analysis
docs.text:
# Generate probability predictions for threshold optimization
y_scores_lg = lg.predict_proba(X_train_scaled)

# Calculate precision-recall curve
precisions_lg, recalls_lg, thresholds_lg = precision_recall_curve(
    y_train, y_scores_lg[:, 1])

# Visualize precision-recall trade-off
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
plt.plot(thresholds_lg, precisions_lg[:-1], 'b--', label='precision')
plt.plot(thresholds_lg, recalls_lg[:-1], 'g--', label='recall')
plt.xlabel('Threshold')
plt.legend(loc='upper left')
plt.ylim([0, 1])
plt.show()

Purpose: Identify optimal classification threshold that balances precision and recall for business objectives.

Flow: 1. Generate probability predictions instead of binary classifications 2. Calculate precision and recall across all possible thresholds 3. Visualize trade-off to identify optimal balance point

Impact: Default threshold (0.5) may not be optimal for business objectives. Threshold optimization can significantly improve recall.

docs.title: Optimized Threshold Application
docs.text:

y_pred_train = lg.predict_proba(X_train_scaled)
metrics_score(y_train, y_pred_train[:, 1] > optimal_threshold)

# Test set with optimized threshold
y_pred_test = lg.predict_proba(X_test_scaled)
metrics_score(y_test, y_pred_test[:, 1] > optimal_threshold)

Purpose: Implement business-optimized classification threshold to maximize recall while maintaining reasonable precision.

Flow: 1. Define optimal threshold based on precision-recall analysis 2. Apply threshold to probability predictions 3. Evaluate performance on both training and test sets

Impact: Threshold of 0.35 (vs default 0.5) prioritizes identifying attrition cases at cost of some precision.

docs.title: RBF Kernel SVM with Probability Calibration
docs.text:
# RBF SVM with probability output
svm_rbf = SVC(kernel='rbf', probability=True)
svm_rbf.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

# Probability predictions for threshold optimization
y_scores_svm = svm_rbf.predict_proba(X_train_scaled)

# Precision-recall curve analysis

    y_train, y_scores_svm[:, 1])

# Visualize trade-off

plt.plot(thresholds_svm, precisions_svm[:-1], 'b--', label='precision')
plt.plot(thresholds_svm, recalls_svm[:-1], 'g--', label='recall')
plt.xlabel('Threshold')
plt.legend(loc='upper left')
plt.ylim([0, 1])
plt.show()

Purpose: Implement non-linear SVM to capture complex decision boundaries with probability calibration for threshold optimization.

Flow: 1. Initialize RBF SVM with probability=True for predict_proba method 2. Fit model and generate probability predictions 3. Perform precision-recall analysis for threshold optimization 4. Visualize threshold trade-offs

Impact: RBF kernel can capture non-linear patterns. Probability calibration enables threshold optimization similar to logistic regression.

docs.title: Decision Tree Implementation
docs.text:
# Decision tree with class weighting for imbalanced data
dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(class_weight={0: 0.17, 1: 0.83}, random_state=1)
dt.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Training evaluation
y_train_pred_dt = dt.predict(X_train)
metrics_score(y_train, y_train_pred_dt)

# Test evaluation
y_test_pred_dt = dt.predict(X_test)
metrics_score(y_test, y_test_pred_dt)

Purpose: Implement interpretable tree-based model with class weighting to handle imbalanced dataset.

Flow: 1. Set class weights inversely proportional to class frequency 2. Fit on unscaled data (trees don't require scaling) 3. Evaluate overfitting by comparing train vs test performance

Impact: Class weights help address 84-16% class imbalance. Trees don't require feature scaling but are prone to overfitting.

docs.title: Feature Importance Analysis

# Extract and visualize feature importance

columns = X.columns
importance_df = pd.DataFrame(importances, index=columns,

# Calculate business impact metrics
def calculate_business_impact(recall, precision, total_employees=2940):
    """
    Calculate business impact of model deployment.

    Parameters:
    recall: Model recall rate
    precision: Model precision rate
    total_employees: Total employee count

    Returns:
    Dictionary with business impact metrics
    """
    # Assume 16% attrition rate
    actual_attrition = int(total_employees * 0.16)

    # Calculate model predictions
    true_positives = int(actual_attrition * recall)
    false_positives = int((true_positives / precision) - true_positives)
    false_negatives = actual_attrition - true_positives

    # Calculate intervention costs (example values)
    intervention_cost_per_employee = 5000  # Retention incentive cost
    missed_opportunity_cost = 25000  # Cost of losing valued employee

    # Calculate total costs
    intervention_costs = false_positives * intervention_cost_per_employee
    missed_opportunities = false_negatives * missed_opportunity_cost
    successful_retentions = true_positives * intervention_cost_per_employee

    return {
        'employees_correctly_identified': true_positives,
        'employees_incorrectly_targeted': false_positives,
        'employees_missed': false_negatives,
        'intervention_costs': intervention_costs,
        'missed_opportunity_costs': missed_opportunities,
        'retention_investment': successful_retentions,
        'total_cost': intervention_costs + missed_opportunities + successful_retentions
    }

# Example calculation for best model
best_model_impact = calculate_business_impact(recall=0.82, precision=0.76)
print("Business Impact Analysis:")
for key, value in best_model_impact.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value:,}")

def generate_attrition_report(model, X_data, feature_names, threshold=0.5):
    """
    Generate comprehensive attrition risk report for business stakeholders.

    Parameters:
    model: Trained model object
    X_data: Feature data for prediction
    feature_names: List of feature names for interpretation
    threshold: Classification threshold

    Returns:
    DataFrame with employee risk scores and recommendations
    """
    # Generate probability predictions
    if hasattr(model, 'predict_proba'):
        probabilities = model.predict_proba(X_data)[:, 1]
    else:
        # For models without probability output
        probabilities = model.decision_function(X_data)

    # Create risk categories
    def categorize_risk(prob):
        if prob >= 0.7:
            return 'High Risk'
        elif prob >= 0.4:
            return 'Medium Risk'
        else:
            return 'Low Risk'

    # Create report DataFrame
    report_df = pd.DataFrame({
        'employee_id': range(len(X_data)),
        'attrition_probability': probabilities,
        'risk_category': [categorize_risk(p) for p in probabilities],
        'predicted_attrition': probabilities > threshold
    })

    # Sort by risk level
    report_df = report_df.sort_values('attrition_probability', ascending=False)

    # Add recommendations
    def get_recommendation(risk_cat):
        recommendations = {
            'High Risk': 'Immediate manager intervention, retention bonus consideration',
            'Medium Risk': 'Career development discussion, workload review',
            'Low Risk': 'Standard engagement activities'
        }
        return recommendations[risk_cat]

    report_df['recommended_action'] = report_df['risk_category'].apply(get_recommendation)

    return report_df

# Example report generation
sample_report = generate_attrition_report(rf_estimator_tuned, X_test.head(10), X.columns)
print(sample_report)

def model_performance_monitor(model, X_new, y_new, baseline_metrics):
    """
    Monitor model performance degradation over time.

    Parameters:
    model: Deployed model object
    X_new: New feature data
    y_new: New actual outcomes
    baseline_metrics: Dictionary of baseline performance metrics

    Returns:
    Performance comparison and alerts
    """
    # Generate new predictions
    y_pred_new = model.predict(X_new)

    # Calculate current metrics
    current_accuracy = metrics.accuracy_score(y_new, y_pred_new)
    current_recall = metrics.recall_score(y_new, y_pred_new)
    current_precision = metrics.precision_score(y_new, y_pred_new)

    # Compare with baseline
    accuracy_change = current_accuracy - baseline_metrics['accuracy']
    recall_change = current_recall - baseline_metrics['recall']
    precision_change = current_precision - baseline_metrics['precision']

    # Generate alerts
    alerts = []
    if accuracy_change < -0.05:
        alerts.append("ALERT: Accuracy decreased by more than 5%")
    if recall_change < -0.10:
        alerts.append("ALERT: Recall decreased by more than 10%")
    if precision_change < -0.10:
        alerts.append("ALERT: Precision decreased by more than 10%")

    monitoring_report = {
        'current_accuracy': current_accuracy,
        'current_recall': current_recall,
        'current_precision': current_precision,
        'accuracy_change': accuracy_change,
        'recall_change': recall_change,
        'precision_change': precision_change,
        'alerts': alerts,
        'recommendation': 'Model retraining recommended' if alerts else 'Model performing within acceptable range'
    }

    return monitoring_report

# Example baseline metrics
baseline = {'accuracy': 0.87, 'recall': 0.82, 'precision': 0.76}

docs.title: Scientific Foundation
docs.text:
This tutorial demonstrates machine learning applications in astronomy through multi-class classification of celestial objects. The objective is to distinguish between Stars, Galaxies, and Quasars using spectroscopic and photometric measurements from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS).

Astronomical Context:

Stars represent luminous plasma spheroids powered by nuclear fusion, with the Sun being our nearest example. The next closest star, Proxima Centauri, lies approximately 4.25 light-years away, illustrating the vast scales involved in astronomical observations.

Galaxies are gravitationally bound systems containing 10^8 to 10^14 stars, along with stellar remnants, interstellar gas, cosmic dust, and dark matter. These structures represent some of the largest organized matter formations in the observable universe.

Quasars (Quasi-stellar objects) are extremely luminous active galactic nuclei powered by supermassive black holes. Their defining characteristic is extreme redshift due to their tremendous distances from Earth, making them observable primarily in the early universe.

docs.title: The Redshift Phenomenon
docs.text:
Critical Insight: Redshift serves as the primary distinguishing feature for quasar identification. This phenomenon occurs because:

  1. Cosmological expansion causes electromagnetic radiation to lose energy over vast distances

  2. Doppler effect creates frequency shifts for objects receding at high velocities

  3. Distance-velocity relationship means more distant objects exhibit higher redshift values

This physical principle becomes the foundation for our machine learning approach, as algorithms can detect patterns in redshift measurements that correlate with object classifications.

docs.title: Problem Formulation
docs.text:
Supervised Classification Challenge: - Input: 17 numerical features from SDSS observations - Output: Categorical classification (Star=2, Galaxy=0, Quasar=1) - Dataset Scale: 250,000 observations with high astronomical data quality - Approach: Non-linear machine learning methods (k-NN and Decision Trees)

The problem represents a moderately imbalanced classification scenario with approximately 50% galaxies, 38% stars, and 12% quasars, reflecting the natural distribution of observable celestial objects.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 1: Environment Setup and Data Loading]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Source: Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS)
docs.text: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey represents one of astronomy's most comprehensive public datasets, utilizing a dedicated 2.5-meter wide-angle optical telescope at Apache Point Observatory, New Mexico. SDSS has catalogued over three million astronomical objects with both spectroscopic and photometric measurements.

docs.title: Feature Architecture Analysis
docs.text:
Spectroscopic Features (5 filters): - u, g, r, i, z: Ultraviolet through infrared photometric measurements - Physical significance: These represent energy emissions across the electromagnetic spectrum - Classification relevance: Different celestial objects exhibit characteristic spectral signatures

Positional Coordinates: - ra (Right Ascension), dec (Declination): Celestial positioning system - Impact on classification: Spatial distribution patterns may reveal object clustering

Technical Metadata: - run, rerun, camcol, field: Survey execution parameters - plate, mjd, fiberid: Observational setup identifiers - Preprocessing implication: These may require removal as non-predictive features

Critical Classification Feature: - redshift: Wavelength shift measurement - Astronomical importance: Primary indicator of cosmic distance and recession velocity - Expected model behavior: Should emerge as the most important predictive feature

docs.title: Data Quality Assessment
docs.text:
Exceptional Quality Characteristics: - Zero missing values: Professional astronomical data collection standards - No duplicate observations: Each celestial object uniquely identified - Large sample size: 250,000 observations provide robust statistical power - Balanced feature types: Entirely numerical features suitable for algorithmic processing

Sampling Strategy: For computational efficiency, the tutorial utilizes a 50,000-observation subsample while maintaining class proportions through stratified sampling. This approach preserves statistical relationships while enabling faster iteration during model development.

docs.title: Class Distribution Analysis
docs.text:
Natural Imbalance Reflection: - Galaxies (50.3%): Most abundant observable objects at current survey sensitivity - Stars (38.2%): Limited to Milky Way objects visible from Earth - Quasars (11.5%): Rare, distant objects requiring sensitive detection methods

This distribution reflects astronomical reality rather than sampling bias, making it an authentic representation of observable celestial object frequencies.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 2: Data Loading and Initial Exploration]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Statistical Distribution Patterns
docs.text:
Key Distribution Characteristics:

Right-Skewed Variables: - redshift, plate, field, dec: Exhibit long tails toward higher values - Astronomical interpretation: Reflects survey design and cosmic object distribution - Modeling implication: May benefit from logarithmic transformation for certain algorithms

Symmetric Distributions: - Photometric filters (u, g, r, i, z): Near-normal distributions - Physical significance: Represents natural variation in stellar brightness measurements - Model advantage: Well-suited for distance-based algorithms without transformation

docs.title: Univariate Analysis Insights
docs.text:
Redshift Distribution: The redshift variable shows extreme right skew with values ranging from near-zero to 6.4. This wide range corresponds to objects from nearby (within our galaxy) to cosmologically distant (early universe). The log-transformation reveals more interpretable patterns, with distinct peaks corresponding to different object classes.

Photometric Filter Analysis: The five photometric filters (u, g, r, i, z) demonstrate correlated but distinct distributions. High correlations between adjacent wavelength bands (g-r: 0.85, r-i: 0.87) reflect the continuous nature of electromagnetic spectra while maintaining independent information for classification.

docs.title: Class-Specific Distribution Patterns
docs.text:
Redshift as Primary Discriminator: - Stars: Extremely low redshift (z ≈ 0), indicating galactic proximity - Galaxies: Moderate redshift distribution reflecting various cosmic distances - Quasars: High redshift tail extending to z > 6, confirming cosmological distances

Photometric Signatures: Each celestial object type exhibits characteristic spectral patterns: - Stars: Relatively consistent brightness across filters - Galaxies: Complex multi-component light profiles - Quasars: Often point-source appearance with unique spectral features

docs.title: Correlation Structure Analysis
docs.text:
High Positive Correlations (>0.8): - Adjacent photometric bands: Physical proximity in electromagnetic spectrum - mjd-plate correlation: Survey execution temporal clustering - Implication: Potential for dimensionality reduction while preserving information

Notable Negative Correlations: - redshift-class relationship: Higher redshift values associate with quasar classification - Strategic importance: Confirms astronomical theory through data-driven discovery

docs.title: Feature Engineering Decisions
docs.text:
Metadata Variable Assessment: Through distribution analysis, several technical variables showed minimal class discrimination: - rerun: Single unique value (constant) - run, field, fiberid, camcol: Uniform distributions across classes - Decision: Remove non-predictive technical metadata - Retention criteria: Keep variables showing class-specific patterns

Dimensionality Optimization: Original 17 features reduced to 10 predictive features by removing: 1. Unique identifiers: objid, specobjid 2. Technical constants: rerun 3. Survey metadata: run, field, fiberid, camcol

This preprocessing maintains astronomical information while eliminating technical artifacts.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3: Comprehensive EDA Implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Label Encoding Strategy
docs.text:
Target Variable Transformation: The categorical target variable undergoes label encoding for algorithmic compatibility: - Galaxy → 0 - Quasar → 1 - Star → 2

Rationale: This numerical encoding preserves class relationships without imposing artificial ordinality, making it suitable for both distance-based and tree-based algorithms.

docs.title: Train-Test Split Methodology
docs.text:
Stratified Sampling Approach: - Split ratio: 90% training, 10% testing - Stratification: Maintains original class proportions in both sets - Random state: Fixed for reproducibility - Result: 45,000 training observations, 5,000 test observations

Why Stratification Matters: Given the natural class imbalance (especially the smaller quasar class), stratified sampling ensures adequate representation of all celestial object types in both training and validation sets.

docs.title: Feature Scaling Considerations
docs.text:
Algorithm-Specific Requirements:

k-Nearest Neighbors: - Scaling necessity: High - distance calculations sensitive to feature magnitude differences - Method: StandardScaler normalization (mean=0, std=1) - Impact: Dramatic performance improvement observed

Decision Trees: - Scaling necessity: Low - tree splits based on threshold comparisons, not distances - Observation: Minimal performance change with/without scaling - Computational benefit: Can skip scaling step for tree-based models

docs.title: Dimensionality Reduction Analysis
docs.text:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) Evaluation:

For k-NN with PCA: - Implementation: Full PCA transformation after standardization - Performance impact: Varies depending on variance retention - Computational trade-off: Reduced feature space vs. information loss

Best Practice: Test PCA impact empirically rather than assuming benefit, as astronomical data often contains meaningful signal across all measured wavelengths.

docs.title: Data Quality Validation
docs.text:
Preprocessing Verification Steps: 1. Missing value confirmation: Zero nulls verified 2. Duplicate detection: No identical observations found 3. Feature distribution assessment: Outliers identified but retained (astronomical extremes often meaningful) 4. Class balance verification: Proportions maintained through stratification

Feature Selection Outcomes: - Initial features: 17 total - After ID removal: 15 predictive candidates - After metadata filtering: 10 core astronomical measurements - Retention criteria: Class discrimination capability and astronomical relevance

[See Code Walkthrough Section 4: Complete Preprocessing Pipeline]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Algorithm Selection Rationale
docs.text:
k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN): - Strength: Captures local patterns in high-dimensional space - Astronomical relevance: Similar objects should cluster in feature space - Non-parametric advantage: No assumptions about underlying data distribution - Computational consideration: Scales poorly with large datasets

Decision Trees: - Strength: Hierarchical decision-making mirrors astronomical classification logic - Interpretability: Clear feature importance and decision pathways - Non-linear capability: Handles complex feature interactions - Efficiency: Computationally scalable for large astronomical datasets

docs.title: k-NN Performance Analysis
docs.text:
Without Preprocessing: - Training Accuracy: Moderate performance - Test Accuracy: Declining performance indicating overfitting - Issue: Different feature scales dominate distance calculations

With Scaling and PCA: - Standardization impact: Significant improvement in classification metrics - PCA considerations: May reduce performance if important spectral information is compressed - Optimal configuration: StandardScaler + selective PCA retention

Performance Metrics Interpretation: - Precision by class: Varies significantly across celestial object types - Recall patterns: Stars and galaxies generally easier to classify than quasars - F1-scores: Balanced measure showing overall classification effectiveness

docs.title: Decision Tree Performance Analysis
docs.text:
Unscaled Performance: - Training Results: High accuracy (>95%) - Test Results: Strong generalization (>90%) - Class-specific performance: Excellent discrimination across all celestial types

Scaled Performance: - Observation: Minimal change confirms scale-invariance of tree algorithms - Implication: Preprocessing overhead unnecessary for tree-based methods - Consistency: Both scaled and unscaled versions achieve similar results

docs.title: Feature Importance Revelations
docs.text:
Redshift Dominance: The decision tree analysis reveals redshift as the overwhelmingly important feature (>70% importance), confirming astronomical theory: - Physical basis: Redshift directly correlates with cosmic distance - Classification logic: Distant objects (high redshift) are typically quasars - Tree structure: Redshift forms the root node split

Secondary Features: - Photometric filters: Provide complementary spectral signature information - Positional coordinates: Minor contribution to classification accuracy - Technical metadata: Negligible importance (correctly filtered out)

docs.title: Cross-Validation Assessment
docs.text:
5-Fold Cross-Validation Results: - Decision Tree: Consistent performance across folds (>90% average) - Stability metric: Low variance between fold performances - Generalization confidence: High reliability for unseen astronomical data

Overfitting Analysis: - Training vs. Test gap: Minimal for Decision Trees - k-NN concern: Higher overfitting tendency, especially without proper preprocessing - Mitigation strategy: Hyperparameter tuning and regularization

docs.title: Algorithm Comparison Summary
docs.text:
Decision Tree Advantages: 1. Superior accuracy: >90% on test set 2. Computational efficiency: Fast training and prediction 3. Interpretability: Clear decision pathways 4. Scale invariance: No preprocessing overhead 5. Astronomical insight: Confirms redshift importance

k-NN Limitations: 1. Preprocessing dependence: Requires careful scaling 2. Computational cost: Increases with dataset size 3. Performance ceiling: Lower maximum accuracy achieved 4. Memory requirements: Stores entire training set

docs.title: Comprehensive Metrics Analysis
docs.text:
Classification Report Interpretation:

def extended_statistics(df):
    """Calculate extended statistical measures for numerical columns."""
    stats = {}
    for col in df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns:
        stats[col] = {
            'mean': df[col].mean(),
            'median': df[col].median(),
            'mode': df[col].mode().iloc[0] if not df[col].mode().empty else np.nan,
            'std': df[col].std(),
            'skewness': df[col].skew(),
            'kurtosis': df[col].kurtosis(),
            'range': df[col].max() - df[col].min(),
            'iqr': df[col].quantile(0.75) - df[col].quantile(0.25)

# Comprehensive correlation analysis
def correlation_analysis():
    """
    Perform comprehensive correlation analysis of astronomical features.

    Returns:
    pd.DataFrame: Correlation matrix
    """
    # Calculate correlation matrix
    corr_matrix = df_astro.corr(numeric_only=True)

    # Create enhanced heatmap
    plt.figure(figsize=(16, 12))
    mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr_matrix, dtype=bool))  # Mask upper triangle

    sns.heatmap(corr_matrix, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt='.2f', center=0,
                square=True, cmap='RdBu_r', vmin=-1, vmax=1)
    plt.title('Feature Correlation Matrix\n(Lower Triangle Only)')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # Identify high correlations
    high_corr_pairs = []
    for i in range(len(corr_matrix.columns)):
        for j in range(i+1, len(corr_matrix.columns)):
            corr_val = corr_matrix.iloc[i, j]
            if abs(corr_val) > 0.7:  # Threshold for high correlation
                high_corr_pairs.append({
                    'Feature 1': corr_matrix.columns[i],
                    'Feature 2': corr_matrix.columns[j],
                    'Correlation': corr_val
                })

    high_corr_df = pd.DataFrame(high_corr_pairs).sort_values('Correlation', 
                                                           key=abs, ascending=False)
    print("High correlation pairs (|r| > 0.7):")
    print(high_corr_df)

    return corr_matrix

# Execute correlation analysis
correlation_matrix = correlation_analysis()

# Analyze correlations with target variable
target_correlations = correlation_matrix['class'].sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False)

def encode_target_variable():

    le = LabelEncoder()

            class_distributions = df_astro.groupby('class')[feature].apply(
                lambda x: x.value_counts(normalize=True)
            ).unstack(fill_value=0)

            # Simple discrimination test: check if distributions are similar
            discrimination_score = class_distributions.var(axis=0).mean()

            if discrimination_score < 0.01:  # Low discrimination threshold
                features_to_remove.append(feature)
                print(f"Low discrimination feature: {feature} (score: {discrimination_score:.4f})")

    return features_to_remove

# Identify features for removal
removal_candidates = feature_selection_analysis()

# Remove identified features
print(f"\nRemoving {len(removal_candidates)} features: {removal_candidates}")
df_astro = df_astro.drop(columns=removal_candidates, errors='ignore')

print(f"Dataset shape after feature removal: {df_astro.shape}")
print(f"Remaining features: {df_astro.columns.tolist()}")

Purpose: Remove non-predictive features to improve model efficiency and reduce overfitting risk.

Flow: 1. Constant detection: Identify features with single unique value 2. Identifier removal: Drop unique ID columns without predictive value 3. Discrimination analysis: Assess technical features for class separation ability 4. Systematic removal: Clean dataset of non-informative features

Impact: Feature removal reduces computational overhead and potential overfitting. Removing important features degrades model performance.

def implement_pca_analysis():
    """
    Implement Principal Component Analysis for dimensionality reduction.

    Returns:
    dict: PCA results and transformed datasets
    """
    from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

    # Full PCA to analyze variance explained
    pca_full = PCA()
    X_train_pca_full = pca_full.fit_transform(scaled_data['standard']['X_train'])

    # Analyze explained variance
    explained_variance_ratio = pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_
    cumulative_variance = np.cumsum(explained_variance_ratio)

    print("PCA Variance Analysis:")
    for i, (individual, cumulative) in enumerate(zip(explained_variance_ratio, cumulative_variance)):
        print(f"PC{i+1}: {individual:.4f} individual, {cumulative:.4f} cumulative")

    # Plot explained variance
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))

    plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
    plt.bar(range(1, len(explained_variance_ratio) + 1), explained_variance_ratio)
    plt.xlabel('Principal Component')
    plt.ylabel('Explained Variance Ratio')
    plt.title('Individual Explained Variance by Component')

    plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
    plt.plot(range(1, len(cumulative_variance) + 1), cumulative_variance, 'bo-')
    plt.axhline(y=0.95, color='r', linestyle='--', label='95% Variance')
    plt.xlabel('Number of Components')
    plt.ylabel('Cumulative Explained Variance')
    plt.title('Cumulative Explained Variance')
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # Determine optimal number of components for 95% variance
    n_components_95 = np.argmax(cumulative_variance >= 0.95) + 1
    print(f"\nComponents needed for 95% variance: {n_components_95}")

    # Apply PCA with optimal components
    pca_optimal = PCA(n_components=n_components_95)
    X_train_pca = pca_optimal.fit_transform(scaled_data['standard']['X_train'])
    X_test_pca = pca_optimal.transform(scaled_data['standard']['X_test'])

    print(f"Original feature space: {scaled_data['standard']['X_train'].shape[1]} dimensions")
    print(f"Reduced feature space: {X_train_pca.shape[1]} dimensions")
    print(f"Variance retained: {cumulative_variance[n_components_95-1]:.4f}")

    return {
        'pca_full': pca_full,
        'pca_optimal': pca_optimal,
        'X_train_pca': X_train_pca,
        'X_test_pca': X_test_pca,
        'n_components': n_components_95,
        'variance_explained': cumulative_variance[n_components_95-1]
    }

# Execute PCA analysis

def metrics_score(actual, predicted, class_names=None):
    """
    Comprehensive model evaluation with multiple metrics.

    Parameters:
    actual (array-like): True class labels
    predicted (array-like): Predicted class labels
    class_names (list): Optional class names for labeling

    Returns:
    None: Prints metrics and displays confusion matrix
    """
    if class_names is None:
        class_names = ['Galaxy', 'Quasar', 'Star']

    # Print classification report
    print("Classification Report:")
    print(classification_report(actual, predicted, target_names=class_names))

    # Create and display confusion matrix
    cm = confusion_matrix(actual, predicted)

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues',
                xticklabels=class_names, yticklabels=class_names)
    plt.ylabel('Actual Class')
    plt.xlabel('Predicted Class')
    plt.title('Confusion Matrix')
    plt.show()

    # Additional metrics
    from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

    accuracy = accuracy_score(actual, predicted)
    precision = precision_score(actual, predicted, average='weighted')
    recall = recall_score(actual, predicted, average='weighted')
    f1 = f1_score(actual, predicted, average='weighted')

    print(f"\nOverall Metrics:")
    print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.4f}")
    print(f"Weighted Precision: {precision:.4f}")
    print(f"Weighted Recall: {recall:.4f}")
    print(f"Weighted F1-Score: {f1:.4f}")

    return {
        'accuracy': accuracy,
        'precision': precision,
        'recall': recall,
        'f1_score': f1,
        'confusion_matrix': cm
    }

Purpose: Provide comprehensive model evaluation with multiple performance metrics and visualization.

Flow: 1. Classification report: Per-class precision, recall, F1-score 2. Confusion matrix: Visual representation of classification errors 3. Overall metrics: Weighted averages for imbalanced classes 4. Return results: Structured output for comparison

Impact: Comprehensive evaluation reveals model strengths and weaknesses. Missing metrics can hide important performance issues.

def comprehensive_cross_validation():

    Implement comprehensive cross-validation for model comparison.

    Returns:
    dict: Cross-validation results for all models
    """
    from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold

    cv_results = {}

    # Define cross-validation strategy
    cv_strategy = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

    # Models to evaluate
    models = {
        'KNN_Basic': KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5),
        'KNN_Optimized': knn_results['optimized']['model'],
        'DT_Basic': DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42),
        'DT_Optimized': dt_results['optimized']['model']
    }

    # Data configurations
    data_configs = {
        'Raw': (X_train, X_test),
        'Scaled': (scaled_data['standard']['X_train'], scaled_data['standard']['X_test']),
        'PCA': (pca_results['X_train_pca'], pca_results['X_test_pca'])
    }

    print("=== Comprehensive Cross-Validation Results ===")

    for model_name, model in models.items():
        cv_results[model_name] = {}

        for data_name, (X_tr, X_te) in data_configs.items():
            try:
                # Perform cross-validation
                scores = cross_val_score(model, X_tr, y_train, cv=cv_strategy, 
                                       scoring='accuracy', n_jobs=-1)

                cv_results[model_name][data_name] = {
                    'mean_score': scores.mean(),
                    'std_score': scores.std(),
                    'scores': scores
                }

                print(f"{model_name} - {data_name}: "
                      f"{scores.mean():.4f} ± {scores.std():.4f}")

            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Error with {model_name} - {data_name}: {str(e)}")
                cv_results[model_name][data_name] = None

    # Create visualization of cross-validation results
    plt.figure(figsize=(15, 8))

    model_names = []
    mean_scores = []
    std_scores = []

    for model_name in models.keys():
        for data_name in data_configs.keys():
            if (model_name in cv_results and

                model_names.append(f"{model_name}_{data_name}")

                std_scores.append(cv_results[model_name][data_name]['std_score'])

def advanced_performance_analysis():

    Conduct detailed performance analysis including learning curves and error analysis.

    Returns:

    analysis_results = {}

    # Select best performing models

    best_dt = dt_results['optimized']['model']

    # Learning curve analysis
    print("=== Learning Curve Analysis ===")

    def plot_learning_curve(model, X, y, title, scoring='accuracy'):
        """Plot learning curves for given model."""
        train_sizes, train_scores, val_scores = learning_curve(
            model, X, y, cv=5, n_jobs=-1, 
            train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10),
            scoring=scoring, random_state=42
        )

        train_mean = np.mean(train_scores, axis=1)
        train_std = np.std(train_scores, axis=1)
        val_mean = np.mean(val_scores, axis=1)
        val_std = np.std(val_scores, axis=1)

        plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
        plt.plot(train_sizes, train_mean, 'o-', label='Training Score', alpha=0.8)
        plt.fill_between(train_sizes, train_mean - train_std, train_mean + train_std, alpha=0.2)

        plt.plot(train_sizes, val_mean, 'o-', label='Validation Score', alpha=0.8)
        plt.fill_between(train_sizes, val_mean - val_std, val_mean + val_std, alpha=0.2)

        plt.xlabel('Training Set Size')
        plt.ylabel('Accuracy Score')
        plt.title(f'Learning Curve: {title}')
        plt.legend()
        plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
        plt.show()

        return {
            'train_sizes': train_sizes,
            'train_scores': train_scores,
            'val_scores': val_scores
        }

    # Generate learning curves
    analysis_results['knn_learning'] = plot_learning_curve(
        best_knn, pca_results['X_train_pca'], y_train, 'k-NN Classifier'

def detailed_error_analysis():
