docs.title: Recommendation System Evaluation Framework
docs.text: Evaluating recommendation systems requires metrics that reflect business objectives rather than just prediction accuracy. This tutorial employs a comprehensive evaluation framework measuring both rating prediction quality and recommendation relevance.

docs.title: Core Evaluation Metrics
docs.text:
Precision@k:

Measures the fraction of recommended items that are actually relevant to the user.

Precision@k = (Relevant items in top k recommendations) / k

Business Interpretation: If you recommend 10 books and 8 are relevant, precision@10 = 0.8. High precision means users won't waste time on irrelevant recommendations.

Recall@k:

Measures the fraction of all relevant items that appear in the top k recommendations.

Recall@k = (Relevant items in top k recommendations) / (Total relevant items)

Business Interpretation: If there are 20 books a user would like and you recommend 12 of them in your top k, recall = 0.6. High recall means you're not missing opportunities.

F1-Score@k:

Harmonic mean balancing precision and recall.

F1@k = 2 * (Precision@k * Recall@k) / (Precision@k + Recall@k)

Relevance Threshold: Items with predicted ratings ≥ 7 are considered "relevant" for precision/recall calculations.

docs.text:

  • Precision@10: 0.86

Optimized Item-Based Collaborative Filtering:

docs.title: Business Metric Interpretation
docs.text:
RMSE Analysis: Matrix factorization achieves the lowest RMSE (1.50), indicating superior rating prediction accuracy. This translates to more accurate predictions of how much users will like specific books.

F1-Score Analysis: User-based collaborative filtering achieves the highest F1-score (0.86), meaning it's best at identifying truly relevant books while minimizing irrelevant recommendations.

Trade-off Implications: The choice between models depends on business priorities:

  • Accuracy-focused: Choose SVD for precise rating predictions
  • Relevance-focused: Choose user-based collaborative filtering for better recommendation quality
  • Efficiency-focused: Choose item-based collaborative filtering for scalable deployment

docs.title: Evaluation Methodology Strengths and Limitations
docs.text:
Strengths:

  • Multi-metric approach - Captures different aspects of recommendation quality
  • Business-relevant thresholds - Uses meaningful rating cutoffs for relevance
  • Statistical rigor - Employs proper train/test splits and cross-validation

Limitations:

  • Offline evaluation - Cannot capture real user engagement or satisfaction
  • Historical bias - Evaluation based on past behavior may not predict future preferences
  • Rating scale assumptions - Threshold of 7 for relevance may not align with all user perceptions
  • No diversity measurement - Doesn't evaluate recommendation diversity or serendipity

docs.text:
A/B Testing: Offline metrics should be validated with A/B tests measuring business KPIs like click-through rates, purchase conversion, and user engagement time.

Multi-Model Strategy: Consider deploying multiple models for different user segments or use cases, leveraging the strengths of each approach.

Continuous Monitoring: Implement real-time monitoring of recommendation performance and user feedback to detect model degradation or bias drift.

def filter_users_by_activity(df, min_ratings=50):
    """
    Filter users based on minimum rating activity.

    Parameters:
    -----------
    df : pandas.DataFrame
        The ratings dataframe
    min_ratings : int
        Minimum number of ratings required per user

    Returns:
    --------
    pandas.DataFrame
        Filtered dataframe with active users only
    """
    # Count ratings per user
    users = df.user_id
    ratings_count = dict()

    for user in users:
        if user in ratings_count:
            ratings_count[user] += 1
        else:
            ratings_count[user] = 1

    # Identify users below threshold
    remove_users = []
    for user, num_ratings in ratings_count.items():
        if num_ratings < min_ratings:
            remove_users.append(user)

    # Filter dataset
    filtered_df = df.loc[~df.user_id.isin(remove_users)]

    print(f"Original users: {df['user_id'].nunique():,}")
    print(f"Users after filtering (≥{min_ratings} ratings): {filtered_df['user_id'].nunique():,}")
    print(f"Removed users: {len(remove_users):,}")

    return filtered_df

# Apply user filtering
df = filter_users_by_activity(df, min_ratings=50)
print(f"Dataset shape after user filtering: {df.shape}")

Purpose: Remove users with insufficient rating history to improve collaborative filtering signal quality.

Flow: Count ratings per user → Identify low-activity users → Filter dataset → Report statistics.

Impact: Reduces noise from casual users while retaining engaged users who provide reliable collaborative signal. The 50-rating threshold ensures sufficient data for similarity calculations.

def top_n_books(data, n, min_interaction=100):

    Generate top N book recommendations based on average ratings.

    # Filter books with sufficient interactions

    print(f"Books meeting criteria (≥{min_interaction} ratings): {len(recommendations)}")

docs.title: Precision and Recall Evaluation Function
docs.text:
def precision_recall_at_k(model, k=10, threshold=7):
    """
    Calculate precision@k and recall@k for recommendation model.

    Parameters:
    -----------
    model : surprise.AlgoBase
        Trained recommendation model
    k : int
        Number of top recommendations to consider
    threshold : float
        Rating threshold for considering item as relevant

    Returns:
    --------
    None (prints metrics)
    """
    # Map predictions to each user
    user_est_true = defaultdict(list)

    # Generate predictions on test set
    predictions = model.test(testset)

    for uid, _, true_r, est, _ in predictions:
        user_est_true[uid].append((est, true_r))

    precisions = dict()
    recalls = dict()

    for uid, user_ratings in user_est_true.items():
        # Sort by estimated rating (descending)
        user_ratings.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)

        # Count relevant items
        n_rel = sum((true_r >= threshold) for (_, true_r) in user_ratings)

        # Count recommended items in top k
        n_rec_k = sum((est >= threshold) for (est, _) in user_ratings[:k])

        # Count relevant and recommended items in top k
        n_rel_and_rec_k = sum(((true_r >= threshold) and (est >= threshold))
                              for (est, true_r) in user_ratings[:k])

        # Calculate precision@k
        precisions[uid] = n_rel_and_rec_k / n_rec_k if n_rec_k != 0 else 0

        # Calculate recall@k
        recalls[uid] = n_rel_and_rec_k / n_rel if n_rel != 0 else 0

    # Calculate overall metrics
    precision = round(sum(prec for prec in precisions.values()) / len(precisions), 3)
    recall = round(sum(rec for rec in recalls.values()) / len(recalls), 3)
    f1_score = round((2 * precision * recall) / (precision + recall), 3) if (precision + recall) > 0 else 0

    # Calculate RMSE
    rmse = accuracy.rmse(predictions, verbose=False)

    print(f'RMSE: {rmse:.3f}')
    print(f'Precision@{k}: {precision}')
    print(f'Recall@{k}: {recall}')
    print(f'F1-Score@{k}: {f1_score}')

    return precision, recall, f1_score, rmse

Purpose: Implement comprehensive evaluation function measuring recommendation quality from multiple perspectives.

Flow: Generate predictions → Group by user → Calculate relevance metrics → Compute averages → Report results.

Impact: This function provides business-relevant metrics that measure both accuracy (RMSE) and recommendation quality (precision/recall).

docs.title: SVD Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
The SVD algorithm models ratings using latent factors:

Rating Prediction Formula: 

r̂_ui = μ + b_u + b_i + q_i^T × p_u

Variable Definitions: - μ = global rating average across all users and items - b_u = user bias term (user's tendency to rate higher/lower than average) - b_i = item bias term (item's tendency to receive higher/lower ratings) - p_u = user latent factor vector (user's preferences in latent space) - q_i = item latent factor vector (item's characteristics in latent space)

docs.title: Recommendation Function Implementation
docs.text:
def get_recommendations(data, user_id, top_n, algo):
    """
    Generate top-N recommendations for a specific user.

    Parameters:
    -----------
    data : pandas.DataFrame
        Rating data with user_id, book_id, rating columns
    user_id : int
        Target user for recommendations
    top_n : int
        Number of recommendations to generate
    algo : surprise.AlgoBase
        Trained recommendation algorithm

    Returns:
    --------
    list of tuples
        List of (book_id, predicted_rating) pairs
    """
    # Create user-item interaction matrix
    user_item_matrix = data.pivot(
        index='user_id', 
        columns='book_id', 
        values='rating'
    )

    # Find books not yet rated by the user
    if user_id not in user_item_matrix.index:
        print(f"Warning: User {user_id} not found in training data")
        return []

    non_interacted_items = user_item_matrix.loc[user_id][
        user_item_matrix.loc[user_id].isnull()
    ].index.tolist()

    print(f"User {user_id} has not rated {len(non_interacted_items)} books")

    # Generate predictions for unrated books
    recommendations = []
    for book_id in non_interacted_items:
        est = algo.predict(user_id, book_id).est
        recommendations.append((book_id, est))

    # Sort by predicted rating (descending)
    recommendations.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)

    return recommendations[:top_n]

Purpose: Generate personalized recommendations by predicting ratings for unrated books.

Flow: Create user-item matrix → Find unrated books → Generate predictions → Sort and return top-N.

Impact: Core function that transforms trained models into actionable recommendations for users.

docs.title: Recommendation Ranking Function
docs.text:
def ranking_books(recommendations, final_rating):
    """
    Rank recommended books using corrected ratings.

    Parameters:
    -----------
    recommendations : list of tuples
        List of (book_id, predicted_rating) pairs
    final_rating : pandas.DataFrame
        DataFrame with avg_rating and rating_count columns

    Returns:
    --------
    pandas.DataFrame
        Ranked recommendations with corrected ratings
    """
    if not recommendations:
        return pd.DataFrame()

    # Extract book IDs from recommendations
    book_ids = [item[0] for item in recommendations]

    # Get rating statistics for recommended books
    ranked_books = final_rating.loc[book_ids].copy()
    ranked_books = ranked_books.sort_values('rating_count', ascending=False).reset_index()

    # Merge with predicted ratings
    rec_df = pd.DataFrame(recommendations, columns=['book_id', 'predicted_ratings'])
    ranked_books = ranked_books.merge(rec_df, on='book_id', how='inner')

    # Calculate corrected ratings (penalize low rating counts)
    ranked_books['corrected_ratings'] = (
        ranked_books['predicted_ratings'] - 
        1 / np.sqrt(ranked_books['rating_count'])
    )

    # Sort by corrected ratings
    ranked_books = ranked_books.sort_values('corrected_ratings', ascending=False)

    return ranked_books

Purpose: Improve recommendation quality by penalizing books with few ratings.

Flow: Extract book IDs → Get rating statistics → Calculate corrected ratings → Sort by corrected scores.

Impact: Balances predicted rating quality with rating reliability, reducing risk of recommending books with insufficient feedback.

docs.title: The Investment Challenge
docs.text: Active portfolio management seeks to outperform broad market indices like the S&P 500 by strategically selecting stocks with higher return potential. Traditional approaches rely on fundamental analysis, technical indicators, or factor models. This tutorial explores an alternative methodology: using network analysis to identify structurally important stocks within the market ecosystem.

docs.title: Core Research Question
docs.text: Can we construct superior portfolios by identifying stocks based on their network topological position (central vs. peripheral) within correlation-based networks?

docs.title: Methodological Foundation
docs.text:
This approach is based on the research paper "Dynamic portfolio strategy using clustering approach" (arXiv:1608.03058), which proposes that:

  • Central stocks act as market hubs, highly connected to many other stocks, reflecting broad market movements

  • Peripheral stocks occupy edge positions in the network, potentially offering diversification benefits

  • Network topology metrics can identify these structural positions more systematically than traditional correlation analysis alone

docs.title: Implementation Workflow
docs.text:
Phase 1: Historical Network Construction (2011-2020)

  • Collect daily price data for all S&P 500 components

  • Compute log returns to ensure statistical properties suitable for analysis

  • Generate correlation matrices for each year

  • Apply Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) filtering to eliminate redundancy

  • Track network evolution over time

Phase 2: Centrality-Based Stock Selection (2011-2020)

  • Calculate multiple centrality measures on the filtered network

  • Identify top-n central stocks (high connectivity, hub-like behavior)

  • Identify top-n peripheral stocks (low connectivity, diversified positions)

Phase 3: Portfolio Performance Simulation (2021)

  • Construct equal-weighted portfolios from selected stocks

  • Simulate performance over 2021

  • Compare against S&P 500 benchmark returns

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Traditional portfolio theory focuses on pairwise correlations and variance-covariance matrices. Network analysis adds a structural dimension, revealing:

  • Which stocks serve as market connectors vs. isolates

  • How market structure changes during crisis vs. stable periods

  • Whether topological position predicts future performance

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Collection Strategy
docs.text:
Source Selection:

The analysis uses Wikipedia's S&P 500 constituent list combined with Yahoo Finance historical data. This approach ensures:

  • Current index composition (as of data collection date)

  • Free, publicly accessible data

  • Adjusted closing prices accounting for splits and dividends

Time Period Rationale:

The 2011-2020 window captures diverse market conditions:

  • 2011: Post-financial crisis recovery

  • 2015-2017: Stable bull market

  • 2018: Volatility spike and correction

  • 2020: COVID-19 pandemic crisis

This variety allows testing whether network-based portfolio selection works across different market regimes.

docs.title: Web Scraping S&P 500 Components
docs.text:
The implementation uses BeautifulSoup to extract the current S&P 500 ticker list from Wikipedia. This automated approach:

  • Eliminates manual data entry errors

  • Can be refreshed easily for updated constituent lists

  • Handles ticker formatting inconsistencies (e.g., replacing "." with "-" for Yahoo Finance compatibility)

Practical Consideration:

The constituent list represents the current S&P 500 composition, not the historical composition. This introduces survivorship bias, as delisted or replaced companies are excluded. For production use, historical constituent data would be preferable.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 1]

docs.title: Historical Price Data Retrieval
docs.text:
Data Specifications:

  • Period: January 1, 2011 to December 31, 2020 (10 years)

  • Frequency: Daily

  • Price Type: Adjusted closing prices

  • Number of Securities: All S&P 500 constituents (approximately 500)

Why Adjusted Close Prices:

Adjusted prices account for:

  • Stock splits (e.g., a 2-for-1 split)

  • Dividend payments

  • Rights offerings

Using adjusted prices ensures that calculated returns reflect true investor experience rather than artificial price changes.

docs.title: Data Storage and Access
docs.text:
The notebook includes commented code to fetch data directly from Yahoo Finance, but relies on a pre-saved CSV file (snp500_price_data_2011_to_2020.csv) for reproducibility. This approach:

  • Advantages: Faster execution, consistent results, no API rate limits

  • Disadvantages: Data becomes stale, requires manual updates

Recommendation: For production systems, implement automated data refresh with proper error handling and data validation.

docs.title: Understanding Index Rebalancing
docs.text:
The S&P 500 is not static. Companies enter and exit the index through:

  • Additions: High-growth companies meeting market cap thresholds

  • Deletions: Bankruptcies, mergers, acquisitions, or falling below thresholds

  • Sector rebalancing: Maintaining sector representation

docs.text:
The heatmap visualization reveals:

  • Vertical gaps: Stocks that weren't part of the S&P 500 for the entire 2011-2020 period

  • Recent additions: Stocks with data only in later years

  • Delistings: Stocks with data only in early years

Interpretation of Patterns:

Concentrated missing data in recent years suggests the current constituent list includes many companies that joined the index mid-period. This is expected given the rise of technology companies and the decline of traditional industrial firms.

docs.title: Data Cleaning Decision
docs.text:
Approach Taken:

Complete column-wise deletion of any stock with missing values.

Impact:

  • Original: ~500 stocks

  • After Cleaning: Depends on the specific dataset, but typically 350-400 stocks

  • Lost Information: Approximately 20-30% of potential securities

Critical Question: Is this the best approach?

Alternative Strategies:

  • Forward filling: Use last known price (problematic for long gaps)

  • Interpolation: Estimate missing values (inappropriate for stock prices)

  • Historical constituent lists: Use only stocks that were in the S&P 500 during each specific time period (more accurate but complex)

  • Partial analysis: Analyze shorter periods where more stocks have complete data

Practical Implication:

The complete-case analysis introduces survivorship bias, as we only analyze stocks that remained continuously in (or eligible for) the S&P 500. These tend to be larger, more stable companies. This may actually benefit the analysis by focusing on liquid, investable securities.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Why Log Returns Instead of Simple Returns
docs.text:
Statistical Foundation:

Stock price movements are better modeled using logarithmic returns rather than simple returns for several reasons:

1. Time Additivity:

Log returns can be summed across time periods:

Log return from t₀ to t₂ = log return(t₀→t₁) + log return(t₁→t₂)

Simple returns require complex compounding calculations.

2. Distribution Properties:

  • Simple returns follow a log-normal distribution (skewed, bounded below at -100%)

  • Log returns approximate a normal distribution (symmetric, unbounded)

  • Normal distribution assumptions enable standard statistical tests

3. Cross-Sectional Analysis:

When analyzing portfolio of multiple stocks, log returns are approximately additive across securities, simplifying portfolio mathematics.

docs.title: Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
Log Return Calculation:

r_t = ln(P_t) - ln(P_{t-1}) = ln(P_t / P_{t-1})

Variable Definitions:

  • r_t = log return at time t

  • P_t = price at time t

  • P_{t-1} = price at previous time period

  • ln = natural logarithm

docs.title: Annual Return Segmentation
docs.text:
The analysis computes log returns separately for each calendar year (2011-2020). This segmentation serves two purposes:

1. Network Construction:

Each year produces an independent correlation network, allowing observation of structural changes over time.

2. Market Regime Analysis:

Different years represent different market conditions:

  • High correlation years (2011, 2020): Crisis periods where most stocks move together

  • Low correlation years (2014, 2017): Stable markets with more stock-specific movements

docs.title: Interpretation of First-Row NaN Values
docs.text:
The log return calculation using .shift(1) produces NaN in the first row of each year because there's no prior day within that year to compare against. These values are implicitly ignored in subsequent correlation calculations.

Design Choice:

Rather than carrying the last day of the previous year into the next year's calculation, the clean break ensures each year's network is independent. This is appropriate for annual network analysis but might miss information if performing rolling window analysis.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 4]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: From Returns to Relationships
docs.text:
Correlation matrices transform individual stock returns into a network representation where:

  • Nodes: Individual stocks (e.g., AAPL, MSFT, JPM)

  • Edges: Correlation strength between stock pairs

  • Edge weights: Correlation coefficient (-1 to +1)

docs.title: Correlation as Network Edges
docs.text:
Interpretation:

  • ρ ≈ +1: Stocks move together (positive correlation)

  • ρ ≈ 0: Stocks move independently

  • ρ ≈ -1: Stocks move opposite (negative correlation, rare in equity markets)

Network Implication:

A fully connected network where every stock connects to every other stock, with edge weights proportional to correlation strength.

docs.title: Year-by-Year Network Evolution
docs.text:
The heatmap visualizations reveal distinct patterns:

High Correlation Years (2011, 2020):

  • Predominantly yellow/red colors across the matrix

  • Indicates system-wide co-movement

  • Interpretation: During crises, diversification breaks down as "everything falls together"

  • Network structure: Dense, highly interconnected

Low Correlation Years (2014, 2017):

  • More blue/green colors, heterogeneous patterns

  • Indicates stock-specific behavior dominates

  • Interpretation: Stable markets allow company fundamentals to differentiate performance

  • Network structure: More modular, distinct clusters

docs.title: Business Insight
docs.text:
Risk Management Perspective:

The temporal variation in correlation has profound implications:

  • Tail Risk: Historical low-correlation assumptions fail during crises

  • Portfolio Diversification: Benefits that exist in normal times disappear when needed most

  • Dynamic Hedging: Correlation-based strategies must account for regime changes

Network Analysis Advantage:

Traditional portfolio theory often assumes stable correlations. Network visualization immediately reveals when this assumption breaks down, potentially providing early warning signals of market stress.

docs.title: Fully Connected Network Problem
docs.text:
Creating a graph directly from the correlation matrix produces a fully connected network where every node connects to every other node. This creates several problems:

1. Information Overload:

With 400+ stocks, this produces 80,000+ edges, making visualization and analysis intractable.

2. Redundancy:

Many weak correlations add noise without information.

3. Computational Cost:

Centrality measures become expensive on dense graphs.

Solution: Apply filtering techniques to extract the most important relationships while preserving network structure. This is where Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) filtering becomes essential.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 5]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: The Minimum Spanning Tree Approach
docs.text:
Definition:

A Minimum Spanning Tree is a subset of edges that:

  • Connects all nodes (stocks) without cycles

  • Minimizes the total edge weight sum

  • Contains exactly (n-1) edges for n nodes

Application to Stock Networks:

By converting correlation to distance and finding the MST, we:

  • Reduce 80,000+ edges to just 400 edges

  • Preserve the most significant relationships

  • Create an interpretable network structure

  • Enable visualization and analysis

docs.title: Distance Transformation
docs.text:
Mathematical Conversion:

d_ij = √(2(1 - ρ_ij))

Variable Definitions:

  • d_ij = distance between stocks i and j

  • ρ_ij = correlation coefficient between stocks i and j

Rationale for This Formula:

  • When ρ = 1 (perfect correlation): d = 0 (zero distance, very similar)

  • When ρ = 0 (no correlation): d = √2 ≈ 1.41 (moderate distance)

  • When ρ = -1 (perfect negative correlation): d = 2 (maximum distance, very different)

This transformation converts correlation (similarity) into distance (dissimilarity), making it suitable for MST algorithms that minimize distance.

docs.title: Why MST for Financial Networks
docs.text:
Theoretical Justification:

Research in econophysics has shown that MSTs effectively capture:

  • Hierarchical market structure (sectors, industries, companies)

  • Key market relationships while filtering noise

  • Temporal evolution of market organization

Practical Benefits:

  • Noise Reduction: Eliminates spurious correlations from short-term market movements

  • Structure Preservation: Maintains the most stable, significant relationships

  • Computational Efficiency: Dramatically reduces graph complexity

Trade-offs:

MST filtering is aggressive, discarding most edges. Alternative approaches include:

  • Thresholding: Keep correlations above a certain level

  • Planar Maximally Filtered Graph (PMFG): Retain more edges while maintaining planarity

  • Community Detection: Cluster-based filtering

The choice depends on whether your goal is simplicity (MST) or comprehensive structure (alternatives).

docs.title: Visual Network Evolution
docs.text:
The filtered network visualizations for 2011-2020 reveal:

Structural Variation:

No two years produce identical networks, confirming that market structure is dynamic rather than static.

Star Topology in Crisis Years:

During 2011 and 2020 (crisis periods), networks tend to show more pronounced hub-and-spoke patterns with a few highly connected central nodes.

Distributed Topology in Stable Years:

During 2014 and 2017 (stable periods), the structure appears more distributed with less pronounced hubs.

Practical Interpretation:

This suggests that during crises, the market becomes dominated by a few key stocks or sectors, while in stable periods, more stocks behave independently.

docs.title: Network Statistics Over Time
docs.text:
Average Shortest Path Length Analysis:

This metric measures how many steps (on average) it takes to get from any stock to any other stock through the network.

Key Observations:

  • 2011-2015: Relatively stable path length (≈6-7)

  • 2016-2017: Significant increase (≈8-9), suggesting more fragmented market structure

  • 2018: Decrease back toward baseline

  • 2020: Increase again during COVID crisis

Interpretation:

  • Lower values: More centralized market with strong hubs connecting everything

  • Higher values: More distributed market with distinct clusters

Financial Implication:

Changes in path length may signal structural market shifts before they're apparent in price movements alone. A sudden increase might indicate emerging market fragmentation or sector divergence.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 6]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Full-Period Network Construction
docs.text:
Unlike the year-by-year analysis, portfolio construction uses the entire 2011-2020 period to build a single correlation network. This approach:

Advantages:

  • More stable estimates based on 10 years of data

  • Captures long-term structural relationships

  • Reduces impact of short-term market noise

Disadvantages:

  • Assumes stationary market structure (contradicts earlier finding of temporal variation)

  • May miss recent structural shifts

  • Could average out important regime-dependent patterns

Critical Assessment:

This is a significant methodological choice with implications for portfolio stability. An alternative approach would use rolling windows or ensemble methods to account for non-stationarity.

docs.title: Multiple Centrality Measures
docs.text:
The analysis computes four different centrality measures, each capturing a different aspect of network importance:

1. Degree Centrality

Measures the number of direct connections a stock has.

High degree stocks:

  • Connect to many other stocks directly

  • Represent broad market exposure

  • Example: HON (Honeywell) shows highest degree centrality

Interpretation:

These are the "popular" stocks that correlate with many others, often representing large-cap, diversified industrial companies or broad sector leaders.

2. Betweenness Centrality

Measures how often a stock lies on shortest paths between other stocks.

High betweenness stocks:

  • Act as bridges between different parts of the network

  • Connect otherwise separated clusters

  • Control information flow in the network

Portfolio Implication:

These stocks might offer diversification by bridging different market sectors or factors.

3. Closeness Centrality

Measures how close a stock is to all other stocks (inverse of average distance).

High closeness stocks:

  • Can reach all other stocks quickly

  • Positioned near the network center

  • Reflect broad market movements efficiently

4. Eigenvector Centrality

Measures importance based on connection quality (being connected to important nodes).

High eigenvector stocks:

  • Connected to other important stocks

  • Part of the network's core

  • Influenced by and influence market leaders

Practical Note:

Eigenvector centrality often identifies blue-chip stocks that form the market's backbone.

docs.title: Visualization and Stock Selection
docs.text:
The bar chart visualization for degree centrality reveals:

Distribution:

Most stocks have low degree centrality, with a few clear outliers at the top.

Top Stocks:

HON (Honeywell) dominates, suggesting it serves as a market hub connecting many sectors (aerospace, building technologies, industrial).

Portfolio Construction Logic:

  • Central Portfolio: Select top-10 or top-20 stocks by centrality measures

  • Peripheral Portfolio: Select bottom-10 or bottom-20 stocks by centrality measures

Expected Behavior:

  • Central Portfolio: Should track the broader market closely, offering stability but limited alpha

  • Peripheral Portfolio: Should show lower correlation with the market, offering diversification and potential for independent performance

docs.text:

Clearly define which stocks comprise the central and peripheral portfolios.

2. 2021 Performance Simulation

  • Calculate equal-weighted portfolio returns

  • Compare against S&P 500 benchmark

3. Performance Metrics

  • Total return

  • Sharpe ratio

  • Maximum drawdown

  • Correlation with benchmark

  • Alpha and beta

4. Results Interpretation

  • Did central or peripheral portfolios outperform?

  • Were results statistically significant?

  • What market conditions drove performance differences?

docs.title: Strengths of the Approach
docs.text:
Novel Perspective:

Network analysis provides structural insights that traditional portfolio theory overlooks. The visualization of market topology is particularly valuable for understanding market organization.

Multi-Metric Analysis:

Using multiple centrality measures rather than relying on a single metric strengthens the approach by capturing different dimensions of network importance.

Temporal Analysis:

The year-by-year network evolution analysis successfully demonstrates that market structure changes over time, particularly during crisis periods.

docs.title: Methodological Limitations
docs.text:
1. Incomplete Analysis

The notebook stops before completing the portfolio simulation and performance comparison, leaving the core research question unanswered.

2. Survivorship Bias

Using the current S&P 500 constituent list for historical analysis excludes failed or delisted companies, potentially overstating historical performance.

3. Look-Ahead Bias Risk

If the portfolio is constructed using information from the same period it's tested on (2011-2020 network for 2021 performance), there's a risk of overfitting.

4. Stationary Assumption Contradiction

The analysis first demonstrates non-stationary market structure (2011-2020 networks differ), then assumes stationarity by building a single 10-year network for portfolio selection.

5. Transaction Costs Ignored

Real portfolio implementation would incur:

  • Trading commissions (minimal with modern brokers)

  • Bid-ask spreads (significant for less liquid stocks)

  • Market impact (especially for larger portfolios)

  • Rebalancing costs (if portfolio composition changes)

6. Limited Backtesting

Testing on only 2021 provides insufficient evidence. A robust analysis would:

  • Test on multiple out-of-sample periods

  • Perform rolling window analysis

  • Assess performance across different market regimes

docs.title: Alternative Approaches
docs.text:
1. Dynamic Network Analysis

Rather than a static 10-year network, use rolling windows to capture evolving market structure.

2. Community Detection

Instead of centrality measures, identify stock communities (clusters) and construct portfolios from different communities for diversification.

3. Risk-Adjusted Optimization

Combine network metrics with traditional mean-variance optimization rather than using centrality alone.

4. Factor Integration

Incorporate fundamental factors (value, momentum, quality) alongside network metrics for a hybrid approach.

5. Machine Learning Enhancement

Use network features as inputs to predictive models rather than direct portfolio selection rules.

docs.title: Computational Requirements
docs.text:
Processing Time:

  • Web scraping: <1 minute

  • Price data loading: <1 minute (with pre-saved CSV)

  • Correlation computation: <1 minute

  • MST construction: <1 minute per year

  • Centrality calculations: 1-2 minutes

Total Runtime: Approximately 15-20 minutes on standard hardware

Memory Requirements:

Minimal; 400 stocks × 10 years of daily data ≈ 10MB. Correlation matrices ≈ 20MB.

Scalability:

The approach scales poorly to universes beyond 1,000 stocks due to quadratic growth in correlation matrix size. For larger universes, consider:

  • Sector-level analysis first

  • Sparse correlation matrices

  • Approximate algorithms for MST construction

docs.title: When This Approach Works Best
docs.text:
Ideal Conditions:

  • Medium-sized stock universe (100-500 stocks)

  • Liquid, well-established securities

  • Sufficient historical data (5+ years)

  • Periodic rebalancing strategy (e.g., annual)

  • Combination with fundamental screening

Questionable Conditions:

  • Small stock universe (network structure less meaningful)

  • High-frequency trading (correlations change too quickly)

  • Illiquid securities (transaction costs dominate)

  • Emerging markets (data quality issues)

docs.title: Reproducibility Considerations
docs.text:
Challenges:

  • S&P 500 composition changes over time (use historical constituent lists)

  • Yahoo Finance API changes (implement robust error handling)

  • Random seed for network layout (affects visualization only, not analysis)

Recommendations for Replication:

  • Pin exact constituent list with dates

  • Save raw data with version control

  • Document exact parameter choices (MST algorithm, centrality normalization)

  • Report all results, not just favorable ones

# Extracting list of S&P 500 companies using BeautifulSoup
resp = requests.get('http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_S%26P_500_companies')
soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, 'lxml')
table = soup.find('table', {'class': 'wikitable sortable'})

docs.title: Code Analysis
docs.text:
Purpose:

This code automatically extracts the current S&P 500 constituent list from Wikipedia, eliminating manual data entry and providing an updateable source of ticker symbols.

Flow - Step by Step:

Step 1: HTTP Request

resp = requests.get('http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_S%26P_500_companies')

  • Sends GET request to Wikipedia's S&P 500 page

  • Returns response object containing HTML content

  • resp.text contains the full HTML as a string

Step 2: HTML Parsing

soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, 'lxml')

  • Parses HTML string into a navigable tree structure

  • Uses 'lxml' parser for speed and robustness

  • Creates soup object that understands HTML structure

Step 3: Table Location

table = soup.find('table', {'class': 'wikitable sortable'})

  • Searches for the first <table> element with CSS classes 'wikitable' and 'sortable'

  • Wikipedia structures its constituent list in this specific table format

  • Returns the table element or None if not found

Step 4: Row Iteration

for row in table.findAll('tr')[1:]:

  • findAll('tr') gets all table row elements

  • [1:] skips the first row (header row with column names)

  • Iterates through each company row

Step 5: Ticker Extraction

ticker = row.findAll('td')[0].text.strip('\n')

  • findAll('td') gets all table cell elements in the row

  • [0] selects the first cell, which contains the ticker symbol

  • .text extracts text content from the HTML element

  • .strip('\n') removes any newline characters

Step 6: List Assembly

tickers.append(ticker)

  • Adds the cleaned ticker symbol to the list

  • Builds a complete list of all S&P 500 tickers

Step 7: Symbol Standardization

tickers = [ticker.replace('.', '-') for ticker in tickers]

  • Replaces periods with hyphens in ticker symbols

  • Example: 'BRK.B' becomes 'BRK-B'

  • Required because Yahoo Finance uses hyphen format

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
Web Scraping Logic:

This implements a simple DOM (Document Object Model) traversal:

HTML Document
  └── <table class="wikitable sortable">
       ├── <tr> (header - skipped)
       ├── <tr>
       │    ├── <td>AAPL</td>  ← Extract this
       │    ├── <td>Apple Inc.</td>
       │    └── ...
       ├── <tr>
       │    ├── <td>MSFT</td>  ← Extract this
       │    └── ...
       └── ...

docs.title: Why These Design Choices
docs.text:
Why Wikipedia instead of direct S&P API?

  • Free and publicly accessible

  • No authentication required

  • Consistently formatted HTML structure

  • Updated regularly by the community

Why 'lxml' parser?

  • Faster than 'html.parser' (default)

  • More lenient with malformed HTML

  • Better for production use

Why .strip('\n')?

HTML formatting often includes newlines for readability. These need removal to ensure clean ticker strings for API calls.

Why replace '.' with '-'?

Yahoo Finance API uses hyphenated format for multi-class stocks (Class A, Class B shares). The conversion ensures compatibility.

  • Different source: You could use alternative data sources (Bloomberg, S&P Global) but would need API credentials

  • Historical constituents: For proper historical analysis, you'd need time-series constituent data

Dependencies:

This code has no dependencies on other sections but provides the tickers list required by all subsequent sections.

Retrieves 10 years of adjusted closing prices for all S&P 500 stocks, providing the raw data foundation for all subsequent analysis.

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
Adjusted Close Price Formula:

Adjusted Close = Close × Adjustment Factor

Where Adjustment Factor accounts for:

Adjustment Factor = (Dividends + Splits + Rights Offerings)

Example:

Stock closes at $100, pays $2 dividend:

Adjusted Close = $100 - $2 = $98 (for all dates before dividend)

This ensures that a return calculation accurately reflects investor experience.

docs.title: Why These Design Choices
docs.text:
Why Adjusted Close instead of Close?

Unadjusted prices create false returns during corporate actions:

  • Split: Stock splits 2-for-1, price drops from $100 to $50

  • Without adjustment: Appears as -50% loss

  • With adjustment: Historical prices halved, showing true continuity

Why Yahoo Finance?

  • Free API access (no subscription required)

  • Comprehensive coverage of U.S. equities

  • Reliable adjusted price calculations

  • Historical data back to 1980s for most stocks

Why CSV caching?

  • Speed: Loading CSV takes ~1 second vs. API fetching takes 5-10 minutes

  • Reliability: Avoids rate limiting and API failures

  • Reproducibility: Ensures all users analyze identical data

Why 2011-2020 period?

  • Post-financial crisis era (cleaner data, stable market structure)

  • Includes both bull markets and corrections

  • 10 years provides sufficient statistical power

  • Leaves 2021 for out-of-sample testing

docs.text:
Purpose:

Identify and remove stocks with incomplete data, ensuring all subsequent calculations use only complete time series.

Flow - Visualization:

Step 1: Transpose for Visualization

price_data.T.isnull()

  • .T transposes DataFrame (swaps rows and columns)

  • Result: Stocks as rows, dates as columns

  • .isnull() creates Boolean matrix (True = missing, False = present)

Why transpose?

With 500 stocks and 2,517 dates:

  • Normal orientation: 2,517 rows × 500 columns (too wide to visualize)

  • Transposed: 500 rows × 2,517 columns (better aspect ratio for heatmap)

Step 2: Heatmap Creation

sns.heatmap(price_data.T.isnull())

  • Creates color-coded matrix visualization

  • Yellow: Missing data (True)

  • Purple/Blue: Present data (False)

  • Immediately reveals patterns in missing data

Flow - Cleaning:

Step 3: Column-wise Deletion

price_data_cleaned = price_data.dropna(axis=1)

Parameters:

  • axis=1 - Operate on columns (default axis=0 operates on rows)

  • No threshold specified - drops any column with any missing value

Effect:

Removes entire stock from dataset if it has even one missing date.

Mathematical Impact:

Original: n₁ stocks × m dates
Cleaned: n₂ stocks × m dates (where n₂ < n₁)
Missing data: n₁ - n₂ stocks completely removed

docs.title: Why These Design Choices
docs.text:
Why complete case analysis (dropna)?

Alternatives considered:

  1. Forward fill: price_data.fillna(method='ffill')

  2. Problem: Creates artificial plateaus during delisting/suspension

  3. Risk: False correlations during actual zero-return periods

  4. Interpolation: price_data.interpolate()

  5. Problem: Stock prices don't follow smooth functions

  6. Risk: Fabricating price movements that never occurred

  7. Mean imputation: Replace with column mean

  8. Problem: Destroys variance structure

  9. Risk: Artificial correlations with other stocks

Complete deletion chosen because:

  • Preserves true price movements (no artificial data)

  • Ensures all correlation calculations use real co-movements

  • Acceptable loss given S&P 500's size (still 350-400 stocks remain)

Why not impute?

For stock returns, missing data typically indicates:

  • Company not yet in index (IPO, promotion from smaller index)

  • Company removed from index (bankruptcy, merger, demotion)

  • Temporary trading suspension (usually indicates crisis)

Imputing values for these situations would misrepresent market reality.

  • No yellow: Confirms successful removal of incomplete series

Statistical implications:

Survivorship Bias:

P(Stock survives 2011-2020) > P(Random stock survival)

Remaining stocks are systematically different:

  • Larger market cap on average

  • Better fundamental performance

  • Lower bankruptcy risk

Correlation Impact:

Removing failed companies may:

  • Increase average pairwise correlation (survivors co-move more)

  • Reduce appearance of tail risk (removed extreme losers)

  • Overestimate diversification benefits

If you change this code:

  • Keep missing data: Correlation calculations will fail or produce NaN

  • Use imputation: Creates artificial relationships that don't reflect market reality

  • Use pairwise deletion: Each correlation uses different stock pairs, making comparisons invalid

  • Example: year=2011 produces '2011-01-01':'2011-12-31'

D = {d₁, d₂, ..., dₙ} (all dates from 2011-01-01 to 2020-12-31)

docs.text:
Why annual segmentation instead of rolling windows?

Annual Approach (Used):

  • Non-overlapping periods

  • Clean temporal comparison

  • Aligns with business/reporting cycles

Rolling Window Alternative:

window_size = 252  # 1 year
for i in range(len(price_data) - window_size):
    window_data = price_data.iloc[i:i+window_size]

Advantages:

  • Smoother temporal evolution

  • More granular analysis

  • Better for detecting gradual changes

Disadvantages:

  • Overlapping periods (not independent)

  • Computational overhead (10× more networks)

  • Complex interpretation

Why function wrapper instead of inline?

snp_500_2012 = price_data_cleaned.loc['2012-01-01':'2012-12-31']

Function approach benefits:

  • DRY principle: Don't Repeat Yourself

  • Maintainability: Change logic once, affects all years

  • Clarity: Function name documents intent

  • Reusability: Can be called elsewhere in notebook

docs.title: Code Analysis
docs.text:
Purpose:

Transform price data into log returns, which have superior statistical properties for correlation analysis and satisfy assumptions of normality and stationarity.

Flow - Step by Step:

Step 1: Time Shift

snp_500_2011.shift(1)

What .shift(1) does:

Moves each row down by 1 position, filling the first row with NaN.

Visual representation:

Original:           After .shift(1):
Date    | Price     Date    | Price
--------|------     --------|------
2011-01-03 | 100       2011-01-03 | NaN
2011-01-04 | 102       2011-01-04 | 100
2011-01-05 | 101       2011-01-05 | 102

Purpose: Aligns today's price with yesterday's price in the same row.

Step 2: Logarithmic Transformation

np.log(snp_500_2011.shift(1))

Applies natural logarithm element-wise to all prices.

Step 3: Log Difference

np.log(snp_500_2011.shift(1)) - np.log(snp_500_2011)

Subtracts today's log price from yesterday's log price.

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
Log Return Formula:

r_t = ln(P_{t-1}) - ln(P_t) = ln(P_{t-1}/P_t)

Note: The code computes negative log returns (t-1 minus t) instead of (t minus t-1). This is unconventional but doesn't affect correlation calculations since:

Corr(X, Y) = Corr(-X, -Y)

Standard log return (should be):

log_returns_2011 = np.log(snp_500_2011) - np.log(snp_500_2011.shift(1))

Properties of Log Returns:

1. Approximate Simple Returns for Small Changes:

r_log ≈ r_simple for |r_simple| < 0.15

Example:

Price: $100 → $105
Simple return: 5%
Log return: ln(105/100) = 4.88%

2. Time Additivity:

r_{t₀→t₂} = r_{t₀→t₁} + r_{t₁→t₂}

Multi-day returns are simply sums of daily returns.

3. Normality:

For small time intervals, log returns approximately follow:

r_t ~ N(μ, σ²)

This enables use of parametric statistical methods.

4. Symmetry:

ln(P₁/P₀) = -ln(P₀/P₁)

A 10% gain followed by a 10% loss returns to the original price in log space (but not simple returns).

docs.title: Why These Design Choices
docs.text:
Why log returns vs simple returns?

Simple Returns:

r_simple = (P_t - P_{t-1}) / P_{t-1}

Problems:

  • Not symmetric: +50% gain needs -33.3% loss to break even

  • Not additive across time

  • Non-normal distribution (bounded below at -100%)

  • Cross-sectional portfolio returns require weighted averages

Log Returns:

r_log = ln(P_t / P_{t-1})

Advantages:

  • Symmetric: magnitude of gain equals magnitude of loss

  • Time-additive: multi-period returns are sums

  • Approximately normal for short intervals

  • Suitable for statistical inference

Why daily returns vs longer periods?

Daily (Used):

  • Maximum sample size: ~252 observations per year

  • Captures high-frequency co-movements

  • Standard in academic finance

Alternative - Weekly:

  • Fewer observations: ~52 per year

  • Less noise from bid-ask bounce

  • Better for less liquid stocks

Alternative - Monthly:

  • Very few observations: ~12 per year

  • Insufficient for reliable correlation estimation

  • Risk of overfitting

If you change the formula:

Correct the sign:

Impact: Changes sign of returns but not correlations.

Use simple returns:

simple_returns_2011 = (snp_500_2011 - snp_500_2011.shift(1)) / snp_500_2011.shift(1)

Impact:

  • Correlation magnitudes change slightly

  • Statistical assumptions violated

  • Less appropriate for academic analysis

  • Provides log return DataFrames for correlation calculation in Section 6

def calculate_log_returns(price_data, correct_sign=True):
    """
    Calculate log returns from price data.

    Parameters:
    -----------
    price_data : pd.DataFrame
        Price data with datetime index
    correct_sign : bool
        If True, use standard convention (today - yesterday)
        If False, use notebook convention (yesterday - today)

    Returns:
    --------
    pd.DataFrame
        Log returns
    """
    if correct_sign:
        log_returns = np.log(price_data) - np.log(price_data.shift(1))
    else:
        log_returns = np.log(price_data.shift(1)) - np.log(price_data)

    # Verify no infinite values
    assert not np.isinf(log_returns).any().any(), "Infinite values detected (zero or negative prices)"

    # Report statistics
    print(f"Mean return: {log_returns.mean().mean():.2%}")
    print(f"Std deviation: {log_returns.std().mean():.2%}")
    print(f"Min return: {log_returns.min().min():.2%}")
    print(f"Max return: {log_returns.max().max():.2%}")

    return log_returns

Purpose:

Compute pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients between all stock returns, creating the foundation for network-based analysis of market structure.

Flow - Correlation Calculation:

return_correlation_2011 = log_returns_2011.corr()

What .corr() does:

Computes Pearson correlation coefficient for every pair of columns (stocks).

Result structure:

           AAPL    MSFT    JPM     ...
AAPL       1.00    0.65    0.52    ...
MSFT       0.65    1.00    0.58    ...
JPM        0.52    0.58    1.00    ...
...

Matrix properties:

  • Symmetric: corr(A,B) = corr(B,A)

  • Diagonal = 1: corr(A,A) = 1

  • Dimensions: n × n where n = number of stocks (~400)

Flow - Visualization:

Step 1: Subplot Grid Creation

figure, axes = plt.subplots(5, 2, figsize=(30, 30))

Parameters:

  • 5, 2 - 5 rows, 2 columns = 10 subplots (one per year)

  • figsize=(30, 30) - Total figure size in inches

  • Returns axes array for subplot addressing

Step 2: Heatmap Plotting

sns.heatmap(return_correlation_2011, ax=axes[0, 0])

Parameters:

  • First argument: Correlation matrix to visualize

  • ax=axes[0, 0] - Plot in specific subplot (row 0, column 0)

Visual encoding:

  • Color intensity represents correlation strength

  • Yellow/Red: High positive correlation

  • Blue/Purple: Low or negative correlation

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
Pearson Correlation Formula:

ρ(X,Y) = Cov(X,Y) / (σ_X × σ_Y)

Where:

  • Cov(X,Y) = Σ[(X_i - μ_X)(Y_i - μ_Y)] / (n-1)

  • σ_X = √[Σ(X_i - μ_X)² / (n-1)]

  • σ_Y = √[Σ(Y_i - μ_Y)² / (n-1)]

Properties:

-1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1

ρ = 1  → Perfect positive linear relationship
ρ = 0  → No linear relationship
ρ = -1 → Perfect negative linear relationship

Matrix form:

For returns matrix R (T observations × N stocks):

R = [r₁, r₂, ..., rₙ]  (each rᵢ is a column vector)

Correlation matrix:
C = [ρᵢⱼ] where ρᵢⱼ = corr(rᵢ, rⱼ)

docs.title: Why These Design Choices
docs.text:
Why Pearson correlation?

Alternatives:

  1. Spearman rank correlation:
log_returns_2011.corr(method='spearman')

  • Captures monotonic relationships

  • Robust to outliers

  • Less common in finance

  • Kendall tau:

log_returns_2011.corr(method='kendall')

  • Measures ordinal association

  • Even more robust

  • Computationally expensive

Pearson chosen because:

  • Standard in portfolio theory and econometrics

  • Directly related to covariance (used in mean-variance optimization)

  • Interpretable linear relationship measure

  • Fast computation even for large matrices

Why visualize all years simultaneously?

Benefits:

  • Immediate visual comparison across time

  • Identify temporal patterns (crisis vs normal)

  • Quality check for data issues

Alternative - Animation:

from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
# Animate transition between years

Trade-off: More dynamic but harder to compare specific years.

docs.title: Computational Complexity
docs.text:
Time complexity:

O(n² × T)

Where:

  • n = number of stocks (~400)

  • T = observations per year (~252)

For this analysis:

400² × 252 ≈ 40 million operations per year
× 10 years = 400 million operations total

Memory:

Each correlation matrix: 400 × 400 × 8 bytes (float64) ≈ 1.3 MB

Total: 10 years × 1.3 MB ≈ 13 MB (negligible)

def analyze_correlation_matrix(corr_matrix, year):
    """
    Compute summary statistics for correlation matrix.

    Parameters:
    -----------
    corr_matrix : pd.DataFrame
        Correlation matrix
    year : int
        Year for labeling

    Returns:
    --------
    dict
        Summary statistics
    """
    # Get upper triangle (excluding diagonal)
    mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr_matrix), k=1).astype(bool)
    upper_tri = corr_matrix.where(mask)

    stats = {
        'year': year,
        'mean_correlation': upper_tri.mean().mean(),
        'median_correlation': upper_tri.median().median(),
        'std_correlation': upper_tri.std().mean(),
        'min_correlation': upper_tri.min().min(),
        'max_correlation': upper_tri.max().max(),
        'pct_negative': (upper_tri < 0).sum().sum() / mask.sum() * 100
    }

    return stats

# Analyze all years

docs.text:
Purpose:

Convert correlation (similarity measure) into distance (dissimilarity measure) suitable for MST algorithms, which minimize total distance.

Flow:

Step 1: Correlation Inversion

1 - return_correlation_2011

Effect:

  • High correlation (ρ ≈ 1) → Low value (≈0)

  • Low correlation (ρ ≈ 0) → Medium value (≈1)

  • Negative correlation (ρ ≈ -1) → High value (≈2)

Step 2: Scaling

2 * (1 - return_correlation_2011)

Doubles the range to [0, 4].

Step 3: Square Root

np.sqrt(2 * (1 - return_correlation_2011))

Takes element-wise square root, producing final distance matrix.

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
Distance Formula:

d_ij = √[2(1 - ρ_ij)]

Derivation from Angular Distance:

This formula comes from the angular interpretation of correlation:

ρ_ij = cos(θ_ij)

Where θ is the angle between two normalized vectors in n-dimensional space.

Euclidean distance between unit vectors:

d² = ||u - v||² = ||u||² + ||v||² - 2u·v
   = 1 + 1 - 2cos(θ)
   = 2(1 - cos(θ))
   = 2(1 - ρ)

∴ d = √[2(1 - ρ)]

Properties of this metric:

1. Range:

ρ = 1  → d = √[2(1-1)] = 0    (identical stocks, zero distance)
ρ = 0  → d = √[2(1-0)] = √2   (uncorrelated, moderate distance)
ρ = -1 → d = √[2(1+1)] = 2    (opposite stocks, maximum distance)

2. Metric Properties:

This is a true metric distance, satisfying:

  • Non-negativity: d(x,y) ≥ 0

  • Identity: d(x,y) = 0 ⟺ x = y

  • Symmetry: d(x,y) = d(y,x)

  • Triangle inequality: d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y) + d(y,z)

3. Preservation of Relationships:

ρ₁ > ρ₂  ⟺  d₁ < d₂

Higher correlation → Lower distance (monotonic transformation)

docs.title: Why These Design Choices
docs.text:
Why this specific formula?

Alternative distance metrics:

  1. Simple inversion:
d = 1 - ρ

  • Range: [0, 2]

  • Not a proper metric (violates triangle inequality)

  • Simpler but less theoretically justified

  • Exponential transformation:

d = -log(ρ) for ρ > 0

  • Emphasizes very high correlations

  • Undefined for ρ ≤ 0

  • Less commonly used

  • Absolute difference:

d = |ρ₁ - ρ₂|

  • Treats positive and negative correlation symmetrically

  • Not appropriate for financial correlations

The chosen formula is preferred because:

  • Established in econophysics literature

  • Proper metric satisfying triangle inequality

  • Geometric interpretation (angular distance)

  • Appropriate weighting of correlation differences

docs.text:
Purpose:

Transform fully-connected dense networks into sparse, interpretable tree structures that preserve the most significant stock relationships while eliminating redundancy.

Flow - Graph Construction:

distance_2011_graph = nx.Graph(distance_2011)

What nx.Graph() does:

Creates an undirected graph from a DataFrame/array:

  • Nodes: Stock tickers (column/row names)

  • Edges: All pairs of stocks

  • Weights: Distance values from the matrix

Result:

Fully connected graph with n nodes and n(n-1)/2 edges.

For 400 stocks: 400 × 399 / 2 = 79,800 edges

Flow - MST Construction:

graph_2011_filtered = nx.minimum_spanning_tree(distance_2011_graph)

What .minimum_spanning_tree() does:

Applies Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm to find the MST.

Algorithm (Kruskal's):

  1. Sort all edges by weight (distance)

  2. Initialize empty tree

  3. For each edge in sorted order:

  4. If adding edge doesn't create cycle: add it

  5. If it creates cycle: skip it

  6. Stop when tree has n-1 edges

Result:

Sparse tree with:

  • Same n nodes

  • Exactly n-1 edges (for 400 stocks: 399 edges)

  • Minimum total edge weight

  • No cycles

Flow - Visualization:

nx.draw_networkx(graph_2011_filtered, with_labels=False, ax=axes[0])

Parameters:

  • graph_2011_filtered - MST to draw

  • with_labels=False - Omit node labels (too many to display)

  • ax=axes[0] - Target subplot

Layout algorithm:

NetworkX uses Fruchterman-Reingold force-directed algorithm by default:

  • Treats edges as springs

  • Nodes repel each other

  • System minimizes energy to find pleasing layout

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
MST Definition:

For graph G = (V, E, w):

  • V = vertices (stocks)

  • E = edges (correlations)

  • w: E → ℝ (weight function, distance values)

Minimum Spanning Tree T is a subgraph where:

T = (V, E_T) such that:
1. E_T ⊆ E
2. |E_T| = |V| - 1
3. T is connected (path exists between any two nodes)
4. T is acyclic (no cycles)
5. Σ_{e∈E_T} w(e) is minimized

Kruskal's Algorithm:

function Kruskal(G):
    T = ∅
    for each vertex v in G.V:
        MAKE-SET(v)

    for each edge (u,v) in G.E sorted by weight:
        if FIND-SET(u) ≠ FIND-SET(v):
            T = T ∪ {(u,v)}
            UNION(u,v)

    return T

Time Complexity:

O(E log E) for sorting edges
+ O(E α(V)) for union-find operations
≈ O(E log V) overall

For this problem:

E ≈ 80,000 edges
V ≈ 400 nodes
Time ≈ 80,000 × log(400) ≈ 700,000 operations (~1 second)

Prim's Algorithm (Alternative):

function Prim(G, start_vertex):
    T = {start_vertex}
    while |T| < |V|:
        find minimum weight edge (u,v) where u ∈ T, v ∉ T
        add v to T
        add edge (u,v) to MST
    return MST

NetworkX Implementation:

Uses Prim's with binary heap for O(E log V) performance.

docs.title: Why These Design Choices
docs.text:
Why MST instead of alternatives?

Alternative 1: Threshold Filtering

threshold = 0.5
filtered_corr = return_correlation_2011[return_correlation_2011 > threshold]
graph = nx.Graph(filtered_corr)

Problems:

  • Arbitrary threshold choice

  • May disconnect graph

  • Still produces dense graphs

Alternative 2: Planar Maximally Filtered Graph (PMFG)

Keeps up to 3(n-2) edges while maintaining planarity.

Advantages:

  • Retains more information than MST

  • Still removes most redundancy

Disadvantages:

  • More complex algorithm

  • Harder to interpret

  • Less established in literature

Alternative 3: K-Nearest Neighbors

Keep k strongest connections per node.

def knn_graph(corr_matrix, k=5):
    for stock in corr_matrix.columns:
        keep_top_k_correlations(stock, k)

Problems:

  • May not be connected

  • Arbitrary k parameter

MST chosen because:

  • Guaranteed connectivity

  • Parameter-free

  • Established in econophysics

  • Interpretable structure

  • Efficient computation

Why draw without labels?

With 400 stock tickers:

  • Labels overlap unreadably

  • Visual clutter dominates

  • Network structure becomes invisible

For detailed analysis, can zoom into specific regions or use interactive plots.

Flow - Metric Computation:

What .average_shortest_path_length() does:

  1. Computes shortest path between every pair of nodes using BFS

  2. Averages all pairwise path lengths

  3. Returns single scalar value

Flow - Visualization:

             data=pd.DataFrame({'year': year,

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
Shortest Path Length:

For nodes u and v in graph G:

d_G(u, v) = minimum number of edges in any path from u to v

Average Shortest Path Length:

L = (1 / (n(n-1))) Σ_{u≠v} d_G(u, v)

Where:

  • n = number of nodes

  • The sum is over all pairs of distinct nodes

For MST with n nodes:

n = 400 nodes
Number of pairs: 400 × 399 / 2 = 79,800 pairs

Algorithm (BFS-based):

function average_shortest_path_length(G):
    total_length = 0
    count = 0

    for each node u in G:
        distances = BFS(G, u)  # Breadth-First Search from u
        for each node v ≠ u:
            total_length += distances[v]
            count += 1

    return total_length / count

Time Complexity:

O(n × (n + edges)) = O(n²) for trees (edges = n-1)

For 400 nodes: 400² ≈ 160,000 operations per graph

docs.title: Why This Metric
docs.text:
Interpretation:

Small L (≈ 4-5):

  • Compact network

  • Stocks quickly reach each other through network

  • Indicates centralized structure with strong hubs

  • Market dominated by few key connections

Large L (≈ 8-10):

  • Elongated network

  • Longer paths between most stocks

  • Indicates fragmented structure

  • Market with distinct separated clusters

Financial Meaning:

L represents how many "steps" of correlation propagation are needed for shocks to spread across the market.

Lower L:

  • Faster contagion

  • Less diversification

  • Higher systemic risk

Higher L:

  • Slower shock propagation

  • More diversification opportunities

  • Segmented market sectors

  • 2016-2017: Sharp increase to L ≈ 8-9

docs.text:
def analyze_network_evolution(graphs, years):
    """
    Comprehensive temporal network analysis.

    Parameters:
    -----------
    graphs : list of nx.Graph
        Filtered network graphs
    years : list of int
        Corresponding years

    Returns:
    --------
    pd.DataFrame
        Time series of network metrics
    """
    metrics = []

    for graph, year in zip(graphs, years):
        metric_dict = {
            'year': year,
            'nodes': graph.number_of_nodes(),
            'edges': graph.number_of_edges(),
            'avg_degree': 2 * graph.number_of_edges() / graph.number_of_nodes(),
            'avg_path_length': nx.average_shortest_path_length(graph),
            'diameter': nx.diameter(graph),
            'radius': nx.radius(graph),
            'avg_clustering': nx.average_clustering(graph),
            'assortativity': nx.degree_assortativity_coefficient(graph),
        }

        # Centrality measures
        degree_cent = nx.degree_centrality(graph)
        between_cent = nx.betweenness_centrality(graph)
        close_cent = nx.closeness_centrality(graph)

        metric_dict.update({
            'max_degree_cent': max(degree_cent.values()),
            'max_between_cent': max(between_cent.values()),
            'max_close_cent': max(close_cent.values()),
            'avg_degree_cent': np.mean(list(degree_cent.values())),
            'avg_between_cent': np.mean(list(between_cent.values())),
            'avg_close_cent': np.mean(list(close_cent.values()))
        })

        metrics.append(metric_dict)

    return pd.DataFrame(metrics)

# Usage
all_graphs = [graph_2011_filtered, graph_2012_filtered, ...]
years = list(range(2011, 2021))
evolution_df = analyze_network_evolution(all_graphs, years)

# Visualize multiple metrics
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(15, 12))
metrics_to_plot = ['avg_path_length', 'diameter', 'avg_clustering', 
                   'assortativity', 'max_degree_cent', 'max_between_cent']

for ax, metric in zip(axes.flat, metrics_to_plot):
    ax.plot(evolution_df['year'], evolution_df[metric], marker='o')
    ax.set_title(metric.replace('_', ' ').title())
    ax.set_xlabel('Year')
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Flow - Centrality Computations:

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
1. Degree Centrality:

C_D(v) = degree(v) / (n - 1)

Where:

  • degree(v) = number of edges incident to node v

  • n = total number of nodes

  • Normalized to [0, 1]

Example:

Node with 10 connections in 400-node network:
C_D = 10 / 399 ≈ 0.025

2. Closeness Centrality:

C_C(v) = (n - 1) / Σ_{u≠v} d(v, u)

Where:

  • d(v, u) = shortest path length from v to u

  • Inverse of average distance

Interpretation:

Measures how quickly node can reach all other nodes.

3. Betweenness Centrality:

C_B(v) = Σ_{s≠v≠t} (σ_st(v) / σ_st)

Where:

  • σ_st = number of shortest paths from s to t

  • σ_st(v) = number of those paths passing through v

Interpretation:

Measures how often node lies on shortest paths between other pairs.

4. Eigenvector Centrality:

Solves eigenvalue problem:

Ax = λx

Where:

  • A = adjacency matrix

  • x = eigenvector (centrality scores)

  • λ = largest eigenvalue

Iterative computation (Power Method):

x^(t+1) = Ax^(t) / ||Ax^(t)||

Interpretation:

Node is important if connected to other important nodes.

docs.title: Centrality Comparison
docs.text:
Use Cases:

Degree Centrality:

  • Best for: Identifying broadly connected hubs

  • Portfolio application: Stocks representing broad market exposure

  • Example stocks: Industrials, financials with broad sector ties

Closeness Centrality:

  • Best for: Identifying central market actors

  • Portfolio application: Stocks that reflect overall market quickly

  • Example stocks: Large-cap tech, major indices components

Betweenness Centrality:

  • Best for: Identifying bridging stocks

  • Portfolio application: Stocks connecting different market sectors

  • Example stocks: Diversified conglomerates, sector bridges

Eigenvector Centrality:

  • Best for: Identifying elite network members

  • Portfolio application: "Quality" stocks connected to other quality stocks

  • Example stocks: FAANG stocks, blue-chip leaders

docs.title: Algorithm Complexity
docs.text:
Degree Centrality:

O(n + edges) = O(n) for trees

Very fast, ~400 operations.

Closeness Centrality:

O(n × (n + edges)) = O(n²)

Requires BFS from each node, ~160,000 operations.

Betweenness Centrality:

O(n × edges) for sparse graphs
O(n³) for dense graphs

Most expensive, ~160,000-400,000 operations.

Eigenvector Centrality:

O(iterations × edges)

Typically converges in 20-50 iterations, ~10,000 operations.

docs.text:
If you use different centrality measures:

PageRank (variant of eigenvector):

pagerank = nx.pagerank(graph, alpha=0.85)

  • Accounts for random jumps

  • Less sensitive to network structure

  • Popular in web analysis

Katz Centrality:

katz = nx.katz_centrality(graph, alpha=0.1)

  • Considers all paths, not just shortest

  • Weights by path length

  • More granular than eigenvector

Harmonic Centrality:

harmonic = nx.harmonic_centrality(graph)

  • Variant of closeness

  • Handles disconnected graphs better

  • Uses sum of inverse distances

Portfolio Construction Strategies:

Central Portfolio:

# Select top N by degree centrality
top_n = 20
central_stocks = dc_data.head(top_n)['stocks'].tolist()

Expected behavior:

  • High correlation with market

  • Low tracking error vs S&P 500

  • Lower volatility

  • Limited alpha potential

Peripheral Portfolio:

# Select bottom N by degree centrality
peripheral_stocks = dc_data.tail(top_n)['stocks'].tolist()

Expected behavior:

  • Lower correlation with market

  • Higher tracking error

  • Potentially higher volatility

  • Higher alpha potential (positive or negative)

Diversified Strategy:

# Combine multiple centrality measures
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Normalize all centrality measures
scaler = StandardScaler()
centrality_matrix = scaler.fit_transform([
    [degree_centrality[stock] for stock in stocks],
    [closeness_centrality[stock] for stock in stocks],
    [betweenness_centrality[stock] for stock in stocks],
    [eigenvector_centrality[stock] for stock in stocks]
]).T

# Compute composite score
composite_score = centrality_matrix.mean(axis=1)

# Select based on composite
top_stocks = [stocks[i] for i in composite_score.argsort()[-20:]]

Dependencies:

  • Requires cleaned price data from Section 3

  • Provides centrality rankings for portfolio construction (incomplete in notebook)

docs.title: Production Code Enhancements
docs.text:
def compute_all_centralities(graph):
    """
    Compute multiple centrality measures for network analysis.

    Parameters:
    -----------
    graph : nx.Graph
        Network graph

    Returns:
    --------
    pd.DataFrame
        Centrality measures for all nodes
    """
    centralities = {
        'degree': nx.degree_centrality(graph),
        'closeness': nx.closeness_centrality(graph),
        'betweenness': nx.betweenness_centrality(graph),
        'eigenvector': nx.eigenvector_centrality_numpy(graph),
        'pagerank': nx.pagerank(graph),
        'harmonic': nx.harmonic_centrality(graph)
    }

    # Convert to DataFrame
    df = pd.DataFrame(centralities)
    df['stock'] = df.index

    # Add rankings
    for col in centralities.keys():
        df[f'{col}_rank'] = df[col].rank(ascending=False)

    # Add composite score
    df['composite'] = df[[col for col in centralities.keys()]].mean(axis=1)
    df['composite_rank'] = df['composite'].rank(ascending=False)

    return df.sort_values('composite', ascending=False)

# Usage
centrality_df = compute_all_centralities(distance_2011_till_2020_graph_filtered)

# Identify central and peripheral stocks
n_stocks = 20
central_portfolio = centrality_df.head(n_stocks)['stock'].tolist()
peripheral_portfolio = centrality_df.tail(n_stocks)['stock'].tolist()

print("Central Portfolio Stocks:")
print(central_portfolio)
print("\nPeripheral Portfolio Stocks:")
print(peripheral_portfolio)

# Visualize centrality correlation
correlation_matrix = centrality_df[[col for col in centralities.keys()]].corr()
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(correlation_matrix, annot=True, cmap='coolwarm', center=0)
plt.title('Correlation Between Centrality Measures')
plt.show()

The notebook stops before final implementation. To complete:

Step 1: Portfolio Selection

# Select stocks for portfolios
n_stocks = 20

# Central portfolio (high degree centrality)
central_portfolio = dc_data.head(n_stocks)['stocks'].tolist()

# Peripheral portfolio (low degree centrality)
peripheral_portfolio = dc_data.tail(n_stocks)['stocks'].tolist()

Step 2: Fetch 2021 Data

# Fetch 2021 prices for selected stocks
price_2021_central = web.DataReader(central_portfolio, 'yahoo', 
                                    start='2021-01-01', end='2021-12-31')['Adj Close']
price_2021_peripheral = web.DataReader(peripheral_portfolio, 'yahoo',
                                       start='2021-01-01', end='2021-12-31')['Adj Close']
price_2021_snp = web.DataReader('^GSPC', 'yahoo',
                                start='2021-01-01', end='2021-12-31')['Adj Close']

Step 3: Compute Portfolio Returns

# Equal-weighted portfolio returns
returns_central = price_2021_central.pct_change().mean(axis=1)
returns_peripheral = price_2021_peripheral.pct_change().mean(axis=1)
returns_snp = price_2021_snp.pct_change()

# Cumulative returns
cumulative_central = (1 + returns_central).cumprod()
cumulative_peripheral = (1 + returns_peripheral).cumprod()
cumulative_snp = (1 + returns_snp).cumprod()

Step 4: Visualization

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
plt.plot(cumulative_central.index, cumulative_central, label='Central Portfolio')
plt.plot(cumulative_peripheral.index, cumulative_peripheral, label='Peripheral Portfolio')
plt.plot(cumulative_snp.index, cumulative_snp, label='S&P 500')
plt.xlabel('Date')
plt.ylabel('Cumulative Return')
plt.title('Portfolio Performance Comparison (2021)')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

Step 5: Performance Metrics

def compute_metrics(returns):
    return {
        'Total Return': (returns.iloc[-1] - 1) * 100,
        'Annualized Return': ((1 + returns.iloc[-1]) ** (252/len(returns)) - 1) * 100,
        'Volatility': returns.std() * np.sqrt(252) * 100,
        'Sharpe Ratio': (returns.mean() / returns.std()) * np.sqrt(252),
        'Max Drawdown': ((returns / returns.cummax()) - 1).min() * 100
    }

metrics_central = compute_metrics(cumulative_central)
metrics_peripheral = compute_metrics(cumulative_peripheral)
metrics_snp = compute_metrics(cumulative_snp)

# Display results
results_df = pd.DataFrame([metrics_central, metrics_peripheral, metrics_snp],
                         index=['Central Portfolio', 'Peripheral Portfolio', 'S&P 500'])
print(results_df)
