docs.title: Introduction and Context
docs.text:
The Enron scandal represents one of the most significant corporate fraud cases in American history. Enron Corporation, once a Wall Street darling and one of America's largest energy companies, experienced a catastrophic collapse in 2001 when massive accounting fraud was uncovered. The company's leadership orchestrated one of the biggest frauds in corporate history, leading to bankruptcy and criminal convictions.

Why Network Analysis Matters:

The Enron email corpus, made public during the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission investigation, provides an unprecedented window into organizational communication patterns. By analyzing the email network of senior officials, we can:

  • Identify key players in the organizational hierarchy
  • Uncover informal communication patterns that may differ from formal org charts
  • Detect central figures who bridge different organizational units
  • Understand information flow within the leadership team

This tutorial focuses on a subset of 50 senior officials from Enron, using their email communication patterns to construct and analyze a social network that reveals organizational structure and key influencers.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Tutorial Objectives and Methodology
docs.text:
Primary Goal:

Build and analyze an email communication network to identify important nodes (individuals) within Enron's senior leadership and understand their roles based on various centrality measures.

Methodology Overview:

This analysis follows a systematic network science approach:

  • Data Loading: Import email communication data showing sender-receiver relationships
  • Network Construction: Transform email data into a graph structure where nodes represent individuals and edges represent email communication
  • Visual Exploration: Create multiple network visualizations to identify patterns and key nodes
  • Quantitative Analysis: Calculate four different centrality measures to objectively identify important individuals
  • Interpretation: Synthesize visual and quantitative findings to understand organizational structure

Why This Approach:

Network analysis is particularly powerful for organizational studies because it:

  • Reveals actual communication patterns rather than formal hierarchies
  • Identifies informal leaders and information brokers
  • Detects communities and subgroups within organizations
  • Provides objective, mathematical measures of individual importance

[See Code Walkthrough Section 1 for implementation details]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Understanding
docs.text:
Dataset Structure:

The dataset consists of email communication records with a simple structure:

  • From: Email sender (node identifier)
  • To: Email recipient (node identifier)
  • Each row represents a directed communication relationship

Dataset Characteristics:

  • 80 nodes representing senior officials at Enron
  • Each node is assigned a numeric identifier
  • The dataset captures email communication patterns, not email content
  • Relationships are based on whether individuals exchanged emails, not frequency

Key Consideration:

This is a subset focusing on senior leadership, not the entire Enron workforce. The network analysis reveals patterns among decision-makers and executives, which is particularly relevant for understanding organizational dynamics at the top.

Interpretation Note:

The numeric identifiers (1-80) anonymize individuals, but centrality analysis can still reveal organizational roles. For instance, the most connected individual likely holds a central organizational position (potentially CEO or a key coordinator).

[See Code Walkthrough Section 2 for data loading implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Network Construction and Visualization
docs.text:
From Data to Network:

The transformation from email records to network graph involves:

  • Nodes: Each unique email address becomes a node in the network
  • Edges: Each email communication creates an edge between sender and receiver
  • Graph Type: Undirected graph (communication goes both ways)

Why Undirected Graph:

The choice of undirected edges treats email communication as bidirectional relationships. This is appropriate when analyzing overall connectivity patterns rather than information flow direction. If directionality matters (who initiates communication), a directed graph would be more appropriate.

Visualization Approaches:

1. Default Layout Visualization:

The initial visualization reveals an immediate pattern: one node appears extraordinarily well-connected while others show varying degrees of connectivity.

Key Observation: Node 1 is connected to virtually all other nodes in the network, suggesting a central organizational role (likely CEO or equivalent).

2. Shell Layout Visualization:

The shell (circular) layout arranges nodes in concentric circles based on their connectivity:

  • Central nodes: Highly connected individuals placed toward the center
  • Peripheral nodes: Less connected individuals placed toward the outside
  • Visual Clarity: This layout better highlights the hierarchical nature of the network

Visual Insights:

From the visualizations, several patterns emerge:

  • Node 1: Universal connector, linked to all other nodes
  • Secondary hubs: Nodes 56, 54, 74, 53, 50 show high connectivity
  • Clustering: Some node groupings suggest team or departmental structures
  • Hierarchy: The network shows clear hierarchical structure rather than flat organization

Interpretation:

The visualizations suggest:

  • A star-like topology with Node 1 at the center (typical CEO pattern)
  • Multiple secondary hubs likely representing department heads or senior VPs
  • Internal team structures visible but not perfectly clear
  • The organization follows traditional hierarchical communication patterns

Limitations of Visual Analysis:

While powerful, visual inspection has limitations:

  • Subjective interpretation
  • Difficult to rank nodes precisely
  • May miss subtle patterns
  • Not scalable to very large networks

This motivates the quantitative centrality analysis that follows.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3 for network construction and visualization code]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Centrality Measures Analysis
docs.text: Centrality measures provide objective, mathematical ways to quantify node importance. This analysis employs four different centrality measures, each capturing a different aspect of "importance" in a network.

docs.title: Understanding Centrality Measures
docs.text:
Why Multiple Measures:

Different centrality measures reveal different types of importance:

  • Some measure direct connections
  • Others measure strategic positioning
  • Some focus on information flow
  • Others consider the importance of neighbors

Using multiple measures provides a more complete picture of organizational structure.

docs.title: Degree Centrality Analysis
docs.text:
What It Measures:

Degree centrality simply counts the number of direct connections a node has. In organizational terms, it identifies individuals who communicate with many others directly.

Results:

Top 5 nodes by degree centrality: 1, 56, 74, 53, 54

Interpretation:

  • Node 1 has the highest degree centrality (connected to almost everyone), confirming visual observation of central organizational role
  • Nodes 56, 74, 53, 54 are secondary hubs with many direct connections
  • These individuals likely hold senior positions requiring broad communication (department heads, senior VPs)

Business Meaning:

High degree centrality indicates:

  • Broad responsibility across multiple areas
  • Role requiring coordination with many people
  • Potential information bottlenecks if these individuals become unavailable

docs.title: Eigenvector Centrality Analysis
docs.text:
What It Measures:

Eigenvector centrality considers not just how many connections you have, but how important your connections are. It's a measure of influence based on being connected to other influential people.

Results:

Top 5 nodes by eigenvector centrality: 1, 56, 74, 53, 54

Interpretation:

The same nodes emerge, suggesting these individuals are:

  • Not only well-connected themselves
  • Connected to other well-connected individuals
  • Part of the "inner circle" of organizational leadership

Why This Matters:

In organizations, being connected to influential people often matters more than the raw number of connections. Eigenvector centrality identifies true influencers, not just communicators.

docs.title: Betweenness Centrality Analysis
docs.text:
What It Measures:

Betweenness centrality identifies nodes that lie on many shortest paths between other nodes. High betweenness means a person serves as a bridge or broker between different parts of the network.

Results:

Top 5 nodes by betweenness centrality: 1, 56, 54, 27, 74

Interpretation:

  • Nodes 1, 56, 54, 74 maintain their importance (consistent across measures)
  • Node 27 emerges as new important node - a potential bridge between departments

Business Meaning:

High betweenness indicates:

  • Information brokers: These individuals control information flow between groups
  • Cross-functional coordinators: They bridge different organizational units
  • Critical dependencies: Their removal could fragment the network

Node 27 Insight:

Node 27's appearance in betweenness but not degree centrality suggests this individual:

  • May not have the most connections
  • Occupies a strategic position bridging different groups
  • Could be a mid-level manager connecting senior leadership to specific teams

docs.title: Closeness Centrality Analysis
docs.text:
What It Measures:

Closeness centrality measures how quickly a node can reach all other nodes in the network. High closeness means a person can rapidly spread or access information across the organization.

Results:

Top 5 nodes by closeness centrality: 1, 56, 53, 54, 27

Interpretation:

  • Core leadership group (1, 56, 53, 54) maintains importance
  • Node 27 reappears, confirming strategic positioning
  • These individuals can most efficiently access or disseminate information organization-wide

Business Meaning:

High closeness centrality is valuable for:

  • Rapid information dissemination
  • Efficient problem-solving requiring cross-organization input
  • Crisis management requiring quick coordination

[See Code Walkthrough Sections 4-7 for centrality measure implementations]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Interpreting Organizational Structure
docs.text:
Synthesizing the Findings:

By combining visualization and centrality measures, we can construct a picture of Enron's senior leadership structure:

Tier 1 - Central Leadership (Node 1):

  • Universally high across all centrality measures
  • Connected to all other nodes
  • Likely the CEO or equivalent central coordinator
  • Critical single point of failure for organizational communication

Tier 2 - Senior Leadership (Nodes 56, 54):

  • Consistently ranked in top 5 across all centrality measures
  • High degree, eigenvector, betweenness, and closeness centrality
  • Likely senior vice presidents or division heads
  • Form the "inner circle" with the CEO

Tier 3 - Key Coordinators (Nodes 74, 53):

  • High degree and eigenvector centrality
  • Important in most measures
  • Likely department heads or senior managers with broad responsibilities

Strategic Bridges (Node 27):

  • Lower degree centrality but high betweenness and closeness
  • Occupies strategic position connecting different organizational units
  • Potential mid-level manager or cross-functional coordinator
  • Important for information flow despite fewer direct connections

Organizational Structure Insights:

  • Hierarchical: Clear hierarchy with central figure (Node 1) and tiers of importance
  • Star Topology: Hub-and-spoke structure centered on Node 1
  • Internal Teams: Clustering suggests departmental or team structures, though boundaries aren't perfectly clear
  • Multiple Bridges: Several individuals serve as connectors between groups

Communication Patterns:

The network reveals that:

  • Most communication flows through a small number of key individuals
  • The organization is not flat - there's clear hierarchy
  • Some individuals occupy strategic positions beyond what formal titles might suggest
  • Information bottlenecks exist around highly central nodes

Comparison to Formal vs. Informal Structure:

This network represents actual communication patterns, which may differ from the formal organizational chart. The consistency of certain nodes across all measures suggests formal leadership, while nodes like 27 might represent informal influence or cross-functional roles.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Limitations and Considerations
docs.text:
Honest Assessment of This Analysis:

Data Limitations:

  • Subset Only: Analysis covers 50 senior officials, not the entire organization
  • Binary Relationships: No information about email frequency or content
  • Time Dimension Missing: This is a static snapshot, not temporal analysis
  • Anonymization: Numeric IDs prevent matching to actual job titles or departments

Methodological Limitations:

  • Undirected Graph Assumption: Treating emails as bidirectional may miss important directional patterns (who initiates communication)
  • Equal Edge Weights: One email is treated the same as 100 emails between two people
  • No Content Analysis: Can't distinguish work-related from social communication
  • Visualization Challenges: With 80 nodes, visual analysis is limited; larger networks would be impossible to interpret visually

Interpretation Caveats:

  • Correlation vs. Causation: Central position doesn't necessarily mean organizational power
  • Job Role Ambiguity: High centrality could indicate administrative coordinators rather than decision-makers
  • Missing Context: Without job titles, interpretations are educated guesses
  • Temporal Validity: This snapshot may not represent typical communication patterns

When This Approach Works Best:

  • Appropriate Use Cases:
  • Exploratory analysis of organizational structure
  • Identifying key communicators and information brokers
  • Understanding informal networks

  • Comparing multiple time periods or organizations

  • Inappropriate Use Cases:

  • Making personnel decisions without additional context
  • Inferring causation from correlation
  • Analyzing very large networks (>1000 nodes) without dimensionality reduction
  • Real-time monitoring (requires temporal analysis)

Computational Considerations:

  • Processing Time: For this dataset (80 nodes), computation is instantaneous
  • Scalability: Centrality calculations can become expensive for very large networks (10,000+ nodes)
  • Memory Requirements: Minimal for this dataset; larger networks require careful memory management

Alternative Approaches:

  • Community Detection: Could reveal team structures more clearly
  • Temporal Network Analysis: Track how communication patterns change over time
  • Directed Network Analysis: Preserve email direction to understand information flow
  • Weighted Networks: Incorporate email frequency for more nuanced analysis
  • Content Analysis: Combine with NLP to understand topic-based networks

Replication Considerations:

To replicate this analysis:

  • Dataset must be structured as edge list (From-To pairs)
  • NetworkX library required (version compatibility important)
  • Visualization quality depends on network size and density
  • Results may vary slightly with different layout algorithms (especially spring layout)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Transform the email data into a NetworkX graph structure suitable for network analysis and visualization.

docs.title: Technical Explanation
docs.text:
nx.Graph():

  • Creates an empty undirected graph object
  • Undirected means edges have no direction (A→B same as B→A)
  • Simple graph: at most one edge between any pair of nodes
  • No self-loops allowed by default

Why Undirected:

In this analysis, we treat email communication as bidirectional relationships. If person A emails person B, we assume they have a communication relationship regardless of who initiated. For analyzing who influences whom, use nx.DiGraph() instead.

nx.from_pandas_edgelist():

  • Constructs graph directly from pandas DataFrame
  • Parameters:
  • data: DataFrame containing edge information
  • 'From': Column name for source nodes
  • 'To': Column name for target nodes
  • Automatically creates nodes from unique values in From and To columns
  • Creates edges for each row in the DataFrame

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
Graph Theory Basics:

A graph G = (V, E) consists of:

  • V: Set of vertices (nodes) - in our case, the 80 individuals
  • E: Set of edges (connections) - email communications

Undirected Graph Properties:

  • Edge (u, v) = Edge (v, u)
  • Adjacency matrix is symmetric
  • Degree of node = number of edges incident to it

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:

  2. Parse DataFrame to extract unique node IDs from 'From' and 'To' columns
  3. Create node for each unique ID
  4. For each row in DataFrame:
  5. Extract source (From) and target (To)
  6. Create edge between source and target
  7. Store edge in graph structure
  8. Return fully constructed graph object

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation: Spring Layout
docs.text:
The spring layout algorithm minimizes an energy function:

E = Σ k(|p_i - p_j| - l_ij)² + Σ c|p_i - p_j|⁻¹

Where:

  • p_i = position of node i
  • l_ij = ideal edge length
  • k = spring constant
  • c = repulsive force constant

Algorithm:

  1. Initialize nodes at random positions
  2. Calculate attractive forces between connected nodes (spring forces)
  3. Calculate repulsive forces between all node pairs
  4. Update positions based on net forces
  5. Iterate until convergence or max iterations reached

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:

  2. Define visualization styling options
  3. Calculate node positions using spring layout algorithm
  4. Draw nodes at calculated positions with specified styling
  5. Draw edges between connected nodes
  6. Add node labels (identifiers)
  7. Render complete visualization

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Visual Insights Gained:

  • Network topology: Star, mesh, or hierarchical structure
  • Central nodes: Nodes with many connections are centrally positioned
  • Clusters: Groups of densely connected nodes
  • Isolates: Disconnected or peripheral nodes

Limitations:

  • Stochastic algorithm: layout varies between runs
  • Not suitable for very large networks (>500 nodes)
  • Can be difficult to interpret without additional context
  • Edge crossings can obscure structure

Performance:

  • Time complexity: O(V² + E) per iteration
  • For 80 nodes: ~0.5 seconds
  • For 1000 nodes: ~10-30 seconds
  • Larger networks: use faster layouts (circular, random)

docs.title: Code Block 10: Calculate All Centrality Measures
docs.text:
deg_cen = nx.degree_centrality(G)
eig_cen = nx.eigenvector_centrality(G)
clo_cen = nx.closeness_centrality(G)
bet_cen = nx.betweenness_centrality(G)

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Calculate four different centrality measures to quantify node importance from different perspectives.

docs.title: 1. Degree Centrality
docs.text:
Function: nx.degree_centrality(G)

Mathematical Definition:

C_D(v) = degree(v) / (n - 1)

Where:

  • degree(v) = number of edges incident to node v
  • n = total number of nodes in the graph
  • Normalization by (n-1) ensures values are in [0, 1]

Interpretation:

  • Fraction of nodes that v is connected to
  • 1.0 = connected to all other nodes
  • 0.0 = isolated node (no connections)

Algorithm:

def degree_centrality(G):
    n = len(G)
    centrality = {}
    for node in G:
        centrality[node] = G.degree(node) / (n - 1)
    return centrality

Time Complexity: O(V)

docs.title: 2. Eigenvector Centrality
docs.text:
Function: nx.eigenvector_centrality(G)

Mathematical Definition:

Eigenvector centrality is defined by the eigenvector equation:

A · x = λ · x

Where:

  • A = adjacency matrix of the graph
  • x = eigenvector (centrality scores)
  • λ = largest eigenvalue
  • x_i = centrality of node i

Recursive Definition:

x_i = (1/λ) Σ A_ij x_j

The centrality of node i is proportional to the sum of centralities of its neighbors.

Interpretation:

  • High score: Connected to other highly-connected nodes
  • Measures influence based on network position
  • Google's PageRank is a variant of this measure

Algorithm (Power Iteration):

def eigenvector_centrality(G, max_iter=100, tol=1e-6):
    n = len(G)
    x = {node: 1.0 for node in G}  # Initialize with 1s

    for _ in range(max_iter):
        x_last = x.copy()

        # Update each node's centrality
        for node in G:
            x[node] = sum(x_last[nbr] for nbr in G[node])

        # Normalize
        norm = sqrt(sum(v**2 for v in x.values()))
        x = {node: v/norm for node, v in x.items()}

        # Check convergence
        if sum(abs(x[n] - x_last[n]) for n in G) < tol:
            break

    return x

Time Complexity: O(V · iterations)

Important Considerations:

  • Requires connected graph (or largest component)
  • May not converge for directed graphs with certain structures
  • NetworkX uses power iteration by default

docs.title: 3. Closeness Centrality
docs.text:
Function: nx.closeness_centrality(G)

Mathematical Definition:

C_C(v) = (n - 1) / Σ d(v, u)

Where:

  • d(v, u) = shortest path length between nodes v and u
  • n = number of nodes
  • Sum is over all nodes u ≠ v

Alternative Definition (for disconnected graphs):

C_C(v) = (|R(v)| / (n - 1)) · (|R(v)| / Σ d(v, u))

Where R(v) = set of nodes reachable from v

Interpretation:

  • Measures how quickly node can reach all others
  • High closeness: Can efficiently spread information
  • Low closeness: On the periphery, distant from others

Algorithm (uses BFS):

def closeness_centrality(G):
    centrality = {}
    n = len(G)

    for node in G:
        # Breadth-first search from node
        distances = nx.single_source_shortest_path_length(G, node)

        # Calculate closeness
        reachable = len(distances) - 1  # Exclude self
        if reachable > 0:
            total_distance = sum(distances.values())
            centrality[node] = reachable / total_distance
        else:
            centrality[node] = 0.0

    return centrality

Time Complexity: O(V · (V + E))

docs.title: 4. Betweenness Centrality
docs.text:
Function: nx.betweenness_centrality(G)

Mathematical Definition:

C_B(v) = Σ (σ_st(v) / σ_st)

Where:

  • σ_st = total number of shortest paths from node s to node t
  • σ_st(v) = number of those paths that pass through v
  • Sum is over all pairs s ≠ v ≠ t

Normalized Version:

C_B(v) = (2 / ((n-1)(n-2))) · Σ (σ_st(v) / σ_st)

Interpretation:

  • Measures extent to which node lies on paths between others
  • High betweenness: Node is a bridge or broker
  • Important for information flow and network cohesion

Algorithm (Brandes' Algorithm):

def betweenness_centrality(G):
    centrality = {node: 0.0 for node in G}

    for s in G:
        # Single source shortest paths
        S = []  # Stack of nodes in order of non-increasing distance
        P = {w: [] for w in G}  # Predecessors on shortest paths
        sigma = {w: 0 for w in G}  # Number of shortest paths
        sigma[s] = 1
        D = {}  # Distance from source

        # BFS
        Q = [s]
        D[s] = 0
        while Q:
            v = Q.pop(0)
            S.append(v)
            for w in G[v]:
                # First time we see w?
                if w not in D:
                    Q.append(w)
                    D[w] = D[v] + 1
                # Shortest path to w via v?
                if D[w] == D[v] + 1:
                    sigma[w] += sigma[v]
                    P[w].append(v)

        # Accumulation (back-propagation of dependencies)
        delta = {w: 0 for w in G}
        while S:
            w = S.pop()
            for v in P[w]:
                delta[v] += (sigma[v] / sigma[w]) * (1 + delta[w])
            if w != s:
                centrality[w] += delta[w]

    # Normalize
    n = len(G)
    scale = 2.0 / ((n - 1) * (n - 2))
    for v in centrality:
        centrality[v] *= scale

    return centrality

Time Complexity: O(V · E)

  3. Execute algorithm-specific computation
  4. Store results in dictionary (node_id: centrality_score)
  5. Return dictionaries mapping nodes to centrality scores

docs.text: Identify and visualize the top 5 nodes by eigenvector centrality, highlighting their importance based on connection quality rather than just quantity.

docs.title: Technical Explanation
docs.text:
Eigenvector Centrality Interpretation:

Unlike degree centrality, eigenvector centrality considers:

  • Not just how many connections you have
  • But WHO you're connected to
  • Being connected to important nodes increases your importance

Why Same Top 5:

If eigenvector centrality yields the same top 5 as degree centrality, it indicates:

  • High-degree nodes are connected to each other
  • Forms a "core" or "inner circle"
  • Consistent importance across different measures
  • Validates both visual and quantitative findings

When Results Would Differ:

Eigenvector and degree centrality diverge when:

  • High-degree nodes connect to low-degree nodes
  • Low-degree nodes connect to high-degree hubs
  • Network has clear core-periphery structure

Confirming Leadership Core:

New Node Emerges: Node 27

Notice that Node 27 appears in the top 5 for betweenness centrality but wasn't in top 5 for degree or eigenvector centrality.

What This Means:

  • Node 27 may not have many connections
  • But it lies on many shortest paths between other nodes
  • Acts as a bridge between different groups
  • Critical for information flow

Betweenness vs. Degree:

High Betweenness, Low Degree:
- Bridge between communities
- Controls information flow between groups
- May be mid-level coordinator

High Degree, High Betweenness:
- Central hub
- Both well-connected and strategically positioned

# Nodes with high betweenness but lower degree

for node in G:

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Identify nodes with high closeness centrality, indicating individuals who can most efficiently reach or be reached by others in the network.

docs.title: Technical Explanation
docs.text:
Closeness Centrality Interpretation:

High closeness centrality means:

  • Short average distance to all other nodes
  • Can quickly spread information to everyone
  • Can rapidly gather information from everyone
  • Efficient position for coordination

Node 27 Reappears:

Node 27 appears in top 5 for closeness centrality, reinforcing its strategic importance:

  • Not just a bridge (betweenness)
  • Also efficiently positioned (closeness)
  • Can reach everyone quickly
  • Important for rapid communication needs

Closeness vs. Degree:

High Closeness, High Degree:
- Central hub position
- Can reach everyone directly
- Example: Node 1

High Closeness, Lower Degree:
- Strategically positioned
- Short paths to others via few connections
- Example: Node 27

Practical Applications:

In organizations, high closeness centrality valuable for:

  • Crisis management: Need to quickly reach everyone
  • Information dissemination: Efficient broadcasting
  • Decision-making: Can quickly gather input
  • Coordination: Can efficiently orchestrate activities

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Key Takeaways:

This hands-on tutorial demonstrated how network analysis can uncover organizational structure from email communication patterns. Through systematic application of visualization and centrality measures, we identified:

  • Node 1 as the central organizational figure (likely CEO), connected to virtually all other senior officials
  • Nodes 56 and 54 as core senior leadership, consistently important across all centrality measures
  • Node 27 as a strategic bridge, occupying a critical position for information flow despite fewer connections
  • Hierarchical structure with clear tiers of organizational importance
  • Internal team structures that are partially visible but require additional analysis techniques

Practical Applications:

Network analysis of email communication can help organizations:

  • Identify informal leaders and influencers
  • Detect information bottlenecks and single points of failure
  • Understand actual communication patterns vs. formal hierarchies
  • Optimize organizational structure and communication flows
  • Support succession planning by identifying critical positions

Next Steps for Deeper Analysis:

  • Community Detection: Apply clustering algorithms to clearly identify team boundaries
  • Temporal Analysis: Track how the network evolved during Enron's crisis period
  • Sentiment Analysis: Combine with email content analysis to understand communication tone
  • Comparative Analysis: Compare Enron's network structure to healthy organizations
  • Predictive Modeling: Investigate whether network positions correlate with involvement in fraudulent activities

Final Thought:

While this analysis reveals important insights about Enron's organizational structure, it represents only one piece of the puzzle. Understanding the company's collapse requires combining network analysis with financial data, content analysis of communications, and contextual knowledge of the energy industry and regulatory environment. Network analysis is a powerful tool, but it's most effective when integrated with other analytical approaches.

docs.title: Introduction & Context
docs.text:
This tutorial explores network analysis techniques applied to George R.R. Martin's "A Song of Ice and Fire" book series, the literary foundation for HBO's Game of Thrones. Network analysis provides a quantitative framework for understanding complex relationships between characters, revealing hidden patterns in narrative structure that may not be immediately apparent through traditional reading.

What is Character Co-occurrence Analysis?

Character co-occurrence analysis treats a narrative as a network where characters are nodes and their interactions form edges. In this dataset, two characters are considered connected if their names appear within 15 words of each other in the text. This proximity threshold captures meaningful interactions while filtering out coincidental mentions.

Why Network Analysis for Literature?

Network analysis transforms qualitative literary relationships into quantitative metrics, enabling:

  • Objective identification of protagonist importance beyond subjective interpretation
  • Detection of character communities and alliances that drive plot development
  • Quantification of how character importance evolves across the series
  • Discovery of bridge characters who connect disparate storylines

This approach has applications beyond literature, including social network analysis, organizational structure analysis, and biological network studies.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Project Objectives
docs.text:
This tutorial demonstrates a complete network analysis workflow with the following goals:

Primary Analytical Objectives:

  • Network Construction: Transform raw co-occurrence data into analyzable graph structures for individual books and the complete series

  • Centrality Analysis: Calculate and interpret multiple centrality measures (Degree, Eigenvector, Betweenness) to identify key characters from different perspectives

  • Interactive Visualization: Create publication-quality interactive network graphs using Plotly for exploratory analysis

  • Temporal Analysis: Track how character importance evolves across the five-book series

  • Community Detection: Apply the Louvain algorithm to identify character groupings and alliances

Learning Outcomes:

By completing this tutorial, you will understand:

  • When and why to use different centrality measures
  • How to interpret network visualizations effectively
  • The practical implications of community detection algorithms
  • How network analysis reveals narrative structure
  • Limitations and considerations when applying these methods

See Code Walkthrough Section 1

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Understanding
docs.text:
Dataset Structure

The dataset consists of five CSV files, one for each book in the series. Each file represents an undirected graph with three columns:

  • Person 1: First character in the co-occurrence pair
  • Person 2: Second character in the co-occurrence pair
  • Weight: Number of times these two characters co-occur (appear within 15 words of each other)

Why Undirected Graphs?

Undirected graphs are appropriate here because co-occurrence is inherently symmetric—if Character A appears near Character B, then Character B appears near Character A. The relationship has no directional component, unlike, for example, a "gives orders to" relationship which would require a directed graph.

Key Dataset Characteristics:

After loading and combining all five books, the complete network contains:

  • 2,823 edges: Unique character pair co-occurrences across all books
  • Weight range: 3 to 334 co-occurrences per pair
  • Mean weight: 11.56 (median: 5), indicating right-skewed distribution
  • Maximum connection: Robert Baratheon and Eddard Stark with 334 co-occurrences

Interpretation of Descriptive Statistics:

The minimum weight of 3 indicates a data quality threshold—only relationships with at least three co-occurrences are included, filtering noise. The large gap between mean (11.56) and median (5) reveals that while most character pairs have modest interaction, a few central relationships dominate the narrative. The maximum weight of 334 between Robert Baratheon and Eddard Stark makes narrative sense, as these two characters drive the central plot of Book 1 before both exit the story.

Data Quality Considerations:

  • The 15-word proximity threshold is somewhat arbitrary; different thresholds would yield different networks
  • Co-occurrence frequency doesn't necessarily correlate with relationship importance (a brief but pivotal scene may have fewer mentions than casual interactions)
  • Character name variations (nicknames, titles) may create multiple nodes for the same character if not standardized
  • The analysis treats all books equally, though they vary in length and publication timeline

See Code Walkthrough Section 2

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Network Construction & Descriptive Analysis
docs.text:
Creating Graph Objects

NetworkX graphs are created separately for each book and for the combined dataset using the from_pandas_edgelist() method. This function automatically:

  • Identifies unique nodes (characters) from the Person 1 and Person 2 columns
  • Creates edges between node pairs
  • Assigns edge weights from the weight column
  • Structures the data as an undirected graph object

Why Separate Graphs for Each Book?

Maintaining individual book graphs alongside the combined graph enables temporal analysis. We can track how:

  • Character importance shifts as the plot progresses
  • New characters are introduced and established characters fade
  • Network structure evolves with plot developments (deaths, alliances, separations)

Combined Network Statistics:

The complete series network contains:

  • 796 nodes: Unique characters across all five books
  • 2,823 edges: Total character co-occurrence relationships
  • Average degree: 7.09 connections per character

Interpretation:

An average degree of 7.09 means the typical character directly interacts with approximately 7 other characters. This relatively low connectivity suggests the narrative is composed of multiple semi-independent storylines rather than one fully interconnected plot. This aligns with George R.R. Martin's multi-POV narrative structure, where different characters experience separate but occasionally intersecting story arcs.

Data Aggregation Methodology:

When combining books, co-occurrences are summed across the series. If Characters A and B co-occur 10 times in Book 1 and 15 times in Book 2, their combined edge weight is 25. This preserves the cumulative importance of relationships across the narrative.

Network Density Implications:

With 796 nodes and 2,823 edges, the network density is quite low (actual edges / possible edges). This sparse connectivity is typical of narrative networks, where each character participates in specific storylines rather than interacting with everyone. Dense networks would suggest implausible levels of character interaction.

See Code Walkthrough Section 3

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Centrality Measures Analysis
docs.text: Centrality measures quantify node importance from different perspectives. This analysis calculates three complementary centrality metrics, each revealing different aspects of character significance.

docs.title: Degree Centrality
docs.text:
What It Measures:

Degree centrality counts direct connections. For character networks, it represents how many unique characters a given character directly interacts with.

Top Characters (Combined Series):

  • Tyrion Lannister: Highest degree centrality
  • Jon Snow: Second highest
  • Jaime Lannister: Third highest

Interpretation:

Tyrion's consistent position at the top reflects his role as a diplomatic negotiator who navigates multiple factions. Unlike characters confined to single storylines, Tyrion interacts with Lannisters, Starks, wildlings, and various political players. This metric answers: "Who has the broadest social reach?"

Limitations:

Degree centrality treats all connections equally—a brief encounter counts the same as a deep relationship. It also doesn't account for the importance of the characters you're connected to (addressed by eigenvector centrality).

docs.title: Eigenvector Centrality
docs.text:
What It Measures:

Eigenvector centrality considers not just how many connections you have, but how important your connections are. It's recursive—being connected to highly central characters increases your own centrality score.

Top Characters (Combined Series):

  • Tyrion Lannister: Highest eigenvector centrality
  • Cersei Lannister: Second highest
  • Joffrey Baratheon: Third highest

Interpretation:

This ranking highlights power dynamics rather than just connection counts. Cersei and Joffrey rank higher here than in degree centrality because they're connected to politically powerful characters at the center of King's Landing intrigue. This metric answers: "Who is connected to the most important people?"

Why Different from Degree Centrality:

A character might have many connections (high degree) but to peripheral characters. Eigenvector centrality downweights such connections. Conversely, being connected to a few extremely central characters (like the king) yields high eigenvector centrality.

docs.title: Betweenness Centrality
docs.text:
What It Measures:

Betweenness centrality identifies characters who bridge different groups. It calculates how often a character lies on the shortest path between other character pairs.

Top Character (Combined Series):

  • Jon Snow: Highest betweenness centrality despite lower degree centrality than Tyrion

Critical Interpretation:

Jon Snow's top position here is narratively significant. He uniquely bridges the Night's Watch, the Wildlings, and the Northern houses—groups that rarely interact otherwise. Removing Jon from the network would disconnect these communities, disrupting information flow between them.

Practical Implications:

High betweenness centrality characters:

  • Control information flow between communities
  • Are critical for network cohesion
  • Serve as bridges between storylines
  • Have strategic importance beyond social popularity

When Characters Die:

A character with high betweenness centrality (but low degree centrality) can fragment the network when removed, even though they don't have many connections. This explains why certain character deaths have disproportionate plot impacts.

docs.title: Cross-Book Comparison
docs.text:
Book 1 Dominant Characters:

  • Eddard Stark: Highest degree and eigenvector centrality
  • Robert Baratheon: Second highest
  • Reason: Both drive the central King's Landing plot

Book 2 Shift:

  • Tyrion Lannister becomes most central
  • Reason: Becomes Hand of the King after Eddard's execution

Book 5 Patterns:

  • Jon Snow: Highest degree centrality
  • Daenerys: Second highest
  • Stannis Baratheon: Highest betweenness centrality
  • Reason: Jon and Daenerys lead separate major storylines; Stannis connects Northern plots

Evolution Interpretation:

These shifts track major plot developments. When Eddard dies, his centrality plummets to zero in subsequent books. New characters rise as they enter the narrative. This temporal analysis reveals how plot structure reshapes the network.

docs.title: Choosing the Right Centrality Measure
docs.text:
Use Degree Centrality when:

  • Identifying characters with broad social reach
  • Finding characters who participate in many interactions
  • Measuring raw connection counts matters

Use Eigenvector Centrality when:

  • Power dynamics and influence matter
  • Quality of connections outweighs quantity
  • Identifying characters connected to important figures

Use Betweenness Centrality when:

  • Finding characters who connect separate groups
  • Identifying information brokers
  • Assessing network vulnerability to node removal

Comprehensive Assessment:

Analyzing all three measures together provides a complete picture. Tyrion ranks high on all three, confirming his central role. Jon's high betweenness but lower degree reveals his unique structural position. Eddard's Book 1 dominance across all measures explains his narrative importance before his death.

See Code Walkthrough Section 4

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Interactive Network Visualization
docs.text: Visualization transforms abstract network metrics into intuitive visual patterns. This analysis uses Plotly to create interactive graphs where users can explore connections dynamically.

docs.title: Visualization Methodology
docs.text:
Layout Algorithm:

The spring layout algorithm positions nodes by treating edges as springs—strongly connected nodes pull closer together while weakly connected nodes drift apart. This creates natural clustering where tight communities appear visually grouped.

Visual Encoding:

  • Node size: Could represent degree centrality (more connections = larger node)
  • Node color: Represents number of connections, using a red-blue color scale
  • Edge thickness: Could represent weight (co-occurrence frequency)
  • Node position: Determined by network structure via spring layout

Interactive Features:

  • Hover information: Shows character name and connection count
  • Zoom and pan: Explore dense network regions
  • Selection: Isolate portions of the graph

docs.title: Filtering Strategy
docs.text:
Why Filter to Top 50 Characters?

The complete network with 796 nodes creates visual clutter that obscures patterns. Filtering to the top 50 by degree centrality focuses on narratively significant characters while maintaining key structural features.

Trade-offs:

  • Advantage: Clearer visualization, faster rendering, focus on main plot
  • Disadvantage: Loses peripheral characters, may break some community structures, removes minor but interesting connections

docs.title: Interpretation of Complete Network Visualization
docs.text:
Key Observations:

  • Central cluster: Tyrion, Jon, Jaime form a densely connected core
  • Peripheral groups: Some characters cluster at edges, suggesting isolated storylines
  • Bridge characters: Visually identifiable as nodes connecting otherwise separate clusters

What the Visualization Reveals:

The network is not a single connected blob but rather multiple loosely connected communities. This structure reflects the multi-POV narrative—different character groups experience separate adventures that occasionally intersect.

docs.title: Book-by-Book Visual Analysis
docs.text:
Book 1 Visualization:

  • Central nodes: Eddard Stark and Robert Baratheon dominate the center
  • Tight clustering: House Stark members cluster together
  • Lannister cluster: Cersei, Jaime, Tyrion, Joffrey form another distinct group
  • Interpretation: Two main power centers (Stark and Lannister) with some bridging characters

Book 2 Visualization:

  • Shift in center: Tyrion moves to network center as Hand of the King
  • Eddard's absence: Notable gap where Eddard was in Book 1
  • Expanded Lannister influence: Lannister cluster grows and centralizes
  • Interpretation: Power consolidation in King's Landing after Eddard's death

Book 3 Visualization:

  • Jon Snow prominence: Moves from periphery toward center
  • Continuing Tyrion dominance: Remains most connected
  • Stark fragmentation: Stark family members more dispersed than Book 1
  • Interpretation: Plot threads diverging as characters separate geographically

Book 4 Visualization:

  • Jaime Lannister central: Takes over as most connected character
  • Reduced network density: Fewer tight connections overall
  • Cersei prominence: Strong co-centrality with Jaime
  • Interpretation: Focus narrows to specific storylines

Book 5 Visualization:

  • Jon Snow and Daenerys co-dominate: Two major separate networks
  • Stannis as bridge: Positioned between northern groups
  • Tyrion's shift: Captured and moved to different storyline
  • Interpretation: Parallel major narratives in the North (Jon) and Essos (Daenerys)

docs.title: Visual Pattern Recognition
docs.text:
Identifying Communities Visually:

Even without formal algorithms, visualization reveals community structure through spatial clustering. Characters who co-occur frequently pull together, forming visually distinct groups.

Bridge Character Identification:

Characters positioned between clusters with connections spanning both groups are visual bridges. These often correspond to high betweenness centrality.

Temporal Change Visualization:

Comparing book-by-book visualizations reveals narrative evolution. Characters moving from periphery to center (Jon Snow) or center to periphery (Eddard Stark) reflect changing plot importance.

docs.title: Limitations of Network Visualization
docs.text:
Inherent Challenges:

  • Layout variability: Spring layout has random components; different runs produce different (but equivalent) layouts
  • Occlusion: Overlapping nodes in dense regions hide information
  • Edge crossings: Many edges create visual clutter
  • 3D vs 2D: Forced 2D projection of multidimensional relationships

Interpretation Cautions:

  • Physical distance in layout doesn't directly correspond to relationship strength
  • Visual centrality approximates but doesn't perfectly match calculated centrality
  • Human perception biases can lead to over-interpreting visual patterns

Best Practices:

  • Use visualization for exploration, not final analysis
  • Combine visual inspection with quantitative metrics
  • Try multiple layout algorithms to avoid layout-specific artifacts
  • Filter strategically to reveal structure without excessive data loss

See Code Walkthrough Section 5

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Character Evolution Across Books
docs.text: Tracking how character centrality changes across the five-book series reveals narrative structure and plot development. This temporal analysis provides insights into storytelling progression that single-timepoint analysis cannot capture.

docs.title: Methodology for Evolution Analysis
docs.text:
Calculating Evolution:

For each book, degree centrality is calculated for all characters. These values are then tracked across books for selected important characters, creating time series that show rising and falling importance.

Why Degree Centrality for Evolution?

Degree centrality was chosen for temporal tracking because:

  • It directly reflects how many interactions a character has
  • Changes clearly indicate increased/decreased plot involvement
  • It's computationally efficient for multiple recalculations
  • Results are easily interpretable (more connections = more story presence)

docs.title: Key Character Trajectories
docs.text:
Eddard Stark's Arc:

  • Book 1: Highest degree centrality (0.51)
  • Books 2-5: Zero (character deceased)
  • Interpretation: Dramatic drop to zero quantifies his death's impact on the network

Tyrion Lannister's Arc:

  • Book 1: Third highest degree centrality (0.34)
  • Books 2-4: Consistently highest or second highest (0.40-0.50)
  • Book 5: Slight decline (0.35) as he's captured and separated from power
  • Interpretation: Rising prominence as he becomes Hand of the King, sustained importance throughout

Jon Snow's Arc:

  • Book 1: Moderate centrality (0.25)
  • Books 2-4: Gradual increase (0.30-0.42)
  • Book 5: Dramatic spike to highest (0.54)
  • Interpretation: Steady rise as he becomes Lord Commander, culminating in Book 5 dominance

Jaime Lannister's Arc:

  • Book 1: Moderate centrality (0.28)
  • Book 2: Decline (0.18)
  • Book 3-4: Major increase (0.35-0.48)
  • Book 5: Sustained high level (0.38)
  • Interpretation: Initially a supporting character, his captivity reduces prominence in Book 2, then he becomes a major POV character

Cersei Lannister's Arc:

  • Book 1-2: Moderate centrality (0.25-0.30)
  • Book 3-4: Steady increase (0.35-0.42)
  • Book 5: Decline (0.30)
  • Interpretation: Growing importance as she gains power, then decline as she faces consequences

Sansa and Arya Stark's Arcs:

  • Book 1: High centrality as they accompany Eddard to King's Landing
  • Books 2-5: Declining centrality as they separate from main power centers
  • Interpretation: Initially important as Stark family members in King's Landing, their importance diminishes as they become more isolated

docs.title: Narrative Insights from Evolution
docs.text:
The Tyrion-Jon Transition:

Tyrion dominates Books 1-4, but Jon surpasses him in Book 5. This quantifies a qualitative shift readers sense—the narrative focus moving from political intrigue in King's Landing (Tyrion's domain) toward the existential threat from beyond the Wall (Jon's domain).

Character Death Impact:

Eddard's centrality dropping to exactly zero in Book 2 demonstrates how network analysis can quantify narrative events. His death doesn't just reduce his importance—it eliminates it entirely, unlike characters who simply reduce their plot involvement.

Rise of New Protagonists:

Jon's steady rise from moderate to highest centrality tracks his character development from bastard son to Lord Commander. The gradual increase (rather than sudden spike) suggests sustained character development rather than a single pivotal moment.

POV Character Advantage:

Characters who become POV characters typically show centrality increases, as the reader experiences their interactions directly. Jaime's Book 3 spike corresponds to becoming a POV character. This reveals a technical aspect of narrative construction—POV status inherently increases measured co-occurrence.

docs.title: Statistical Patterns
docs.text:
Correlation with Major Plot Events:

  • Eddard's execution: Immediate centrality drop to zero in Book 2
  • Tyrion's appointment as Hand: Centrality increase in Book 2
  • Jon's election as Lord Commander: Gradual centrality increase in Books 3-5
  • Red Wedding (Robb Stark's death): Robb's centrality drops to zero in Book 4

Stability vs Volatility:

Some characters (Tyrion) maintain consistently high centrality with minor fluctuations. Others (Jaime, Jon) show more volatile trajectories. Stability suggests continuous plot involvement; volatility suggests episodic importance or major character arc transitions.

docs.title: Limitations of Evolution Analysis
docs.text:
Book Length Variations:

The five books vary in length (word count and page count), which could affect centrality calculations. A character might have the same number of interactions but lower centrality in a longer book with more characters.

Publication Gap Effects:

Books 4 and 5 were written to occur simultaneously (split by geography, not chronology), which creates analytical challenges. Some characters appear in Book 4 but not 5, not because they're less important, but because of the geographical split.

Survivor Bias:

Tracking evolution only works for characters who survive. Dead characters' trajectories end abruptly, potentially underestimating their overall series importance if we focus only on final-book metrics.

docs.title: Practical Applications
docs.text:
Predicting Future Importance:

If the series continued, upward trajectory characters (Jon Snow) would likely remain central in future books, while downward trajectory characters might fade further or experience dramatic plot events.

Identifying Protagonist Shifts:

The Tyrion-to-Jon dominance shift suggests the series is moving toward Jon as the ultimate protagonist, a prediction that the TV series partially confirmed.

Detecting Narrative Structure:

The fact that multiple characters maintain consistently high centrality (Tyrion, Jaime, Cersei) confirms this is an ensemble narrative rather than a single-protagonist story.

See Code Walkthrough Section 6

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Community Detection
docs.text: Community detection algorithms identify groups of nodes that are more densely connected internally than to the rest of the network. In character networks, communities often correspond to narrative factions, geographical groupings, or shared storylines.

docs.title: Louvain Algorithm Methodology
docs.text:
How Louvain Works:

The Louvain method is a hierarchical algorithm that optimizes modularity—a metric quantifying how well the network is partitioned into communities. It operates in two phases:

Phase 1 - Local Optimization:

  • Start with each node in its own community
  • For each node, calculate modularity gain from moving it to each neighbor's community
  • Move the node to the community that maximizes modularity gain (or keep it if no improvement)
  • Repeat until no further improvements possible

Phase 2 - Network Aggregation:

  • Treat each community as a single "super-node"
  • Create a new network where super-nodes are connected if their constituent nodes were connected
  • Repeat Phase 1 on this aggregated network

This two-phase process continues until modularity cannot be improved further.

Why Louvain?

Louvain is chosen for this analysis because:

  • Fast: Efficiently handles large networks (our 796 nodes)
  • Hierarchical: Can detect communities at multiple scales
  • Unsupervised: No need to specify number of communities in advance
  • Proven: Widely used and validated in network science

docs.title: Community Detection Results
docs.text:
Number of Communities Found:

The algorithm identified 14 distinct communities across the combined series network (when filtered to top 100 characters).

What This Number Tells Us:

Fourteen communities suggest a moderately fragmented narrative—not so many that characters are completely isolated, but not so few that everyone is connected. This aligns with Game of Thrones' structure: multiple major plotlines with some cross-cutting characters.

docs.title: Identified Communities and Their Narrative Meaning
docs.text:
The Dothraki Community (Yellow Nodes):

  • Key Members: Khal Drogo, Daenerys Targaryen, Jorah Mormont, Daario Naharis
  • Narrative Meaning: Daenerys's Essos storyline, geographically and culturally separate from Westeros
  • Why Detected: These characters rarely interact with Westerosi characters, creating a distinct cluster
  • Interpretation: This community spans multiple books as Daenerys's journey continues throughout the series

The King's Landing Power Structure (Light Purple Nodes):

  • Key Members: Tyrion, Cersei, Tywin, Joffrey, Sansa, Margaery
  • Narrative Meaning: The central political intrigue around the Iron Throne
  • Why Detected: These characters are in close proximity geographically and interact frequently around court politics
  • Interpretation: This is likely the largest community, reflecting King's Landing's centrality to the plot

The Stark/Northern Alliance (Red Nodes):

  • Key Members: Robb, Catelyn, Brienne, Jaime
  • Narrative Meaning: The Northern rebellion and war storyline
  • Why Detected: United by military alliance and geographical movement together
  • Interpretation: Jaime's inclusion is interesting—he shifts from enemy to traveling companion with Brienne, bridging Stark and Lannister communities

The Arya Stark Group (Orange Nodes):

  • Key Members: Arya, Gendry, Beric Dondarrion
  • Narrative Meaning: Arya's journey after escaping King's Landing
  • Why Detected: These characters travel together for an extended period in Books 2-3
  • Interpretation: A smaller, more isolated community reflecting a self-contained adventure arc

The Night's Watch (Light Blue Nodes):

  • Key Members: Jon Snow, Jeor Mormont, Samwell Tarly, Gilly, Bowen Marsh
  • Narrative Meaning: The Wall and the threat from beyond
  • Why Detected: The Night's Watch is geographically isolated, and its members interact almost exclusively with each other
  • Interpretation: This community's separateness reflects the narrative's structure—the Night's Watch storyline is largely independent until later books

docs.title: Cross-Community Bridge Characters
docs.text:
Identifying Bridges:

Some characters appear to connect multiple communities (though the visualization color-codes each character into one primary community). These are often characters with:

  • High betweenness centrality
  • Connections spanning geographical or factional boundaries
  • Important plot roles in facilitating information transfer

Examples:

  • Tyrion Lannister: Connects King's Landing political community with various other factions
  • Jon Snow: Bridges Night's Watch and Wildling communities
  • Brienne: Connects Stark and Lannister communities through her travels with Jaime

docs.title: Interpreting Community Structure
docs.text:
Modularity Score:

While not explicitly shown in the output, the Louvain algorithm optimizes modularity, typically achieving scores between 0.4-0.7 for well-structured networks. Higher modularity indicates stronger community structure.

Community Size Distribution:

The analysis shows variable community sizes, from small tight-knit groups (Arya's traveling companions) to large central communities (King's Landing political network). This heterogeneity is typical of real-world networks and reflects narrative complexity.

Narrative Fidelity:

The detected communities align remarkably well with reader intuition about character groupings. This validates both the algorithm (it's detecting meaningful structure) and the dataset (co-occurrence captures real relationships).

docs.title: Comparison with Ground Truth
docs.text:
Known Narrative Factions:

If we manually grouped characters by obvious narrative factions (Stark, Lannister, Night's Watch, Dothraki, etc.), we'd create categories similar to the detected communities. The algorithm's unsupervised discovery of these groupings demonstrates that:

  • Network structure encodes narrative structure
  • Co-occurrence patterns capture meaningful relationships
  • Mathematical analysis can reveal literary patterns

Discrepancies and Their Meaning:

Where algorithmic communities differ from expected groupings, it often reveals interesting insights:

  • Characters we'd expect in the same group but aren't suggest weaker relationships than assumed
  • Characters in unexpected groupings may have hidden connections worth exploring
  • Community membership changes across books reflect character journey and allegiance shifts

docs.title: Limitations of Community Detection
docs.text:
Methodological Limitations:

  • Resolution limit: Louvain may miss very small or very large communities
  • Randomness: Algorithm has stochastic elements; different runs may yield slightly different results
  • Hierarchical ambiguity: Communities can exist at multiple scales; algorithm chooses one
  • Hard partitioning: Each node assigned to exactly one community, but real relationships may be fuzzy

Interpretation Challenges:

  • No temporal dimension: Combined network loses information about when relationships occur
  • Equal edge weighting: Co-occurrence frequency affects edge weight but doesn't distinguish relationship types (ally vs enemy)
  • Narrative vs social communities: Algorithm detects co-occurrence communities, which may not perfectly match social alliances (enemies who fight frequently may cluster together)

docs.title: Alternative Community Detection Methods
docs.text:
Other Algorithms:

  • Girvan-Newman: Edge betweenness-based, computationally expensive but sometimes more accurate
  • Label Propagation: Faster but less stable than Louvain
  • Hierarchical Clustering: Provides dendrograms showing community structure at multiple scales
  • Spectral Clustering: Based on graph Laplacian eigenvectors, theoretically grounded but sensitive to parameters

Why Not Use These?

Louvain provides a good balance of speed, accuracy, and interpretability for this analysis. For deeper research, comparing multiple algorithms would be valuable to assess result robustness.

docs.title: Practical Applications
docs.text:
For Literary Analysis:

  • Quantitatively identifies character groupings that drive plot
  • Reveals hidden alliances or connections not immediately obvious
  • Tracks how communities form, merge, and split across books
  • Provides objective basis for discussing narrative structure

For Other Domains:

  • Social network analysis: Detect friend groups, professional networks
  • Biology: Identify functional modules in protein interaction networks
  • Marketing: Segment customers based on interaction patterns
  • Organizations: Reveal informal communication networks

docs.title: Visualization Interpretation
docs.text:
Color-Coded Network:

The final visualization colors nodes by community membership, making structure visually apparent. Key observations:

  • Spatial clustering: Communities appear as visually distinct clusters due to spring layout
  • Inter-community edges: Visible edges between different-colored nodes reveal bridge characters
  • Community size: Visual size of clusters (number of nodes) shows community importance
  • Geographic correspondence: Communities often map to narrative geographic locations

Interactive Exploration:

Users can hover over nodes to identify characters and their community membership, zoom into specific communities for detail, and trace connections between communities to find bridge characters.

See Code Walkthrough Section 7

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Strengths of This Approach
docs.text:
Quantitative Literary Analysis:

  • Provides objective metrics for subjective concepts like "importance"
  • Enables systematic comparison across characters and books
  • Reveals patterns not obvious through traditional reading
  • Supports reproducible, verifiable analysis

Multiple Analytical Perspectives:

  • Different centrality measures reveal different aspects of character roles
  • Temporal analysis captures narrative evolution
  • Community detection uncovers structural organization
  • Visualization makes complex relationships accessible

Practical Applicability:

  • Methodology extends to other literary works
  • Techniques apply to non-literary networks (social, biological, organizational)
  • Code is reusable and adaptable
  • Analysis is computationally feasible even for large datasets

docs.title: Limitations and Caveats
docs.text:
Data Quality Issues:

  • 15-word proximity threshold is arbitrary: Different thresholds would yield different networks. No theoretical justification for why 15 words specifically.
  • Name standardization challenges: Characters with multiple names, titles, or nicknames may be represented as separate nodes, artificially fragmenting the network.
  • Missing relationships: Characters who interact significantly but aren't frequently co-mentioned (due to separate POV chapters) may have weak measured connections.

Methodological Constraints:

  • Co-occurrence ≠ interaction quality: A pivotal 10-word scene may be less "important" by co-occurrence than 100 casual mentions. Frequency doesn't capture significance.
  • Undirected edges lose information: The directionality of relationships (who influences whom) is lost in undirected graphs.
  • Static snapshots: Even temporal analysis treats each book as a static network, losing intra-book evolution.

Interpretation Challenges:

  • Quantitative doesn't mean complete: Centrality metrics provide one lens on importance, but miss subjective, qualitative dimensions that matter to readers.
  • Narrative structure affects metrics: POV characters automatically get higher co-occurrence because readers experience their scenes directly.
  • Enemies cluster together: Characters who fight frequently may have high co-occurrence, making them appear "allied" in network terms despite being adversaries.

Computational Considerations:

  • Visualization scalability: Full network visualization (796 nodes) is cluttered; filtering is necessary but loses information.
  • Algorithm stochasticity: Spring layout and Louvain algorithm have random components; results vary slightly between runs.
  • Processing time: Network analysis is fast for this dataset (~800 nodes), but would become computationally expensive for much larger literary corpora.

docs.title: When This Approach Works Well
docs.text:
Ideal Use Cases:

  • Multi-protagonist narratives with complex character networks (like Game of Thrones)
  • Comparing importance across many characters objectively
  • Detecting communities and factions in large casts
  • Tracking character evolution across series installments
  • Exploratory analysis to generate hypotheses for deeper literary study

Less Suitable For:

  • Single-protagonist narratives (network structure is trivial)
  • Works where internal monologue matters more than interaction
  • Analysis requiring understanding of relationship quality (love/hate/neutral)
  • Studies focused on themes, symbolism, or other non-relational literary elements

docs.title: Alternative and Complementary Approaches
docs.text:
Alternative Network Definitions:

  • Dialogue networks: Link characters who speak to each other (requires different data)
  • Scene networks: Link characters who appear in the same scene (requires scene segmentation)
  • Sentiment networks: Weight edges by relationship positivity/negativity (requires sentiment analysis)

Complementary Analyses:

  • Topic modeling: Identify themes associated with character communities
  • Sentiment analysis: Understand relationship emotional valence
  • NLP-based character analysis: Extract character traits from descriptions
  • Narrative arc modeling: Track plot structure mathematically

Advanced Network Techniques:

  • Temporal networks: Represent time explicitly rather than as separate snapshots
  • Weighted centrality: Use edge weights (co-occurrence frequency) more sophisticatedly
  • Network embedding: Create vector representations of characters for downstream ML tasks
  • Signed networks: Model positive (ally) vs negative (enemy) relationships

docs.title: Recommendations for Future Work
docs.text:
Methodological Improvements:

  • Sensitivity analysis: Test multiple proximity thresholds to assess result robustness
  • Name entity resolution: Carefully standardize character names to avoid artificial node splitting
  • Temporal network analysis: Use proper temporal network methods rather than separate snapshots
  • Qualitative validation: Combine quantitative findings with close reading to validate interpretations

Extended Analysis:

  • Comparison across series: Apply methodology to other multi-book fantasy series for comparative literary studies
  • Prediction tasks: Use network features to predict character survival, importance in later books, or TV adaptation casting prominence
  • TV vs book comparison: Analyze TV series network and compare to book network to understand adaptation choices

Deeper Statistical Analysis:

  • Null model comparison: Compare observed network to randomized networks to assess statistical significance of community structure
  • Centrality correlation: Systematically test correlations between different centrality measures
  • Book-length normalization: Control for varying book lengths in temporal analysis

This document provides complete implementation coverage of the Game of Thrones Network Analysis. Each code block includes technical explanations, mathematical foundations, and design rationale. Document Structure:

docs.title: Installing Required Libraries
docs.text:
!pip install plotly
!pip install community
!pip install python-louvain
!pip install colorlover

Purpose:

This code installs four libraries not included in standard Python or Google Colab environments:

  • plotly: Interactive visualization library for creating network graphs with hover effects and zoom capabilities
  • community: Package providing the Louvain community detection algorithm
  • python-louvain: Alternative/additional implementation ensuring Louvain algorithm availability
  • colorlover: Utility for generating color scales for community visualization

Flow:

  1. The !pip install command runs shell commands from within Jupyter/Colab notebooks
  2. pip (Python's package installer) downloads packages from PyPI (Python Package Index)
  3. Each library is installed to the notebook's environment
  4. Installation output shows download progress and dependency resolution

Impact:

  • Required once per session: In Colab, installations persist only for the current runtime. If runtime restarts, reinstall.
  • Dependency conflicts: These packages have their own dependencies. If other incompatible versions are installed, errors may occur.
  • Removal implications: Without these libraries, visualization and community detection code will fail with ImportError.

Design Choices:

  • Why plotly? Matplotlib could create static graphs, but Plotly's interactivity allows users to explore large networks by zooming and hovering.
  • Why Louvain? Among community detection algorithms (Girvan-Newman, Label Propagation, etc.), Louvain offers the best balance of speed and accuracy for networks of this size.
  • Why colorlover? Provides convenient color palette generation for distinguishing multiple communities visually.

Technical Notes:

  • Installation is idempotent—running multiple times won't break anything, just shows "already installed" messages
  • The community package is actually python-louvain, so installing both ensures availability regardless of import syntax

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Core Library Imports
docs.text:
import networkx as nx
from decorator import decorator
from networkx.utils import create_random_state, create_py_random_state
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import os

Purpose:

Import essential libraries for network analysis, data manipulation, and visualization.

Library-by-Library Explanation:

NetworkX (nx):

  • Core graph theory library for creating and analyzing networks
  • Provides graph classes (Graph, DiGraph, MultiGraph)
  • Implements centrality measures, shortest paths, clustering coefficients
  • Why imported as 'nx': Convention in network analysis community for concise code

decorator:

  • Utility for creating decorators (functions that modify other functions)
  • Used internally by NetworkX for some algorithms
  • Rarely called directly in user code

networkx.utils functions:

  • create_random_state: Ensures reproducible randomness in algorithms
  • create_py_random_state: Python-specific random state creation
  • Important for getting consistent results from stochastic algorithms (like spring layout)

NumPy (np):

  • Numerical computing library providing array operations
  • Foundation for pandas and many other scientific libraries
  • Used for mathematical operations on network metrics

pandas (pd):

  • Data manipulation library for tabular data
  • Provides DataFrame structure for storing centrality results
  • Handles CSV reading and data aggregation

Matplotlib (plt) and Seaborn (sns):

  • Matplotlib: Foundational plotting library for static visualizations
  • Seaborn: Higher-level interface to matplotlib with better defaults
  • Both used for any quick exploratory plots (though Plotly handles main visualizations)

os:

  • Operating system interface module
  • Used to list files in directories and navigate file systems
  • Critical for loading the five book CSV files

Impact:

Removing any of these imports will cause failures in downstream code. These form the foundational stack for the entire analysis.

docs.title: Pandas Display Configuration
docs.text:
pd.options.display.float_format = '{:,.2f}'.format

Purpose:

Configure how pandas displays floating-point numbers in DataFrames.

Flow:

  1. Access pandas global options via pd.options
  2. Set display.float_format option to a custom format string
  3. Format string '{:,.2f}' means:
  4. :, - Use comma as thousands separator
  5. .2f - Display 2 decimal places

Impact:

  • Before: Numbers display with many decimal places and scientific notation: 0.1234567, 1.23456e-4
  • After: Clean display: 0.12, 123.46
  • Scope: Affects all DataFrame displays in the notebook after this line
  • Removal: Numbers would display with full precision, making tables harder to read

Example:

# Before: 0.123456789
# After:  0.12

Set the default visual style for matplotlib/seaborn plots.

Flow:

Style Options:

  • darkgrid: Gray grid on white background (chosen here)
  • whitegrid: Gray grid on white background with lighter tones

Without init_notebook_mode(), Plotly visualizations won't render. The connected=True parameter requires internet access but keeps notebook file size smaller.

docs.title: Combining Books
docs.text:
books = [book1, book2, book3, book4, book5]

books_combined = pd.DataFrame()

for book in books:
    books_combined = pd.concat([books_combined, book])

books_combined = books_combined.groupby(["Person 2", "Person 1"], as_index=False)["weight"].sum()

Purpose:

Combine all five books into a single DataFrame, aggregating weights for character pairs that appear in multiple books.

Flow - Step by Step:

Step 1: Create list of DataFrames

books = [book1, book2, book3, book4, book5]
  • Organizes all book DataFrames into an iterable list
  • Enables loop-based processing

Step 2: Initialize empty DataFrame

books_combined = pd.DataFrame()
  • Creates empty container for concatenated data
  • Starts with no rows or columns

Step 3: Concatenate DataFrames

for book in books:
    books_combined = pd.concat([books_combined, book])
  • pd.concat() stacks DataFrames vertically (append rows)
  • Iterates through each book, adding its rows to combined DataFrame
  • After loop, books_combined contains all rows from all books

Step 4: Aggregate weights

books_combined = books_combined.groupby(["Person 2", "Person 1"], as_index=False)["weight"].sum()
  • groupby(): Groups rows by unique combinations of Person 1 and Person 2
  • ["weight"].sum(): Sums the weight column for each group
  • as_index=False: Keeps grouped columns as regular columns, not index

Mathematical Operation:

For characters A and B appearing in multiple books:

Book 1: A-B weight = 5
Book 2: A-B weight = 8
Book 3: A-B weight = 3
---
Combined: A-B weight = 5 + 8 + 3 = 16

Impact:

  • Essential for series-wide analysis: Creates single network representing entire series
  • Preserves cumulative importance: Characters with consistent presence across books get higher weights
  • Order matters: Groupby on ["Person 2", "Person 1"] treats (A,B) and (B,A) as different, but since graph is undirected, they represent the same edge

Potential Issue:

If names are spelled differently across books (e.g., "Jon Snow" vs "Jon-Snow"), they won't aggregate properly. Data should be preprocessed for consistency.

Alternative Implementation:

# More efficient single-step approach:
books_combined = pd.concat(books).groupby(["Person 1", "Person 2"], as_index=False)["weight"].sum()
