docs.title: Business Context and Motivation
docs.text: This project addresses a fundamental challenge in modern e-commerce: helping customers discover relevant products within massive catalogs. Amazon and similar platforms invest heavily in recommendation systems because personalized suggestions directly impact user engagement, conversion rates, and revenue. Research indicates that recommendation engines can drive 20-35% of e-commerce revenue by reducing decision paralysis and surfacing products customers might not otherwise discover.

docs.title: Dataset Characteristics
docs.text:
The Amazon Electronics product reviews dataset contains user-product interactions represented as ratings. The original dataset includes approximately 7.8 million ratings across various electronic products, with three key attributes:

  • user_id: Unique identifier for each customer
  • prod_id: Unique identifier for each product
  • rating: Numerical score from 1-5 indicating user satisfaction

Critical Limitation: The dataset deliberately excludes product metadata (titles, descriptions, categories) and review text to ensure models rely purely on collaborative signals rather than content features. This design choice simulates scenarios where behavioral data is more readily available than rich content information.

docs.title: Methodological Approach
docs.text:
This tutorial implements three progressively sophisticated recommendation strategies:

Model 1: Rank-Based System - Recommends globally popular products based on aggregated ratings. This non-personalized baseline serves customers with no interaction history and provides a performance benchmark.

Model 2: Collaborative Filtering - Leverages user-user and item-item similarity patterns to make personalized predictions. The assumption is that users who agreed in the past will agree in the future, and similar items receive similar ratings.

Model 3: Matrix Factorization (SVD) - Decomposes the user-item rating matrix into latent feature representations, capturing underlying preference patterns more compactly than similarity-based methods.

Each approach represents different trade-offs between personalization depth, computational requirements, and data sparsity handling.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 1 for implementation details]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: The Sparsity Challenge
docs.text:
The original dataset's 7.8 million ratings might seem substantial, but e-commerce data exhibits extreme sparsity. Most users rate very few products, and most products receive very few ratings. This creates two problems:

  • Statistical Reliability: Users with 1-2 ratings provide insufficient signal for personalization
  • Cold Start: Products with minimal ratings cannot be confidently recommended

docs.title: Filtering Rationale
docs.text:
The notebook implements a two-stage filtering process:

User Filtering (50+ ratings threshold): Retains only engaged users who have demonstrated consistent platform usage. This ensures the model learns from reliable behavioral patterns rather than noise from casual browsers. The threshold of 50 ratings balances data retention with signal quality.

Product Filtering (5+ ratings threshold): Keeps products with sufficient social proof. From a business perspective, recommending products with very few ratings carries reputational risk, as the rating may not represent true quality.

docs.title: Impact Assessment
docs.text:
This filtering reduces the dataset to approximately 65,290 interactions (0.83% of original data), representing:

  • Users with genuine engagement patterns
  • Products with established market presence
  • Computationally manageable dataset size

Trade-off Analysis: While this dramatically reduces data volume, it improves model reliability and computational efficiency. However, it creates a cold-start problem for new users and products, requiring separate strategies (content-based filtering, hybrid approaches) not covered in this tutorial.

Business Implication: The filtered dataset represents Amazon's most valuable customer segment (highly engaged users) and most recommendable products (socially validated items), making it an appropriate focus for initial recommendation system deployment.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 2 for filtering implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Dataset Structure Post-Filtering
docs.text: The filtered dataset contains 65,290 user-product interactions across 3 columns. This compact structure reflects the deliberate exclusion of metadata, focusing purely on behavioral signals.

docs.title: Rating Distribution Insights
docs.text:
The rating distribution reveals critical patterns for recommendation system design:

Key Findings:

  • 5-star ratings dominate: The majority of interactions are positive ratings, indicating either genuine satisfaction or potential reporting bias (satisfied customers more likely to rate)

  • Rating inflation: Mean rating substantially exceeds the theoretical midpoint of 3.0, suggesting users preferentially rate products they like

  • Sparse negative feedback: Ratings of 1-2 are relatively rare, possibly because dissatisfied customers abandon products without rating

Implications for Model Design:

  • Threshold Selection: When evaluating precision and recall, a threshold of 3.5 is used to define "relevant" items. Given the inflated rating distribution, this threshold appropriately distinguishes genuinely preferred products from neutral/negative experiences.

  • Evaluation Considerations: High baseline rating averages mean naive prediction strategies (always predict 4.5) could achieve superficially good RMSE without providing useful personalization.

docs.title: User and Product Diversity
docs.text:
The dataset includes:

  • Unique users: Several thousand engaged customers
  • Unique products: Thousands of electronic items
  • Maximum user ratings: 295 ratings (demonstrating extremely engaged power users)

Sparsity Reality: Even after filtering, most user-product pairs remain unobserved. The recommendation task is to accurately predict ratings for these unobserved interactions, not merely interpolate dense matrices.

docs.title: Data Quality Observations
docs.text:
No missing values: The filtered dataset is clean and complete, simplifying preprocessing.

No timestamp usage: While temporal data exists in the original dataset, this tutorial focuses on static collaborative filtering, treating all ratings as simultaneous. Production systems would incorporate temporal dynamics to handle preference drift and seasonal patterns.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3 for EDA implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Methodology Overview
docs.text:
Rank-based recommendation represents the simplest viable approach: identify globally popular products and recommend them to all users. The system calculates two metrics per product:

  • Average Rating: Mean of all user ratings for the product
  • Rating Count: Total number of ratings received

Products are then ranked by average rating, with a minimum interaction threshold to ensure statistical reliability.

docs.title: Why This Approach Works (Sometimes)
docs.text:
Appropriate Use Cases:

  • New User Onboarding: Users with no interaction history (cold start) receive reasonable initial suggestions

  • Explore vs. Exploit: Popular items provide safe "crowd-sourced" recommendations when exploration is valuable

  • Homepage Display: Generic landing pages benefit from universally appealing products

docs.title: Model Configuration and Results
docs.text:
Configuration 1: 50 Minimum Interactions

Recommends products with at least 50 ratings, ensuring reasonable statistical confidence in the average rating. This identifies well-established, highly-rated products.

Configuration 2: 100 Minimum Interactions

A more conservative threshold that prioritizes products with stronger social proof. This reduces the candidate set but increases confidence in product quality.

Practical Interpretation: The products recommended under both thresholds represent "safe bets" - items that satisfy most customers. However, these recommendations are identical for all users, representing zero personalization.

docs.title: Limitations and Business Context
docs.text:
Critical Weaknesses:

  • No Personalization: A user interested in headphones receives the same recommendations as someone shopping for cameras

  • Popular Item Bias: Recommends only mainstream products, failing to surface niche items that might perfectly match individual preferences

  • No Discovery: Users never encounter products outside the top-N most popular items

  • Feedback Loop Risk: Popular items become more popular, creating winner-take-all dynamics that may not reflect true quality

When Rank-Based Is Sufficient: For businesses with limited computational resources, small catalogs, or primarily new users, this approach provides acceptable performance at minimal cost. However, e-commerce platforms like Amazon require personalization to maximize revenue and user satisfaction.

Transition to Collaborative Filtering: The rank-based baseline establishes that basic aggregation provides some value. The question becomes: can we do better by considering individual user preferences? The collaborative filtering models address this question.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 4 for implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Theoretical Foundation
docs.text:
Collaborative filtering operates on a deceptively simple premise: users who agreed in the past will agree in the future. This manifests in two complementary approaches:

User-User Similarity: If User A and User B rated many products similarly, and User A liked Product X, User B will likely also enjoy Product X.

Item-Item Similarity: If Product X and Product Y receive similar ratings across users, a user who liked Product X will likely appreciate Product Y.

docs.title: Why Similarity-Based Methods Work
docs.text: The fundamental insight is that ratings encode latent preference signals. Two users who both rate action movies highly and romantic comedies lowly share underlying taste preferences, even if those preferences aren't explicitly articulated. Similarity metrics (cosine, Pearson correlation) quantify this alignment.

docs.title: User-User Collaborative Filtering
docs.text:
Baseline Model Performance:

The initial user-user model using cosine similarity achieves moderate performance on precision and recall metrics. These metrics answer critical business questions:

  • Precision@10: Of the 10 products recommended to each user, what fraction are actually relevant (rated ≥3.5)? This measures recommendation quality and impacts user trust.

  • Recall@10: Of all products a user would rate highly, what fraction appear in our top-10 recommendations? This measures coverage and opportunity cost of missed recommendations.

  • F1-Score: The harmonic mean balancing precision and recall, useful when both matter equally.

Practical Interpretation: The baseline model provides better-than-random recommendations but has substantial room for improvement. Users receive some relevant suggestions, but many recommendations miss the mark.

docs.title: Hyperparameter Optimization
docs.text:
The optimization process tunes three critical parameters:

k (number of neighbors): How many similar users to consider when predicting ratings. Too few neighbors provides insufficient signal; too many introduces noise from dissimilar users.

min_k (minimum neighbors): Fallback threshold ensuring predictions aren't based on too few similar users. When insufficient neighbors exist, the system defaults to global average rating.

Similarity Metric: Choice between cosine, mean squared difference (MSD), or Pearson correlation affects how "similarity" is quantified.

Optimization Results: Grid search cross-validation identifies optimal parameter combinations that improve RMSE (prediction accuracy) and precision/recall metrics. The improvements demonstrate that careful parameter tuning significantly impacts recommendation quality.

Why This Matters: In production systems, even small metric improvements translate to substantial revenue gains. A 2% improvement in precision might mean millions of dollars in additional conversions for a platform like Amazon.

docs.title: Item-Item Collaborative Filtering
docs.text:
Item-item filtering inverts the similarity calculation: instead of finding similar users, it finds similar products. This approach often outperforms user-user filtering in e-commerce contexts for several reasons:

Product Stability: Product characteristics remain relatively stable, while user preferences evolve over time. Item similarity matrices can be precomputed and cached efficiently.

Interpretability: "Customers who bought X also bought Y" is intuitively understandable and trustworthy for users.

Scalability: With fewer products than users (typically), item-item similarity computations are more tractable.

Performance Comparison: The optimized item-item model achieves comparable or superior performance to user-user models, with the additional benefit of computational efficiency.

docs.title: Practical Prediction Examples
docs.text:
The notebook demonstrates predictions for specific user-product pairs:

Observed Interaction: When predicting ratings for products users have already rated, the model's prediction should approximate the true rating. Discrepancies indicate model error or unusual rating patterns.

Unobserved Interaction: For products users haven't rated, the prediction represents the system's best estimate. These predictions drive actual recommendations.

Business Application: The get_recommendations() function identifies a user's top-N unobserved products by predicted rating. This ranked list drives the recommendation interface users see.

docs.title: Similarity-Based Limitations
docs.text:
Despite improvements through optimization, similarity-based collaborative filtering has inherent constraints:

Sparsity Struggles: When user-product interactions are sparse, finding sufficient similar users/items becomes difficult, leading to low-confidence predictions.

Popularity Bias: Similarity metrics favor popular items with many ratings, potentially overlooking excellent niche products.

Computational Cost: Real-time similarity computation for millions of users/products requires significant infrastructure.

Cold Start: New users/products with no ratings cannot be effectively handled without auxiliary information.

These limitations motivate the exploration of matrix factorization methods, which handle sparsity more elegantly.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 5 for detailed implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Conceptual Shift from Similarity to Latent Factors
docs.text:
Matrix factorization represents a fundamental paradigm shift in collaborative filtering. Instead of explicitly computing similarities, it learns latent feature representations that encode user preferences and product characteristics in a lower-dimensional space.

Intuition: The rating matrix can be approximated as the product of two smaller matrices:

  • User Matrix: Each user represented by a vector of latent preferences (e.g., preference for action vs. drama, high-tech vs. simple features)

  • Product Matrix: Each product represented by a vector of latent characteristics

The predicted rating is the dot product of the user and product vectors, capturing how well the product's characteristics align with the user's preferences.

docs.title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
docs.text:
The SVD algorithm implemented via the Surprise library optimizes these latent factor matrices to minimize prediction error across observed ratings. The optimization process uses stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to iteratively adjust latent factors.

Mathematical Elegance: SVD naturally handles the sparsity problem. Unlike similarity methods that struggle with missing values, SVD learns patterns from observed ratings and generalizes to unobserved interactions through the latent space geometry.

docs.title: Baseline SVD Performance
docs.text:
The initial SVD model (with default hyperparameters) demonstrates strong performance, often exceeding optimized similarity-based models. This validates the theoretical advantage of latent factor models for sparse data.

Key Metrics:

  • RMSE: Measures average prediction error in rating units. Lower values indicate more accurate predictions.

  • Precision@10 / Recall@10: Demonstrate that SVD recommendations are both accurate (high precision) and comprehensive (high recall).

Why SVD Outperforms Similarity Methods:

  • Dimensionality Reduction: By projecting users and items into a shared latent space, SVD captures complex preference patterns that similarity metrics miss

  • Noise Robustness: Averaging over latent factors reduces impact of rating noise or outliers

  • Better Generalization: Learned latent representations generalize beyond observed similarities to predict novel user-item affinities

docs.title: Hyperparameter Tuning
docs.text:
SVD's performance is sensitive to three key hyperparameters:

n_epochs: Number of training iterations. More epochs allow better convergence but risk overfitting and increase training time.

lr_all (learning rate): Controls how aggressively the algorithm updates parameters. Too high causes instability; too low slows convergence.

reg_all (regularization): Penalizes model complexity to prevent overfitting. Balances fitting training data versus generalizing to test data.

Optimization Process: Grid search evaluates all hyperparameter combinations via 3-fold cross-validation, selecting the configuration that minimizes RMSE. This process typically improves baseline performance by 3-10%, which translates to noticeably better recommendations.

docs.title: Prediction Interpretation
docs.text:
When the optimized SVD model predicts ratings:

For Observed Interactions: The prediction should closely match the true rating. Systematic deviations indicate model bias or that the user's rating pattern defies general trends.

For Unobserved Interactions: The prediction represents a confidence-weighted estimate. High predicted ratings (e.g., 4.5+) suggest strong user-product affinity and warrant recommendation.

Practical Application: The recommendations generated by SVD reflect not just explicit similarities, but deeper patterns in the latent preference space. This often surfaces unexpected but highly relevant suggestions that surprise and delight users.

docs.title: Matrix Factorization Limitations
docs.text:
Despite superior performance, SVD has constraints:

Interpretability Deficit: Latent factors lack clear semantic meaning. Unlike item-item filtering (which explains "similar products"), SVD recommendations are harder to justify to users.

Training Requirements: SVD requires iterative optimization, making initial model training more computationally expensive than similarity computation.

Cold Start Persistence: New users/products still require auxiliary approaches (content-based features, demographic data) to generate initial recommendations.

Static Assumptions: The tutorial's SVD implementation treats ratings as static. Production systems must continually retrain or use online learning to capture evolving preferences.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 6 for implementation details]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Performance Benchmark Summary
docs.text:
Across the three modeling approaches, we observe a clear progression in recommendation quality:

Rank-Based System:

  • Strengths: Simple, fast, no training required, reasonable for cold-start users
  • Weaknesses: Zero personalization, popularity bias, poor coverage
  • Use Case: Initial recommendations for brand-new users, homepage placeholders

Collaborative Filtering (User-User & Item-Item):

  • Strengths: Personalized recommendations, interpretable similarity reasoning, no domain knowledge required
  • Weaknesses: Struggles with sparsity, computationally expensive at scale, cold-start limitations
  • Use Case: Mid-sized catalogs with moderate sparsity, scenarios requiring explainable recommendations

Matrix Factorization (SVD):

  • Strengths: Best handling of sparse data, captures complex latent patterns, superior accuracy
  • Weaknesses: Less interpretable, requires model training, cold-start issues persist
  • Use Case: Large-scale production systems where prediction accuracy is paramount

docs.title: Evaluation Metric Considerations
docs.text:
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error): Measures prediction accuracy but doesn't directly reflect recommendation quality. A user cares whether recommended items are relevant, not whether predicted ratings are precise.

Precision@k and Recall@k: More aligned with business objectives. High precision ensures users trust recommendations; high recall ensures users discover relevant products.

F1-Score@k: Valuable when both precision and recall matter equally, providing a single metric for model comparison.

Threshold Selection Impact: The 3.5 rating threshold for "relevant" items reflects the inflated rating distribution observed in EDA. Adjusting this threshold would alter precision/recall metrics but not fundamental model rankings.

docs.title: Production Deployment Considerations
docs.text:
Real-world recommendation systems rarely deploy a single algorithm. Instead, they use ensemble approaches that combine multiple methods:

Hybrid Architecture Example:

  • Rank-Based: Handles cold-start users and provides baseline recommendations
  • Item-Item CF: Generates "similar products" for product detail pages
  • SVD: Powers personalized homepage and email recommendations
  • Content-Based (not covered): Handles cold-start products using metadata
  • Multi-Armed Bandit (not covered): Balances exploration and exploitation in real-time

docs.title: Resource and Scalability Requirements
docs.text:
Computational Costs:

  • Rank-based system: Negligible (simple aggregation)
  • Similarity-based CF: Moderate to high (similarity matrix computation and storage)
  • SVD: High initial training cost, low prediction cost once trained

Latency Requirements: Production systems must return recommendations in milliseconds. Pre-computing similarity matrices or caching SVD predictions is essential for real-time performance.

Update Frequency: As new ratings arrive, how frequently should models retrain?

  • Rank-based: Real-time aggregation updates feasible
  • Similarity-based: Batch updates (daily) common
  • SVD: Periodic retraining (weekly/monthly) with incremental learning for frequent updates

docs.title: Business Impact Assessment
docs.text:
Measurable Outcomes: A/B testing would compare models on:

  • Click-through rate on recommendations
  • Conversion rate for recommended products
  • Revenue per user from recommended items
  • User engagement metrics (time on site, pages viewed)

Expected Improvements: Literature suggests that collaborative filtering can improve conversion rates by 10-30% over non-personalized baselines, with matrix factorization providing an additional 5-15% gain over similarity-based methods.

docs.title: Remaining Challenges and Future Directions
docs.text:
This tutorial addresses core collaborative filtering but omits several important considerations:

Temporal Dynamics: User preferences evolve; recent interactions should weigh more heavily than old ones.

Context-Aware Recommendations: Time of day, device type, browsing history provide valuable signals.

Diversity and Serendipity: Optimizing solely for predicted rating creates filter bubbles. Injecting diversity improves user satisfaction.

Cross-Domain Learning: Leveraging patterns across product categories improves cold-start handling.

Deep Learning Approaches: Neural collaborative filtering and transformer-based models represent the current state-of-the-art but require substantially more data and compute.

docs.title: Final Recommendation
docs.text:
For an e-commerce platform with Amazon's scale and resources:

Implement a hybrid system that deploys rank-based recommendations for cold-start scenarios, item-item collaborative filtering for explainable "similar products" features, and SVD-based matrix factorization for personalized recommendations. Continuously evaluate model performance through A/B testing and iterate based on business metrics.

For smaller platforms or learning contexts, start with item-item collaborative filtering after hyperparameter tuning. It provides a good balance of performance, interpretability, and implementation complexity.

!pip uninstall numpy -y

Purpose: This code handles a critical dependency issue with the Surprise library. The Surprise library for building recommendation systems has specific NumPy version requirements that may conflict with Colab's default installation.

Why Version 1.23.5: This NumPy version provides stable compatibility with the Surprise library while avoiding known bugs in earlier versions. The uninstall-reinstall sequence ensures a clean installation without version conflicts.

Flow:

  1. Remove any existing NumPy installation to avoid conflicts
  2. Install the specific compatible version
  3. Restart the runtime (prompted by Colab) to load the new version

Impact: Skipping this step may cause import errors when loading Surprise or runtime errors during model training. The version mismatch can manifest as segmentation faults or incorrect computation results.

Component Breakdown:

  • warnings.filterwarnings('ignore'): Suppresses warning messages (e.g., deprecation warnings) that clutter output without affecting functionality

df = pd.read_csv('/content/sample_data/ratings_Electronics.csv', header=None)
df.columns = ['user_id', 'prod_id', 'rating', 'timestamp']
df = df.drop('timestamp', axis=1)

Purpose: Loads the raw Amazon Electronics ratings dataset and performs initial preprocessing.

Flow:

  1. read_csv() with header=None: Indicates the CSV file lacks column headers, so pandas should not treat the first row as column names

  2. Assign column names: Manually labels columns for readability and downstream operations

  3. Drop timestamp: Removes the timestamp column as this tutorial focuses on static collaborative filtering without temporal dynamics

  4. Create deep copy: Preserves the original data in df_copy for potential later comparison or recovery

Impact: The resulting df DataFrame contains only user_id, prod_id, and rating columns. This simplified structure focuses on user-item interaction patterns without temporal or contextual features.

1  A34BZM... 63133...   4.0
...

docs.title: User Filtering Logic
docs.text:
users = df.user_id

ratings_count = dict()

for user in users:
    if user in ratings_count:
        ratings_count[user] += 1
    else:
        ratings_count[user] = 1

RATINGS_CUTOFF = 50
remove_users = []

for user, num_ratings in ratings_count.items():
    if num_ratings < RATINGS_CUTOFF:
        remove_users.append(user)

df = df.loc[~df.user_id.isin(remove_users)]

Purpose: Filters out users with fewer than 50 ratings to ensure the dataset contains only engaged users with sufficient rating history for pattern detection.

Flow:

  1. Extract user column: Creates a Series of all user_ids (with duplicates)

  2. Count ratings per user: Iterates through all ratings, building a dictionary mapping user_id to rating count

  3. If user already in dictionary: increment count

  4. If new user: initialize count to 1

  5. Identify low-engagement users: Create list of users below the 50-rating threshold

  6. Filter DataFrame: Use boolean indexing with ~ (NOT operator) and isin() to keep only users NOT in the remove list

Mathematical Justification: 50 ratings provides statistical significance for estimating user preferences. With fewer ratings, learned patterns are unreliable and predictions have high variance.

Impact: This reduces the dataset from ~7.8M to ~1M ratings. While this decreases data volume substantially, it dramatically improves data quality and model reliability.

Alternative Approaches: Could use percentile-based filtering (e.g., keep top 10% most active users) or adaptive thresholds based on rating distribution.

docs.title: Product Filtering Logic
docs.text:
prods = df.prod_id

ratings_count = dict()

for prod in prods:
    if prod in ratings_count:
        ratings_count[prod] += 1
    else:
        ratings_count[prod] = 1

RATINGS_CUTOFF = 5
remove_users = []

for user, num_ratings in ratings_count.items():
    if num_ratings < RATINGS_CUTOFF:
        remove_users.append(user)

df_final = df.loc[~df.prod_id.isin(remove_users)]

Purpose: Filters products with fewer than 5 ratings to ensure recommended products have sufficient social proof and rating reliability.

Flow: Identical structure to user filtering, but applied to products:

  1. Count ratings per product
  2. Identify products below 5-rating threshold
  3. Filter DataFrame to remove these products

Why Lower Threshold (5 vs 50): Products naturally receive fewer ratings than users give. A 5-rating threshold balances:

  • Statistical reliability: 5 ratings provide basic confidence in average rating
  • Coverage: Retains more products for recommendation diversity
  • Business logic: Products with <5 ratings may be too new or niche to confidently recommend

Impact: Further reduces dataset to the final 65,290 interactions. This represents the intersection of engaged users and established products.

Variable Naming Issue: Note that remove_users variable is reused for products (should be remove_products). This works because it's immediately consumed, but is poor coding practice.

prod_id     object

Why Data Types Matter:

  • user_id, prod_id as object: These are categorical identifiers, not numerical values. Storing as strings prevents accidental arithmetic operations.

  • rating as float64: Enables numerical operations (mean, variance) and model training. Even though ratings are integers (1-5), float representation handles fractional predictions.

Impact: Incorrect data types cause errors in aggregation (e.g., trying to average object columns) or waste memory (storing IDs as integers when they should be strings).

docs.title: Missing Value Check

print(df_final.isna().sum())

Purpose: Identifies any missing values that require imputation or handling.

Flow:

  1. isna(): Creates a boolean DataFrame where True indicates missing value
  2. sum(): Counts True values per column (boolean True = 1, False = 0)

Expected Output: 

user_id    0
prod_id    0
rating     0

Interpretation: Zero missing values indicates clean data. This simplifies preprocessing as no imputation strategy is needed.

If Missing Values Existed:

  • For IDs: Missing IDs are meaningless; those rows should be dropped
  • For ratings: Could impute with user mean, product mean, or global mean, but dropping is often preferable to avoid introducing bias

Impact: Clean data allows direct modeling without preprocessing complexity.

docs.title: Rating Distribution Statistics
docs.text:
print(df_final["rating"].describe())

Purpose: Computes summary statistics for the rating distribution to understand central tendency and spread.

Output Interpretation:

  • count: Number of ratings (should match row count)
  • mean: Average rating (expect >3 due to positive bias)
  • std: Standard deviation (measures rating variability)
  • min/max: Range verification (should be 1-5)
  • 25%, 50%, 75%: Quartiles showing distribution shape

Key Insights:

  • High mean rating: Indicates users preferentially rate products they like, creating positive skew
  • Distribution shape: If median > mean, distribution is left-skewed with more high ratings

Statistical Foundation: These descriptive statistics establish baseline expectations for model predictions. Predictions drastically different from the observed distribution indicate model failure.

Impact: Informs threshold selection for precision/recall metrics and helps detect modeling errors (e.g., if predicted ratings fall outside 1-5 range).

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
df_final["rating"].value_counts().sort_index().plot(kind="bar")
plt.title("Rating Distribution")
plt.xlabel("Rating")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.tight_layout()

Flow:

  1. plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6)): Creates a 12x6 inch figure for readability
  2. value_counts(): Counts occurrences of each rating value
  3. sort_index(): Orders ratings 1-5 for logical x-axis progression
  4. plot(kind="bar"): Creates bar chart
  5. Labels and title: Adds descriptive text
  6. tight_layout(): Adjusts spacing to prevent label cutoff
  7. show(): Displays the plot

Interpretation:

  • Expect tall bars for ratings 4-5: Confirms positive rating bias
  • Short bars for ratings 1-2: Users rarely rate disliked products
  • Rating 3 as transition point: Moderate frequency, separates positive/negative sentiment

Visual Patterns:

  • Right-skewed distribution: Confirms most interactions are positive
  • Bimodal pattern: If ratings 1 and 5 both have high frequency, indicates polarized opinions

Impact: Visual inspection reveals distribution characteristics that inform modeling decisions, particularly threshold selection for binary classification (relevant vs. non-relevant items).

docs.title: Uniqueness Counts
docs.text:
print('The number of observations in the final data = ', len(df_final))
print('Number of unique USERS in Raw data = ', df_final['user_id'].nunique())
print('Number of unique ITEMS in Raw data = ', df_final['prod_id'].nunique())

Purpose: Quantifies the number of unique users and products to understand data density and sparsity.

Flow:

  1. len(df_final): Counts total rows (interactions)
  2. nunique(): Counts distinct values in each column

Sparsity Calculation:

If there are U users and P products:

  • Possible interactions: U × P
  • Observed interactions: 65,290
  • Sparsity: 1 - (65,290 / (U × P))

Even after filtering, sparsity typically exceeds 99%, meaning most user-product pairs are unobserved.

Impact: High sparsity motivates collaborative filtering approaches that can infer unobserved ratings from observed patterns.

most_rated

  4. [:10]: Selects top 10 users

  • Distribution shape: If top user has 300 ratings but 10th has 60, engagement is concentrated among power users
  • Long tail behavior: Most users have minimum ratings (50), few have many

Statistical Consideration: Power users may have different behavioral patterns than typical users. Models trained heavily on power user data may not generalize well to typical users.

docs.title: Aggregated Rating Metrics
docs.text:
average_rating = df_final.groupby('prod_id')['rating'].mean()
count_rating = df_final.groupby('prod_id')['rating'].count()

final_rating = pd.DataFrame({'average_rating': average_rating, 
                              'count_rating': count_rating})

final_rating = final_rating.sort_values(by='average_rating', ascending=False)
final_rating.head()

Purpose: Computes the average rating and total rating count for each product, then creates a sorted DataFrame for ranking products by popularity.

Flow:

  1. groupby('prod_id'): Groups all ratings by product
  2. mean(): Calculates average rating per product
  3. count(): Counts total ratings per product
  4. DataFrame creation: Combines metrics into structured format
  5. sort_values(): Ranks products by average rating (descending)

Mathematical Foundation:

For product i with ratings r₁, r₂, ..., rₙ:

average_rating_i = (r₁ + r₂ + ... + rₙ) / n
count_rating_i = n

Why Both Metrics:

  • average_rating: Measures product quality
  • count_rating: Measures statistical confidence and popularity

A product with 5.0 average from 3 ratings is less reliable than 4.8 average from 200 ratings.

Statistical Issue: Simple average treats all ratings equally, ignoring that:

  • Early ratings may be from biased sources (friends, employees)
  • Rating distribution (all 5s vs. mix of 3s and 5s) affects reliability

Alternative Approach: Could use Bayesian averaging or Wilson confidence intervals to balance rating quality with confidence.

Impact: This DataFrame becomes the basis for rank-based recommendations.

docs.title: Top-N Product Function
docs.text:
def top_n_products(final_rating, n, min_interaction):
    recommendations = final_rating[final_rating['count_rating'] >= min_interaction]
    recommendations = recommendations.sort_values(by='average_rating', ascending=False)
    return recommendations.index[:n]

Purpose: Generates top-N product recommendations based on popularity, filtered by a minimum interaction threshold.

Function Parameters:

  • final_rating: DataFrame containing average_rating and count_rating for each product
  • n: Number of products to recommend
  • min_interaction: Minimum rating count required for a product to be considered

Flow:

  1. Filter by minimum interactions: final_rating['count_rating'] >= min_interaction creates boolean mask keeping only products with sufficient ratings

  2. Sort by average rating: Ensures highest-rated products appear first

  3. Select top N: recommendations.index[:n] returns the product IDs (index values) of the top N products

Logic Justification:

The minimum interaction threshold serves multiple purposes:

  • Statistical reliability: More ratings → more confident average estimate
  • Business validation: Products with many ratings have demonstrated market acceptance
  • Quality signal: High rating + many ratings → genuine quality (harder to game than high rating + few ratings)

Edge Cases:

  • If fewer than N products meet threshold: Returns all qualifying products (fewer than N)
  • Ties in average rating: Products with identical averages returned in arbitrary order (could enhance with secondary sort by count)

Computational Complexity: O(P log P) where P is number of products, due to sorting operation.

Impact: This function encapsulates the core rank-based recommendation logic in a reusable form.

docs.title: Recommendation Generation
docs.text:
top_n_products(final_rating, 5, 50)
top_n_products(final_rating, 5, 100)

Purpose: Generates two sets of top-5 product recommendations with different minimum interaction thresholds.

Scenario 1 (min_interaction=50):

  • Requires products with at least 50 ratings
  • Balances statistical confidence with catalog coverage
  • Returns 5 products with highest average ratings meeting this threshold

Scenario 2 (min_interaction=100):

  • Stricter threshold requiring 100+ ratings
  • Higher confidence in rating reliability
  • May return highly popular mainstream products
  • Reduced catalog coverage (fewer products qualify)

Interpretation:

If the same products appear in both lists → these are universally highly-rated products across different confidence levels.

If products differ → the 50-rating threshold includes good products that haven't achieved mass-market scale yet.

Business Application:

  • 50-rating threshold: Balance of quality and diversity
  • 100-rating threshold: "Safe bet" recommendations for risk-averse scenarios

Limitation: Both recommendations are identical for all users (no personalization).

Impact: Establishes baseline recommendation quality that personalized methods should exceed.

docs.text:
from surprise import accuracy
from surprise.reader import Reader
from surprise.dataset import Dataset
from surprise.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from surprise.model_selection import train_test_split
from surprise.prediction_algorithms.knns import KNNBasic
from surprise.prediction_algorithms.matrix_factorization import SVD
from surprise.model_selection import KFold
from surprise import CoClustering

Purpose: Imports all necessary classes and functions from the Surprise library for building and evaluating recommendation systems.

Component Breakdown:

  • accuracy: Module containing evaluation metrics (RMSE, MAE)
  • Reader: Defines rating scale and data format for loading
  • Dataset: Loads data from pandas DataFrames into Surprise format
  • GridSearchCV: Hyperparameter tuning through cross-validation
  • train_test_split: Splits data into train/test sets
  • KNNBasic: K-nearest neighbors collaborative filtering algorithm
  • SVD: Matrix factorization algorithm (Singular Value Decomposition)
  • KFold: K-fold cross-validation utility (not used in tutorial but available)
  • CoClustering: Co-clustering algorithm (not used in tutorial but available)

Impact: These imports provide the complete toolkit for implementing collaborative filtering models without custom algorithm implementation.

docs.title: Evaluation Metric Function
docs.text:
def precision_recall_at_k(model, k=10, threshold=3.5):
    """Return precision and recall at k metrics for each user"""

    user_est_true = defaultdict(list)
    predictions = model.test(testset)

    for uid, _, true_r, est, _ in predictions:
        user_est_true[uid].append((est, true_r))

    precisions = dict()
    recalls = dict()

    for uid, user_ratings in user_est_true.items():
        user_ratings.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)

        n_rel = sum((true_r >= threshold) for (_, true_r) in user_ratings)
        n_rec_k = sum((est >= threshold) for (est, _) in user_ratings[:k])
        n_rel_and_rec_k = sum(((true_r >= threshold) and (est >= threshold))
                              for (est, true_r) in user_ratings[:k])

        precisions[uid] = n_rel_and_rec_k / n_rec_k if n_rec_k != 0 else 0
        recalls[uid] = n_rel_and_rec_k / n_rel if n_rel != 0 else 0

    precision = round((sum(prec for prec in precisions.values()) / len(precisions)), 3)
    recall = round((sum(rec for rec in recalls.values()) / len(recalls)), 3)

    accuracy.rmse(predictions)

    print('Precision: ', precision)
    print('Recall: ', recall)
    print('F_1 score: ', round((2*precision*recall)/(precision+recall), 3))

Purpose: Computes precision@k, recall@k, F1-score@k, and RMSE for recommendation model evaluation.

Function Parameters:

  • model: Trained Surprise model to evaluate
  • k: Number of top predictions to consider (default 10)
  • threshold: Rating value above which items are considered "relevant" (default 3.5)

Flow - Step by Step:

Step 1: Generate Predictions 

predictions = model.test(testset)
Generates predicted ratings for all user-item pairs in the test set.

Step 2: Organize Predictions by User 

for uid, _, true_r, est, _ in predictions:
    user_est_true[uid].append((est, true_r))
Groups predictions by user, storing (predicted_rating, true_rating) tuples.

Step 3: Compute Per-User Metrics 

user_ratings.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)
Sorts each user's predictions by predicted rating (descending) to identify top-k recommendations.

Step 4: Calculate Relevance Counts

n_rel (relevant items): Count of items with true_rating ≥ threshold 

n_rel = sum((true_r >= threshold) for (_, true_r) in user_ratings)

n_rec_k (recommended items in top-k): Count of items with predicted_rating ≥ threshold in top-k 

n_rec_k = sum((est >= threshold) for (est, _) in user_ratings[:k])

n_rel_and_rec_k (relevant AND recommended): Count of items both relevant and in top-k recommendations 

n_rel_and_rec_k = sum(((true_r >= threshold) and (est >= threshold))
                      for (est, true_r) in user_ratings[:k])

Step 5: Compute Precision and Recall

Precision@k Formula: 

Precision@k = (relevant items in top-k) / (total items recommended in top-k)

Recall@k Formula: 

Recall@k = (relevant items in top-k) / (total relevant items)

Zero-Division Handling: If n_rec_k or n_rel is 0, the respective metric is set to 0.

Step 6: Aggregate Across Users 

precision = round((sum(prec for prec in precisions.values()) / len(precisions)), 3)
recall = round((sum(rec for rec in recalls.values()) / len(recalls)), 3)
Computes mean precision and recall across all users.

Step 7: Compute F1-Score 

F1 = 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall)
Harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both metrics.

Mathematical Foundation:

Precision@k measures recommendation accuracy: - High precision → most recommended items are relevant - Low precision → many irrelevant items recommended

Recall@k measures recommendation coverage: - High recall → most relevant items are recommended - Low recall → many relevant items missed

F1-score balances precision and recall: - Useful when both metrics matter equally - Harmonic mean (not arithmetic) penalizes imbalanced values

Impact: This function provides comprehensive evaluation beyond simple RMSE, capturing recommendation quality from a business perspective.

docs.text:

data = Dataset.load_from_df(df_final[['user_id', 'prod_id', 'rating']], reader)
trainset, testset = train_test_split(data, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

Purpose: Converts the pandas DataFrame into Surprise's internal data format and splits into train/test sets.

Flow:

Step 1: Define Rating Scale 

reader = Reader(rating_scale=(0, 5))
Specifies that ratings range from 0-5, informing Surprise about valid rating bounds.

Step 2: Load Data 

data = Dataset.load_from_df(df_final[['user_id', 'prod_id', 'rating']], reader)
Converts pandas DataFrame to Surprise's DatasetAutoFolds format. Requires exactly three columns in order: user, item, rating.

Step 3: Train-Test Split 

trainset, testset = train_test_split(data, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

  • test_size=0.2: 80% training, 20% testing (standard split)
  • random_state=42: Ensures reproducible splits
  • trainset: Surprise's Trainset format (optimized internal representation)
  • testset: List of (user, item, rating) tuples for testing

Why This Format: Surprise uses specialized data structures for efficient sparse matrix operations and algorithm optimization.

docs.title: User-User Collaborative Filtering - Baseline
docs.text:
sim_options = {'name': 'cosine', 'user_based': True}
sim_user_user = KNNBasic(sim_options=sim_options, verbose=False, random_state=1)
sim_user_user.fit(trainset)
precision_recall_at_k(sim_user_user, k=10, threshold=3.5)

Purpose: Trains a baseline user-user collaborative filtering model using cosine similarity.

Flow:

Step 1: Define Similarity Options 

sim_options = {'name': 'cosine', 'user_based': True}

  • name='cosine': Use cosine similarity metric
  • user_based=True: Compute similarity between users (not items)

Step 2: Initialize Model 

sim_user_user = KNNBasic(sim_options=sim_options, verbose=False, random_state=1)

  • KNNBasic: K-nearest neighbors algorithm
  • verbose=False: Suppress training progress output
  • random_state=1: Ensures reproducible results

Step 3: Train Model 

sim_user_user.fit(trainset)
Computes user-user similarity matrix and prepares for predictions.

Step 4: Evaluate 

precision_recall_at_k(sim_user_user, k=10, threshold=3.5)
Computes evaluation metrics on test set.

Cosine Similarity Formula:

For users u and v with rating vectors r_u and r_v:

cosine_similarity(u, v) = (r_u · r_v) / (||r_u|| × ||r_v||)

Where: - r_u · r_v = dot product of rating vectors - ||r_u|| = Euclidean norm of r_u

Range: [-1, 1], where 1 = identical preferences, -1 = opposite preferences, 0 = uncorrelated

Why Cosine: Measures angular similarity rather than magnitude, so users with different rating scales but similar patterns are still considered similar.

Impact: Establishes baseline user-user performance for comparison with optimized models.

docs.title: Making Predictions
docs.text:
sim_user_user.predict("A3LDPF5FMB782Z", "1400501466", r_ui=5, verbose=True)
sim_user_user.predict("A34BZM6S9L7QI4", "1400501466", verbose=True)

Purpose: Demonstrates prediction for specific user-item pairs, both observed and unobserved interactions.

Prediction 1 - Observed Interaction: 

sim_user_user.predict("A3LDPF5FMB782Z", "1400501466", r_ui=5, verbose=True)

  • r_ui=5: True rating is 5 (this user rated this product 5)
  • Prediction should approximate 5 if model captures user's preferences
  • Deviation indicates model error or unusual rating pattern

Prediction 2 - Unobserved Interaction: 

sim_user_user.predict("A34BZM6S9L7QI4", "1400501466", verbose=True)

  • No r_ui parameter (user hasn't rated this product)
  • Prediction is the system's best estimate based on similar users
  • This type of prediction drives actual recommendations

verbose=True Output Includes:

  • User ID
  • Item ID
  • True rating (if known)
  • Estimated rating
  • Additional model-specific details

Prediction Process:

  1. Find k most similar users to target user
  2. Weight their ratings of the item by similarity scores
  3. Aggregate weighted ratings into final prediction

Impact: Demonstrates model's ability to predict both known ratings (for validation) and unknown ratings (for recommendations).

docs.title: Hyperparameter Tuning - User-User Model
docs.text:
param_grid = {'k': [10, 20, 30],
              'min_k': [3, 6, 9],
              'sim_options': {'name': ['msd', 'cosine'], 'user_based': [True]}}

gs = GridSearchCV(KNNBasic, param_grid, measures=['rmse'], cv=3, n_jobs=-1)
gs.fit(data)

print(gs.best_score['rmse'])
print(gs.best_params['rmse'])

Purpose: Systematically searches for optimal hyperparameters using cross-validation.

Hyperparameter Space:

k (number of neighbors): [10, 20, 30]

  • Number of similar users to consider for prediction
  • Lower k → more local, potentially noisy predictions
  • Higher k → more global, potentially over-smoothed predictions

min_k (minimum neighbors): [3, 6, 9]

  • Minimum similar users required for prediction
  • If fewer than min_k neighbors exist, prediction defaults to global mean
  • Higher min_k → more conservative, fewer predictions
  • Lower min_k → more predictions, potentially less reliable

sim_options (similarity measure): ['msd', 'cosine']

  • msd (mean squared difference): Measures rating vector distance
  • cosine: Measures angular similarity

Cross-Validation Process:

  • cv=3: 3-fold cross-validation
  • measures=['rmse']: Optimize for RMSE
  • n_jobs=-1: Use all CPU cores for parallelization

Grid Search Algorithm:

  1. Generate all parameter combinations: 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 combinations
  2. For each combination:
  3. Perform 3-fold cross-validation
  4. Compute average RMSE
  5. Select combination with lowest average RMSE

Output Interpretation:

  • best_score['rmse']: Lowest RMSE achieved across all combinations
  • best_params['rmse']: Hyperparameters that achieved this score

Computational Cost: 18 combinations × 3 folds = 54 model trainings. Parallelization reduces wall-clock time.

Impact: Improves model performance through systematic hyperparameter optimization rather than arbitrary choices.

  • Lower RMSE than baseline
  • Higher precision and/or recall
  • Better F1-score

Why Optimization Helps:

  • Appropriate k: Balances local pattern capture with noise reduction
  • Appropriate min_k: Avoids unreliable predictions from too few neighbors
  • Optimal similarity metric: MSD may outperform cosine for this specific dataset's characteristics

Impact: Demonstrates that careful hyperparameter tuning yields measurable performance gains.

docs.title: Item-Item Collaborative Filtering
docs.text:
sim_options = {'name': 'cosine', 'user_based': False}
sim_item_item = KNNBasic(sim_options=sim_options, random_state=1, verbose=False)
sim_item_item.fit(trainset)
precision_recall_at_k(sim_item_item, k=10, threshold=3.5)

Purpose: Implements item-item collaborative filtering by computing similarities between products instead of users.

Key Difference: 

'user_based': False
This single parameter change transforms the algorithm from user-user to item-item similarity.

Item-Item Logic:

  1. Compute similarity between all product pairs based on co-rating patterns
  2. For prediction, identify products similar to those the user rated highly
  3. Weight these similar products' ratings by similarity scores

Why Item-Item Often Outperforms User-User:

  • Stability: Product characteristics are more stable than user preferences
  • Sparsity: Typically fewer items than users, creating denser similarity matrix
  • Interpretability: "Similar products" is intuitive to users
  • Precomputation: Item similarity matrix can be cached and updated incrementally

Impact: Provides an alternative collaborative filtering approach that may perform better depending on data characteristics.

docs.title: Recommendation Generation Function
docs.text:
def get_recommendations(data, user_id, top_n, algo):
    recommendations = []

    user_item_interactions_matrix = data.pivot(index='user_id', columns='prod_id', 
                                               values='rating')

    non_interacted_products = user_item_interactions_matrix.loc[user_id][
        user_item_interactions_matrix.loc[user_id].isnull()].index.tolist()

    for item_id in non_interacted_products:
        est = algo.predict(user_id, item_id).est
        recommendations.append((item_id, est))

    recommendations.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
    return recommendations[:top_n]

Purpose: Generates top-N product recommendations for a specific user by predicting ratings for all unobserved products.

Flow:

Step 1: Create User-Item Matrix 

user_item_interactions_matrix = data.pivot(index='user_id', columns='prod_id', values='rating')
Transforms long-format data into wide matrix with users as rows, products as columns, ratings as values.

Step 2: Identify Unobserved Products 

non_interacted_products = user_item_interactions_matrix.loc[user_id][
    user_item_interactions_matrix.loc[user_id].isnull()].index.tolist()

  • Select user's row from matrix
  • Find columns (products) with null values (not rated)
  • Extract product IDs as list

Step 3: Predict Ratings 

for item_id in non_interacted_products:
    est = algo.predict(user_id, item_id).est
    recommendations.append((item_id, est))
For each unobserved product, predict rating and store (product_id, predicted_rating) tuple.

Step 4: Rank by Predicted Rating 

recommendations.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
return recommendations[:top_n]
Sort predictions descending by rating, return top N.

Computational Consideration: If a user hasn't interacted with 10,000 products, this generates 10,000 predictions. For production systems, candidates are pre-filtered or sampled.

Impact: Encapsulates the complete recommendation pipeline in a reusable function.

docs.title: SVD Baseline Model
docs.text:
svd = SVD(random_state=1, verbose=False)
svd.fit(trainset)
precision_recall_at_k(svd, k=10, threshold=3.5)

Purpose: Trains a baseline matrix factorization model using Singular Value Decomposition.

SVD Algorithm Overview:

SVD decomposes the user-item rating matrix R (dimensions U × I) into three matrices:

R ≈ P × Σ × Q^T

Where: - P (U × f): User latent factor matrix - Σ (f × f): Diagonal matrix of singular values - Q (I × f): Item latent factor matrix - f: Number of latent factors (dimensionality of latent space)

Prediction Formula:

For user u and item i: 

r̂_ui = μ + b_u + b_i + p_u · q_i

Where: - μ: Global rating mean - b_u: User bias (tendency to rate higher/lower than average) - b_i: Item bias (tendency to receive higher/lower ratings) - p_u · q_i: Dot product of user and item latent factor vectors

Training Process:

Uses Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) to minimize: 

Σ(r_ui - r̂_ui)² + λ(||p_u||² + ||q_i||² + b_u² + b_i²)

This is sum of squared errors plus L2 regularization to prevent overfitting.

Why SVD Works for Sparse Data:

  • Learns latent representations from observed ratings
  • Generalizes to unobserved entries through latent space geometry
  • Captures complex preference patterns in lower-dimensional space

Default Hyperparameters:

  • n_factors: 100 (latent factor dimensionality)
  • n_epochs: 20 (training iterations)
  • lr_all: 0.005 (learning rate)
  • reg_all: 0.02 (regularization)

Expected Performance: SVD typically outperforms similarity-based methods due to superior sparse data handling.

Impact: Establishes matrix factorization baseline for comparison with optimized version.

docs.title: SVD Predictions
docs.text:
svd.predict("A3LDPF5FMB782Z", "1400501466", r_ui=5, verbose=True)
svd.predict("A34BZM6S9L7QI4", "1400501466", verbose=True)

Purpose: Demonstrates SVD predictions for observed and unobserved user-item pairs.

Prediction Components:

When verbose=True, output shows:

  • User and item IDs
  • True rating (if known)
  • Estimated rating from model
  • Additional details specific to SVD (may include individual bias terms)

Interpretation:

For observed interaction: Compare prediction to true rating. Close values indicate good model fit; large deviations suggest the interaction is unusual or that the model has systematic bias.

For unobserved interaction: Predicted rating is the recommendation confidence score. Higher predictions suggest stronger user-item affinity.

Impact: Validates that SVD produces reasonable predictions consistent with learned user/item patterns.

docs.title: SVD Hyperparameter Tuning
docs.text:
param_grid = {'n_epochs': [10, 20, 30], 
              'lr_all': [0.001, 0.005, 0.01],
              'reg_all': [0.2, 0.4, 0.6]}

gs = GridSearchCV(SVD, param_grid, measures=['rmse'], cv=3, n_jobs=-1)
gs.fit(data)

print(gs.best_score['rmse'])
print(gs.best_params['rmse'])

Purpose: Optimizes three critical SVD hyperparameters through grid search cross-validation.

Hyperparameter Space:

n_epochs: [10, 20, 30]

  • Number of SGD training iterations
  • More epochs → better convergence but longer training and potential overfitting
  • Fewer epochs → faster training but potential underfitting

lr_all (learning rate): [0.001, 0.005, 0.01]

  • Step size for gradient descent updates
  • Higher learning rate → faster convergence but risk of overshooting/instability
  • Lower learning rate → stable convergence but slow and may get stuck in local minima

reg_all (regularization): [0.2, 0.4, 0.6]

  • L2 penalty on model parameters
  • Higher regularization → simpler model, less overfitting, potentially underfits
  • Lower regularization → complex model, better training fit, risk of overfitting

Grid Search Process:

  • Total combinations: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27
  • Cross-validation: 3-fold for each combination = 81 model trainings
  • Optimization target: Minimize RMSE
  • Parallelization: n_jobs=-1 uses all CPU cores

Mathematical Insight:

The three hyperparameters interact:

  • High learning rate + low regularization → unstable, overfits
  • Low learning rate + high regularization → underfits, doesn't learn
  • Optimal zone balances convergence speed, stability, and generalization

Output:

  • best_score: Lowest RMSE achieved
  • best_params: Optimal hyperparameter combination

Impact: Systematic optimization typically improves RMSE by 3-10% and improves precision/recall metrics meaningfully.

docs.title: Optimized SVD Model
docs.text:
svd_optimized = SVD(n_epochs=20, lr_all=0.005, reg_all=0.4, 
                    random_state=1, verbose=False)
svd_optimized.fit(trainset)
precision_recall_at_k(svd_optimized, k=10, threshold=3.5)

Purpose: Trains final SVD model using optimal hyperparameters identified by grid search.

Optimal Configuration (example values):

  • n_epochs=20: Sufficient iterations for convergence
  • lr_all=0.005: Balanced learning rate
  • reg_all=0.4: Moderate regularization preventing overfitting

Expected Results:

  • RMSE: Lower than baseline SVD
  • Precision@10: Higher than baseline
  • Recall@10: Higher than baseline
  • F1-Score: Improved balance of precision and recall

Why Optimization Matters:

Even small RMSE improvements (e.g., 0.95 → 0.92) correspond to:

  • More accurate rating predictions
  • Better top-N recommendation quality
  • Improved user satisfaction and conversion rates

In production systems serving millions of users, such improvements generate substantial business value.

Comparison to Similarity-Based Models:

Optimized SVD typically outperforms optimized collaborative filtering because:

  • Better sparse data handling through dimensionality reduction
  • Captures complex interaction patterns in latent space
  • More efficient computation once trained

Impact: Represents the best-performing model in this tutorial and likely the best choice for production deployment.

docs.title: RMSE Computation
docs.text:
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) measures the average magnitude of prediction errors:

RMSE = √(Σ(r̂_ui - r_ui)² / N)

Where: - r̂_ui: Predicted rating for user u, item i - r_ui: True rating - N: Number of predictions

Interpretation:

  • RMSE in rating units (e.g., RMSE = 0.95 means average error of 0.95 rating points)
  • Lower is better
  • Squared errors penalize large deviations more than small ones

Why RMSE Matters:

  • Standard metric for regression problems
  • Directly measures prediction accuracy
  • Enables comparison across different models

Limitations:

  • Doesn't directly measure recommendation quality
  • Treats all prediction errors equally (but predicting 3 vs 4 may matter less than predicting 2 vs 5)
  • Can be dominated by a few large errors

docs.title: Precision@k Deep Dive
docs.text:
Precision@k measures the fraction of recommended items that are relevant:

Precision@k = |{recommended items that are relevant}| / k

Business Interpretation:

  • High precision: Users see mostly relevant recommendations → trust system
  • Low precision: Users see many irrelevant recommendations → lose trust, stop clicking

Example:

If k=10 and a user rates 7 of the 10 recommended items ≥3.5, then Precision@10 = 0.7

Trade-offs:

  • Easy to achieve high precision by only recommending "safe" popular items
  • But this sacrifices discovery and personalization
  • Balance precision with diversity and coverage

docs.title: Recall@k Deep Dive
docs.text:
Recall@k measures the fraction of relevant items that are recommended:

Recall@k = |{relevant items that are recommended}| / |{all relevant items}|

Business Interpretation:

  • High recall: System surfaces most products user would like → maximizes opportunity
  • Low recall: Many products user would like are never shown → lost sales

Example:

If a user has 20 relevant items in the test set and 8 appear in top-10 recommendations, Recall@10 = 8/20 = 0.4

Trade-offs:

  • Easy to achieve high recall by recommending many items (large k)
  • But this dilutes precision and overwhelms users
  • Must balance with precision

docs.title: F1-Score@k
docs.text:
F1-Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall:

F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

Why Harmonic Mean:

Penalizes imbalanced values more than arithmetic mean:

  • If Precision=0.9, Recall=0.1: Arithmetic mean=0.5, Harmonic mean=0.18
  • Forces systems to balance both metrics

When to Use F1:

  • When precision and recall are equally important
  • When you want a single metric summarizing recommendation quality
  • For comparing models when precision/recall trade-offs differ

Limitations:

  • May not reflect business priorities if precision and recall have different costs
  • Threshold selection (e.g., 3.5) significantly impacts results

docs.title: Cross-Validation
docs.text:
K-Fold Cross-Validation provides robust performance estimates:

Process:

  1. Split data into K equal folds
  2. For each fold:
  3. Train on K-1 folds
  4. Test on remaining fold
  5. Average metrics across K folds

Benefits:

  • Uses all data for both training and testing
  • Reduces variance in performance estimates
  • Detects overfitting (large train-test metric gap)

In This Tutorial:

GridSearchCV uses 3-fold cross-validation (cv=3), meaning each hyperparameter combination is evaluated on 3 different train-test splits, and the average RMSE is reported.

docs.title: What This Project Is
docs.text:
• A hands‑on topic modeling case study using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) on a corpus of academic papers.
  • You’ll see how to move from raw text → numeric features → probabilistic topics → human‑readable insights.
  • Two styles are common in this folder:
  • A practical scikit‑learn LDA runner (fast, good defaults).
  • (Optionally) a more educational SVI LDA implementation to see how the math runs step‑by‑step.

docs.title: How to Run Locally
docs.text:
↩ Back to Top The core script is run_lda.py (see code below). Typical runs:

# default (5 topics, unigrams)
python run_lda.py

# more topics
python run_lda.py --topics 8

# include bigrams
python run_lda.py --ngrams 2

# export artifacts
python run_lda.py --topics 8 --ngrams 2 \
  --save-csv lda_terms_8_bigram.csv \
  --save-doc-topics doc_topic_scores.csv

# optional visualization (if pyLDAvis is installed in your env)
python run_lda.py --topics 8 --ngrams 2 --out mit_topics.html

docs.title: Concepts You’ll Learn
docs.text:
↩ Back to Top LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation): an unsupervised probabilistic model where - each document is a mixture of topics, - each topic is a mixture of words.

Why it’s useful: It surfaces latent themes in large text corpora, helping you search, cluster, summarize, and discover.

Variational Inference (VI): an optimization-based approach to approximate the intractable posterior in LDA. - You posit a simpler family (variational distribution), then optimize it to be close to the true posterior. - Stochastic/online flavors process mini-batches for scalability.

docs.title: Pipeline: From Raw Text to Topics
docs.text: ↩ Back to Top 1. Load Data: read data/papers (JSON list of documents). 2. Preprocess: lowercasing, tokenization, removing stopwords, optionally include bigrams. 3. Vectorize: CountVectorizer → Document‑Term Matrix (rows=docs, cols=terms, values=counts). 4. Fit LDA: learn topic distributions over words and document distributions over topics. 5. Inspect: print top words, view top documents per topic, write CSVs. 6. Visualize (optional): pyLDAvis to explore the learned topics interactively. 7. Iterate: adjust K, pruning thresholds, n‑grams; compare results.

docs.title: “Compilation” vs “Execution” in ML Projects
docs.text:
There’s no C/C++ style compilation here. Instead, think in terms of data/ML pipeline construction:

  • Build phase (akin to compilation): Set up dependencies, load data, construct features (vectorizers), define model and hyperparameters.
  • Fit/Train phase: Run the optimizer/VI to estimate hidden variables and parameters.
  • Evaluation/Export phase (execution artifacts): Print topics, save CSVs, render HTML viz.
  • Reproducibility: Lock random seeds and versions to “re‑build” the same model later.

This “build → fit → evaluate → export” loop is the ML analog of compile → link → execute.

docs.title: Hyperparameters & Practical Tips
docs.text:
• --topics (K): higher K = finer granularity; too high fragments themes.
  • --ngrams: set to 2 to include bigrams; helpful for phrases like “neural network”.
  • --max_df / --min_df: prune ubiquitous/rare terms for cleaner topics.
  • --max_features: cap vocabulary if memory is tight.
  • --words-per-topic & --csv-words: control output verbosity.
  • Sanity checks: read the top documents for each topic; if they don’t make sense, tune pruning or K.

docs.title: Artifacts & How to Read Them
docs.text:
• Console topics: a quick glance at themes (top N terms).
  • lda_top_terms.csv (--save-csv): ranked words per topic for reports.
  • doc_topic_scores.csv (--save-doc-topics): topic mixture per document for filtering/ranking.
  • mit_topics.html: interactive topic map (if pyLDAvis available).

docs.title: Case Study - Data Analysis with Human-Generated Text/svilda.py
docs.text:
import random
import numpy as n
from scipy.special import psi
from nltk.tokenize import wordpunct_tokenize

meanchangethresh = 1e-3

def dirichlet_expectation(alpha):
    '''see onlineldavb.py by Blei et al'''
    if (len(alpha.shape) == 1):
        return (psi(alpha) - psi(n.sum(alpha)))
    return (psi(alpha) - psi(n.sum(alpha, 1))[:, n.newaxis])

class SVILDA():
    def __init__(self, vocab, K, D, alpha, eta, tau, kappa, iterations):
        self._vocab = vocab
        self._V = len(vocab)
        self._K = K
        self._D = D
        self._alpha = alpha
        self._eta = eta
        self._tau = tau+1
        self._kappa = kappa
        self._lambda = 1* n.random.gamma(100., 1./100., (self._K, self._V))
        self._Elogbeta = dirichlet_expectation(self._lambda)
        self._expElogbeta = n.exp(self._Elogbeta)
        self.ct = 0
        self._iterations = iterations

    def updateLocal(self, doc): #word_dn is an indicator variable with dimension V
        (wordids, wordcts) = doc
        batchD = len(wordids)

        # Initialize the variational distribution q(theta|gamma) for
        # the mini-batch
        gamma = 1*n.random.gamma(100., 1./100., (batchD, self._K))
        Elogtheta = dirichlet_expectation(gamma)
        expElogtheta = n.exp(Elogtheta)

        sstats = n.zeros(self._lambda.shape)
        # Now, for each document d update that document's gamma and phi
        it = 0
        meanchange = 0
        for d in range(0, batchD):
            # These are mostly just shorthand (but might help cache locality)
            ids = wordids[d]
            cts = wordcts[d]
            gammad = gamma[d, :]
            Elogthetad = Elogtheta[d, :]
            expElogthetad = expElogtheta[d, :]
            expElogbetad = self._expElogbeta[:, ids]
            # The optimal phi_{dwk} is proportional to 
            # expElogthetad_k * expElogbetad_w. phinorm is the normalizer.
            phinorm = n.dot(expElogthetad, expElogbetad) + 1e-100
            # Iterate between gamma and phi until convergence
            for it in range(0, 100):
                lastgamma = gammad
                # We represent phi implicitly to save memory and time.
                # Substituting the value of the optimal phi back into
                # the update for gamma gives this update. Cf. Lee&Seung 2001.
                gammad = self._alpha + n.multiply(expElogthetad, expElogbetad) * cts / phinorm
                Elogthetad = dirichlet_expectation(gammad)
                expElogthetad = n.exp(Elogthetad)
                phinorm = n.dot(expElogthetad, expElogbetad) + 1e-100
                # If gamma hasn't changed much, we're done.
                meanchange = n.mean(abs(gammad - lastgamma))
                if (meanchange < meanchangethresh):
                    break
            gamma[d, :] = gammad
            # Contribution of document d to the expected sufficient
            # statistics for the M step.
            sstats[:, ids] += n.multiply(expElogthetad, expElogbetad) * cts / phinorm

        # This step finishes computing the sufficient statistics for the
        # M step, so that
        # sstats[k, w] = \sum_d n_{dw} * phi_{dwk} 
        # = \sum_d n_{dw} * exp{Elogtheta_{dk} + Elogbeta_{kw}} / phinorm_{dw}.

        return gamma, sstats

    def updateGlobal(self, sstats, doc):
            # print 'updating global parameters'
        (words, counts) = doc

        rhot = (self.ct + self._tau) **(-self._kappa)

        self._lambda = self._lambda * (1-rhot) + rhot * (self._eta + self._D * sstats / len(words))

        self._Elogbeta = dirichlet_expectation(self._lambda)
        self._expElogbeta = n.exp(self._Elogbeta)


    def runSVI(self, doc_vecs):

        for i in range(self._iterations):            
            randint = random.randint(0, self._D-1)
            if (i%100)==0: 
                print("ITERATION", i, " running document number ", randint)

            doc = doc_vecs[randint]
            gamma_d, sstats = self.updateLocal(doc)
            self.updateGlobal(sstats, doc)
            self.ct += 1

docs.title: Enhanced Runner We Used (run_lda.py)
docs.text:
The enhanced runner you executed in this project (with flags for CSV, doc‑topic, top‑docs, etc.):

# Enhanced run_lda.py (used in your successful runs)
# - optional pyLDAvis
# - --save-csv, --save-doc-topics
# - --top-docs with de-duplication
# - words-per-topic controls
import os, json, argparse, csv, numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import LatentDirichletAllocation
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
HAS_VIZ = True
try:
    import pyLDAvis, pyLDAvis.sklearn
except Exception:
    HAS_VIZ = False
def topk_unique(scores, k, texts, snippet_len=120):
    if k <= 0: return []
    k = min(k, scores.shape[0])
    idx = np.argpartition(scores, -k)[-k:]
    idx = idx[np.argsort(scores[idx])][::-1]
    seen, out = set(), []
    for i in idx:
        key = texts[i][:snippet_len]
        if key not in seen:
            seen.add(key); out.append(i)
        if len(out) == k: break
    return out
def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--topics", type=int, default=5)
    p.add_argument("--max_df", type=float, default=0.95)
    p.add_argument("--min_df", type=int, default=2)
    p.add_argument("--max_features", type=int, default=20000)
    p.add_argument("--ngrams", type=int, choices=[1,2], default=1)
    p.add_argument("--words-per-topic", type=int, default=12)
    p.add_argument("--csv-words", type=int, default=20)
    p.add_argument("--save-csv", default="")
    p.add_argument("--top-docs", type=int, default=0)
    p.add_argument("--save-doc-topics", default="")
    p.add_argument("--out", default="lda_topics.html")
    p.add_argument("--mds", choices=["mmds","tsne"], default="mmds")
    args = p.parse_args()
    ROOT = os.path.dirname(__file__)
    data_file = os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "papers")
    if not os.path.exists(data_file):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Missing data file: {data_file}")
    with open(data_file, "r") as f:
        papers = json.load(f)
    vectorizer = CountVectorizer(
        max_df=args.max_df, min_df=args.min_df, max_features=args.max_features,
        stop_words="english", ngram_range=(1, args.ngrams)
    )
    X = vectorizer.fit_transform(papers)
    lda = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=args.topics, learning_method="batch", random_state=0).fit(X)
    feature_names = vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()
    for k, topic in enumerate(lda.components_):
        top = topic.argsort()[-args.words_per_topic:][::-1]  # bug to remind this is illustrative
        terms = ", ".join(feature_names[i] for i in top)
        print(f"\\nTopic {k+1}: {terms}")
    if args.save_csv:
        with open(args.save_csv, "w", newline="") as f:
            w = csv.writer(f); w.writerow(["topic","rank","term"])
            for k, topic in enumerate(lda.components_):
                top = topic.argsort()[-args.csv_words:][::-1]
                for r, i in enumerate(top, start=1):
                    w.writerow([k+1, r, feature_names[i]])
        print(f"\\nSaved topic-term CSV: {args.save_csv}")
    doc_topic = lda.transform(X)
    if args.save_doc_topics:
        with open(args.save_doc_topics, "w", newline="") as f:
            w = csv.writer(f); header = ["doc_index"]+[f"topic_{i+1}" for i in range(lda.n_components)]
            w.writerow(header)
            for i, row in enumerate(doc_topic):
                w.writerow([i]+[f"{v:.6f}" for v in row])
        print(f"Saved doc→topic CSV: {args.save_doc_topics}")
    if args.top_docs>0:
        for t in range(doc_topic.shape[1]):
            top_idx = topk_unique(doc_topic[:,t], args.top_docs, papers)
            print(f"\\nTop {args.top_docs} docs for Topic {t+1}:")
            for i in top_idx:
                snippet = papers[i][:140].replace("\\n"," ")
                print(f"  • Doc {i}: {snippet}...")
    if HAS_VIZ:
        print(f"\\nSaving interactive visualization to: {args.out}")
        vis = pyLDAvis.sklearn.prepare(lda, X, vectorizer, mds=args.mds)
        pyLDAvis.save_html(vis, args.out); print("Done.")
    else:
        print("\\n(pyLDAvis not installed in this environment; printed topics only.)")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import numpy as np
from glob import glob
from PIL import Image
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import copy
import utils


def computeEigenFaces(S):
    dbx = np.array(S) #Converting into numpy array
    A = dbx # Note that the dbx here is transposed as compared to the original M script

    # Covariance matrix C=A'A, L=AA'
    covariance_matrix = np.matmul(A, A.T)

    A=None

    #Compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors from the covariance matrix
    eigen_values, eigen_vectors = np.linalg.eig(covariance_matrix)     


    # Sort and eliminate those whose eigenvalue is small based on the threshold.
    nonzero_eigenvals = eigen_values > 1e-4
    v = eigen_vectors[:,nonzero_eigenvals]
    d = eigen_values[nonzero_eigenvals]

    # Sort eigenvalues already sorted, but in descending order, so let's change this into ascending
    d = d[::-1]
    v = v[:,::-1] 


    # Reducing the number of dimensions by multiplying original vales and eigenvectors.
    u = []
    for i in range(len(d)):
        temp = np.sqrt(d[i])
        u.append(np.matmul(dbx.T, v[:,i])/temp) 

    # Normalization of reduced dimensions.
    for i in range(len(u)):
        kk = u[i]
        temp = np.sqrt(np.sum(np.square(kk)))
        u[i] = u[i]/temp

    return u


def reconstructNewFaces(u, mean_face, input_image = 'new_image.jpg'):

    eigen_face = np.array(u)

    # Read the input image and convert to gray scale     
    im = Image.open(input_image)
    InputImage = im.convert('L')

    # Converting to numpy array
    im_raw = np.asarray(InputImage)

    # Reshaping to vector
    InImage = np.reshape(im_raw.T,im_raw.shape[0]*im_raw.shape[1])

    # Normalization of the vector
    temp = InImage
    me=np.mean(temp)
    st=np.std(temp)
    temp=(temp-me)*st/(st+me)
    NormImage = temp

    # obtain the weights by dotting the normalized image with the eigenfaces
    weights = np.matmul(u, NormImage.T)

    # To reconstruct a face, we dot the weights with the eigenfaces, and add the mean face.
    ReshapedImage = mean_face + np.matmul(weights, u)

    # Converting back to image
    ReshapedImage = np.reshape(ReshapedImage,im_raw.shape)
    ReshapedImage = ReshapedImage.T

    return ReshapedImage

grid_im = utils.gray_images_square_grid(np.array(all_faces))
plt.imshow(grid_im, cmap='gray')


# Normalize the images

# Compute average face

# Calling the above function which results the eigenfaces
EigenFaces = computeEigenFaces(S)

# Now render the eigenfaces
EigenFacesIm = []

#Visualizaing the eigenfaces
for i in range(len(EigenFaces)):
    img = np.reshape(EigenFaces[i], (300,300))
    img = img.T
    # Scale the image
    img = utils.convertImageToU8bit(img)
    # convert and save
    im = Image.fromarray(img)
    im.convert('RGB').save('eigenfaces/eigen_{}.jpeg'.format(i+1))

    EigenFacesIm.append(img)

_, eigen_faces = utils.loadFaces('.\\eigenfaces\\')
grid_im = utils.gray_images_square_grid(np.array(eigen_faces))
plt.imshow(grid_im, cmap='gray')
