docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Continuous human review is critical for maintaining and improving Large Language Model (LLM) pipelines, as automated evaluators alone cannot catch subtle errors, surface unexpected issues, or refine nuanced quality definitions. As outlined in Lesson 10 - Interfaces for Continuous Human Review and Error Analysis, human oversight complements the Analyze-Measure-Improve lifecycle (Figure 2) by addressing LLM-as-Judge drift and evolving quality criteria. The challenge is to involve humans effectively given the vast number of production traces, as slow or cumbersome review processes can stall the Improve phase.

Back to Top

docs.title: The Case for Custom Review Interfaces
docs.text:
Investing in custom-built review interfaces maximizes the speed, quality, and impact of human feedback.

  • Limitations of Existing Tools:
  • Common tools like spreadsheets and generic log viewers struggle with complex LLM traces (long inputs, intermediate reasoning, tool calls, RAG context, final outputs).
  • They make navigation tedious, structured/free-form feedback difficult, and lack LLM-specific features, leading to reviewer fatigue and lower-quality annotations.
  • Benefits of Custom Interfaces: Improve consistency and efficiency by presenting trace information in digestible, visually intuitive ways (e.g., displaying emails as formatted emails, using color-coded tags for document annotations).
  • Ease of Creation: Modern web frameworks or LLMs can rapidly generate basic interfaces from natural language prompts, reducing the need for extensive frontend development.

Back to Top

docs.title: Principles of Effective Review Interfaces
docs.text:
Effective review interfaces are guided by Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) principles:

  • Visibility of System Status: Show which trace is being reviewed, how many remain, and feedback status.
  • Match Between System and Real World: Use familiar terms from rubrics and evaluation criteria.
  • User Control and Freedom: Allow easy navigation, undo actions, and deferring uncertain cases.
  • Consistency and Standards: Maintain consistent layouts and terminology across traces.
  • Error Prevention: Use distinct labeling controls and require rationales for “Fail” judgments.
  • Recognition Rather Than Recall: Visually present predefined failure modes to reduce cognitive load.
  • Flexibility and Efficiency of Use: Offer keyboard shortcuts and intuitive design for novices and experts.
  • Aesthetic and Minimalist Design: Emphasize signal over noise, clearly highlighting inputs and outputs.
  • Essential Interface Elements: Display full LLM traces (collapsing less important sections by default), support structured feedback (checkboxes, buttons, quick ratings like thumbs up/down), and include open-ended feedback fields.
  • Features to Improve Speed and Quality:
  • Inline annotation for highlighting issues.
  • Keyboard shortcuts for rapid actions.
  • Visual hierarchy to emphasize key trace components.
  • Batch review and bulk actions for labeling multiple examples.
  • Progressive disclosure to simplify the interface.
  • Feedback templates for common comments.
  • “Defer” option for uncertain cases to maintain label accuracy.
  • Contextual metadata display and filters.
  • Progress indicators for reviewed counts.

The speed of data review directly correlates with the engineering velocity of an AI application.

Back to Top

docs.title: Case Study: EvalGen Interface and Insight
docs.text:
EvalGen is a lightweight, early-stage interface for human evaluation, showing one output at a time, supporting binary feedback, open-ended comments, editable labels, and a basic rubric builder. It prioritizes traces where multiple automated LLM judges disagree.

  • Insight: User studies revealed that human reviewers experience criteria drift, refining their understanding of “correctness,” revising past judgments, and adding new failure categories. Review tools must treat evaluation as an evolving sensemaking process, not a static labeling task.
  • Features: EvalGen supports dynamic rubric updates, allowing reviewers to propose new failure modes during review. It logs reviewer comments to track evolving quality criteria, enabling iterative refinement of evaluation standards and integration with the Analyze-Measure-Improve cycle.

Back to Top

docs.title: Selecting Traces from the “Firehose” for Human Review
docs.text:
Given the impossibility of reviewing every production trace, smart strategies prioritize traces likely to uncover quality issues or improve the system:

  • Random Sampling: Provides an unbiased overview of performance but may miss rare issues.
  • Uncertainty Sampling: Focuses on traces where automated evaluators disagree or are unsure (e.g., failing some criteria but not others, inconsistent LLM judge results with temperature > 0, or conflicting evaluators). These are often the most informative for human review.
  • Failure-Driven Sampling: Targets obviously problematic cases identified by guardrail failures, timeouts, or user feedback. High-precision but may miss subtle issues.

Back to Top

docs.title: Navigating Trace Groups and Discovering Patterns
docs.text:
Many issues become visible only when examining groups of traces:

  • Clustering: Groups traces by metadata (e.g., client persona, feature used) or semantic similarity (using embeddings of inputs/outputs) to reveal latent categories and systematic failures.
  • Search and Similarity Tools: Enable reviewers to find similar examples by keyword, metadata filters, or conceptual content. Blending group-level tools with targeted sampling directs attention to the most informative data.
  • Pattern Discovery: Interfaces should support visualizations (e.g., failure heatmaps, clustering plots) to highlight recurring issues, such as consistent misinterpretations in specific contexts.

Back to Top

docs.title: Integrating Human Review into the Bigger Engineering Workflow
docs.text:
For human review to be valuable, it must integrate into the team’s engineering workflow:

  • Automated Systems: Schedule daily/weekly trace selection and notify reviewers.
  • Alerts: Route high-priority issues (e.g., guardrail failures) to on-call reviewers immediately.
  • Feedback Flow:
  • Golden Dataset: Add human-labeled traces (especially failures) to the CI golden dataset for regression testing.
  • LLM-as-Judge Evaluators: Use human labels to monitor judge accuracy, revising prompts or few-shot examples if True Positive Rate (TPR) or True Negative Rate (TNR) drops.
  • Lightweight Actions: Support actions like adding traces to the CI golden set or filing prefilled bug reports. Dashboards should show review activity and trends to prioritize fixes.

Back to Top

docs.title: Example Walkthrough: Reviewing Real Estate Assistant Emails
docs.text:
This section illustrates the evolution from a basic spreadsheet (awkward, slow, error-prone) to a lightweight custom UI (clear layout, faster decisions) and an advanced interface. The advanced UI features:

  • Rich, readable layouts for traces, including intermediate reasoning/tool usage.
  • Visual formatting for key entities (e.g., property details).
  • Structured feedback options (predefined tags, hotkeys, metadata).
  • Group-level exploration tools (clustering, search) for pattern detection and bulk labeling.

Small UI improvements significantly enhance review speed and label quality.

Back to Top

docs.title: Case Study: DocWrangler for Prompt Refinement
docs.text:
DocWrangler, an IDE for LLM-powered document processing, accelerates iterative development by displaying the original document, generated output, and prompt side-by-side. It supports:

  • Open Coding: Reviewers jot natural-language comments on outputs to identify recurring issues.
  • Prompt Refinement: Uses comments and the current prompt to suggest updates, presenting both versions side-by-side to close the feedback loop.

This approach helps reviewers refine their understanding of errors and improve prompts iteratively.

Back to Top

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Continuous human review is critical for high-quality LLM applications, as automated evaluation alone is insufficient. Custom interfaces designed with HCI principles enable efficient, high-quality feedback by presenting clear trace context, structured feedback mechanisms, and features to reduce cognitive load. Smart sampling (random, uncertainty-based, failure-driven) focuses human attention on valuable traces. Integrating review into the engineering workflow via automated scheduling, alerts, and feedback loops (e.g., updating golden datasets, refining LLM-as-Judge prompts) ensures actionable insights. By enabling rapid problem identification and iteration, these interfaces build more reliable LLM systems.

Back to Top

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Introduction
  • Accuracy Optimization
  • Quick Wins and Best Practices for Cost Reduction
  • Leveraging LLM Provider Caching
  • Advanced Strategy: Implementing Model Cascades
  • Summary

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Improve phase, as outlined in Lesson 11 - Improvement, is where insights from the Analyze and Measure phases of the Analyze-Measure-Improve lifecycle (Figure 2) are applied to enhance Large Language Model (LLM) pipelines. This phase focuses on improving both the quality of results (accuracy optimization) and system efficiency (cost optimization). Effective improvements rely on established evaluators and monitoring systems to ensure robust and cost-effective LLM systems.

Back to Top

docs.title: Accuracy Optimization
docs.text:
Improving accuracy increases the likelihood of the LLM producing correct, helpful, or expected outputs. Strategies progress from quick, low-effort wins to significant structural and model-level changes.

  • Quick Wins (Prompt Refinement):
  • Clarify Ambiguous Wording: Update prompts with explicit language or disambiguating examples to address LLM misunderstandings.
  • Add a Few Examples: Include 2-3 representative input/output pairs targeting observed failure cases (distinct from CI test cases) to guide the model.
  • Use Role-Based Guidance: Assign a persona (e.g., “You are a careful tax advisor...”) to steer tone and reasoning for open-ended tasks.
  • Ask for Step-by-Step Reasoning: For logical or multi-step tasks, instruct the LLM to “think step by step” to improve correctness and completeness.
  • Structural Changes:
  • Break Task into Smaller Steps: Decompose complex tasks into a sequence of smaller LLM calls for targeted prompts and easier error isolation (e.g., extracting preferences, querying a database, filtering results, generating a message).
  • Tune RAG Steps: Enhance retrieval quality by reworking the retriever query, adjusting document chunking, changing the number of retrieved chunks, or adding a re-ranking step.
  • Fix Tool Misuse: Clarify tool prompt descriptions (e.g., acceptable values/formats) to address incorrect tool calls or argument errors.
  • Add Lightweight Checks: Implement validations (e.g., regexes for malformed outputs, length constraints, blacklists) to catch common failure modes.
  • Heavier Fixes:
  • Fine-Tuning: For persistent issues in high-value tasks with hundreds of labeled examples, fine-tune the model to lock in improvements (slower, more expensive).
  • Add Human Review Loops: For high-stakes or subtle failure modes, build lightweight interfaces for regular human review of sampled outputs to inform fine-tuning datasets.
  • Prompt Optimization: Treat prompts as tunable artifacts, testing variations against golden sets using formal techniques (e.g., grid search, reinforcement learning) after exhausting other methods.

Back to Top

docs.title: Quick Wins and Best Practices for Cost Reduction
docs.text:
Cost optimization delivers the same quality more efficiently with low-effort strategies.

  • Tiered Model Selection:
  • Assess task requirements within the pipeline.
  • Use smaller, faster, cheaper models for simple, high-volume tasks (e.g., text classification, data extraction, intent recognition).
  • Reserve premium models for tasks requiring sophisticated reasoning or high-stakes accuracy (e.g., routing complex chatbot queries to a more expensive model).
  • Divide and Conquer with Task Decomposition:
  • Break workflows into sub-tasks, assigning cheaper models to intermediate stages.
  • For RAG, use a cost-effective embedding model for retrieval, a fast LLM or re-ranker for filtering, and a capable model only for final answer synthesis to reduce tokens sent to expensive models.
  • Cutting Tokens in Prompts:
  • Optimize Input/Prompt Tokens: Use concise instructions and tune the number of retrieved documents in RAG.
  • Pre-process Inputs into Summaries: Use a cheaper model to summarize long documents for subsequent calls.
  • Optimize Output Tokens: Instruct the LLM to be concise or use compact formats like YAML instead of prose or JSON to reduce generated tokens.

Back to Top

docs.title: Leveraging LLM Provider Caching
docs.text:
Many LLM API providers use caching to reduce latency and cost by reusing intermediate key/value (KV) states.

  • Mechanism: Reuses cached KV states for prompts starting with the same token sequence (prefix), computing states only for new suffixes.
  • Maximizing Cache Reuse: Place constant instructions before user-provided or changing data and maintain consistent formatting/phrasing across requests.

Back to Top

docs.title: Advanced Strategy: Implementing Model Cascades
docs.text:
Model cascades approximate the accuracy of a trusted, expensive “oracle” model at lower cost using a cheaper “proxy” model.

  • Workflow: The proxy model attempts to answer a query. If confident, its answer is returned; otherwise, the query escalates to the oracle model.
  • Confidence Quantification: Use log probabilities from LLM APIs to estimate confidence. For classification tasks, convert logprobs to normalized probabilities. For generative tasks, use heuristics like average log probability per token or total sequence log probability, requiring experimentation.
  • Building and Tuning the Cascade: Set confidence thresholds for the proxy model, tuning separate thresholds for classification classes or a global threshold for generative tasks. Evaluate proxy predictions against oracle outputs using a binary scoring function (e.g., LLM-as-Judge checking if proxy output matches oracle information). Aim for a desired match rate with the oracle while maximizing proxy usage. Extend to multi-stage cascades with models ordered by cost.

Back to Top

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Improve phase is a continuous process covering accuracy and cost optimization. Accuracy improvements start with prompt refinement (clarifying wording, adding examples, role-based guidance, step-by-step reasoning), progress to structural changes (task decomposition, RAG tuning, tool fixes, lightweight checks), and may require heavier fixes (fine-tuning, human review loops, prompt optimization). Cost optimization includes tiered model selection, task decomposition, token reduction, caching, and model cascades. All improvements rely on robust evaluation and monitoring, with successful changes integrated into the CI pipeline to ensure persistence. This iterative process adapts to changes in models, data, and use cases, maintaining reliable LLM systems.

Back to Top

docs.title: Introduction: Importance of Evaluations
docs.text:
GitHub Copilot evolved from a basic code completer to a robust AI-assisted coding tool through rigorous evaluations. Originally met with skepticism, it matured as evaluations offered strong, consistent signals to engineers. Evaluations became the foundation for iterative product improvement and were seen as essential for shaping Copilot's development direction.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: Categories of Evaluation
docs.text:
Evaluations at GitHub Copilot spanned a gradient from purely programmatic to deeply subjective:

  • Algorithmic: Validate outputs using schema rules, length checks, or compilation tests.
  • Verifiable: Ensure code behaves correctly through real executions and test validations.
  • LLM as Judge: Use LLMs for qualitative judgments when human review doesn't scale.
  • AB Testing: Industry-standard user-based feedback loop for real-world performance.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: Harness Lib: Offline Verifiable Evaluation
docs.text:
A modular library used for offline testing code completions:

  • Test Sample Pipeline:
  • Filtered high-quality open-source repos.
  • Extracted functions tied to passing unit tests.

  • Generated completions and validated with preexisting unit tests.

  • Key Learnings:

  • Avoided training data contamination by working closely with OpenAI.
  • Balanced subjective realism (production-like traffic) and flexibility.
  • Offered both notebook experimentation and pipeline automation.
  • Highlighted the need for modularity and caching.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: AB Testing for Shipping Changes
docs.text:
AB testing played a vital role in deploying updates gradually:

  • Key Metrics:
  • Completion acceptance rate.
  • Characters retained post-edit.

  • Latency.

  • Guardrail Metrics:

  • Dozens of secondary diagnostics to detect anomalies.

  • Tradeoffs:

  • Maximizing one metric could compromise another.
  • Required detective work and robust data science analysis.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: LLM as Judge for Subjective Evaluation
docs.text:
As Copilot Chat emerged, subjective evaluation grew vital:

  • Challenges:

  • Judging conversation usefulness and productivity, not just output.

  • Evolution:

  • Started with manual comparison.
  • GPT-4 initially failed with vague rubrics.

  • Bullet-point grading criteria improved consistency.

  • Outcome:

  • LLMs became scalable judges for non-code tasks.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: Key Learnings and Meta Insights
docs.text:
• Two Personas of Eval:
  • Regression-safe engineers.

  • Experimental prototype builders.

  • Timing Matters:

  • "Vibe checks" early on, structured evals after prototype stabilization.

  • Surprises:

  • Users prefer shorter completions.

  • Many guardrail metrics were born from past failures.

  • Ultimate Insight:

  • Evals are tools for building, not blockers to innovation.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: Motivation for Error Analysis
docs.text:
Experts argue that manual inspection of model outputs is the highest ROI activity in AI product development. Focusing on the data—rather than tools or frameworks—prevents many early pitfalls. Observing raw outputs reveals patterns faster than any metric or automation.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: What is Error Analysis?
docs.text:
A practical and iterative technique for dealing with errors in AI systems. It:

  • Guides where to invest engineering time.
  • Helps convert "bad vibes" into actionable fixes.
  • Informs what to measure and track over time.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: Multi-Stage Process
docs.text:
1. Manual Review: Inspect model outputs and jot down observations.
  2. Categorization: Group similar issues, potentially with LLM support.
  3. Pivot Table: Map outputs to issue categories and count them.
  4. Iterative Fixes: Adjust prompts, models, or frameworks. Create new metrics if needed.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: Case Study: AI Email Recruiter
docs.text:
Using Llama 370B, emails to candidates often sounded off:

  • Sounded like rejections unintentionally.
  • Confused sender/recipient.
  • Referenced irrelevant resume info.
  • Contained generic, verbose language.

Without error analysis, prompt changes led to new issues—a "whack-a-mole" problem.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: Importance of Custom Annotation Tools
docs.text:
Generic tools slow the process. Instead:

  • Build interfaces tailored to your data type.
  • Render natural formats (emails, plots, code).
  • Add:
  • Open-ended feedback box.
  • Hotkeys and navigation.
  • Save/export options.

Fast to build with AI coding tools; often <10 mins.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: Annotation Best Practices
docs.text:
• Start Free-form: Don't classify too early.
  • Manual is Mandatory: Don’t LLM your first pass.
  • Record Critical Feedback: Look for high-severity problems early.
  • Use Voice Transcription if needed.
  • Stop When You Stop Learning: Not at a fixed number.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: From Notes to Eval Metrics
docs.text:
• Convert notes into failure modes.
  • Build a pivot table to prioritize fixes.
  • Develop concrete, domain-specific metrics.
  • Decide whether it's a retrieval or prompt issue.
  • Use LLMs to scale evaluations post-categorization.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Build your own annotation UI.
  2. Delay categorization—start with free-form notes.
  3. Keep annotating until discoveries taper off.
  4. Error analysis is the foundation of model improvement.
  5. It's the highest ROI task in AI development.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This guide summarizes key research papers and insights in generative AI, large language models (LLMs), and related fields, focusing on their contributions to AI development, safety, ethics, and applications. The selected works span foundational concepts, system architectures, governance, and domain-specific implementations, providing a comprehensive overview for researchers and practitioners.

Back to Top

docs.title: Shankar & Sim (2024/2025) – Generative AI on the Loose
docs.text:
Generative AI on the Loose: Impact of Improved AI and Expert Oversight on Knowledge Sharing

  • Overview: An empirical study analyzing the interplay between advanced GenAI systems (e.g., GPT-4) and expert moderation on platforms like Stack Overflow.
  • Core Findings:
  • Combining high-performing GenAI with strict expert oversight reduces content volume but improves quality and reliability.
  • Relaxed moderation leads to a surge in lower-quality or hallucinated content.
  • Novice users benefit most from expert moderation for quality maintenance.
  • Methodology: Natural experiment around GPT-4 adoption and Stack Overflow policy changes, using mixed methods to measure content volume and quality across user skill tiers.
  • Implications: GenAI requires moderation for quality; platform design (e.g., moderation policies) significantly impacts content trustworthiness.
  • Reference: Shankar & Sim (June 2024 / Feb 2025 revision), SSRN: Generative AI on the Loose

Back to Top

docs.title: Shankar et al. (2024d) – Clarification
docs.text:
No separate publication titled Shankar et al. (2024d) is indexed in generative AI or AI safety literature as of July 2025. It likely refers to: - The fourth revision of Shankar & Sim (2024/2025), “Generative AI on the Loose.” - An unpublished or internal work not yet public.

  • Known Public Record: The Shankar & Sim (2024/2025) SSRN paper is the most likely source.

Back to Top

docs.title: Bommasani et al. (2021) – Foundation Models
docs.text:
On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models

  • Overview: A landmark Stanford report introducing foundation models—large-scale models pretrained via self-supervised learning, adaptable for downstream tasks.
  • Key Contributions:
  • Defines foundation models (e.g., BERT, GPT-3, CLIP).
  • Highlights emergent behaviors and transfer capabilities across modalities.
  • Warns of homogenization risks from shared base models.
  • Urges interdisciplinary study across ethics, policy, and technical design.
  • Risks Highlighted:
  • Model biases and societal inequities.
  • Lack of interpretability and safety mechanisms.
  • Environmental costs of training.
  • Over-centralization in deployment and research.
  • Use Case Domains: Education, healthcare, legal systems, human-AI interaction.
  • Reference: Bommasani et al., 2021 (arXiv)

docs.title: Q: Reconciling Scores & Rubrics
docs.text:
How do you reconcile having concrete scores with iteratively improving the rubric during inter-annotator discussions... Does a low Cohen's Kappa signal a rubric issue?

A: - Low Cohen’s Kappa often signals poor rubric clarity or misaligned annotator understanding. - Disagreement might stem from large surface area or non-expert annotation. - High-enough agreement is acceptable; perfect alignment is not required and often too costly. - The goal is shared understanding, not perfection.

📚 Reference: - Cohen’s Kappa Explained – StatQuest

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: AWS vs Notebooks for Prototyping
docs.text:
Should you fight through AWS Bedrock complexity or use a notebook to keep learning momentum?

A: - Use notebooks to keep progressing. - AWS is complex—even experienced engineers struggle with it. - You can move to deployment later.

📚 Reference: - Why AWS is hard – Forrest Brazeal

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: User Engagement Prediction
docs.text:
How to build binary evaluations around response likelihood? Should you begin with error analysis?

A: - Yes—start with error analysis. - It’s the most impactful way to guide what you build and test. - Use it to balance unit tests vs trace-level analysis.

📚 Reference: - Open Coding in Practice (YouTube)

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: Error Analysis: End-to-End
docs.text:
Should error analysis be trace-level rather than on every single LLM step?

A: - Yes, review trace start and end. - If end is good, skip; if bad, find the first error, code it, and move on. - Keeps analysis tractable and fast.

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: Universal Tracing & Logging
docs.text:
Is it worth building a universal trace logger? Are logging standards emerging?

A: - Python/TypeScript dominate vendor SDKs. - Vendor lock-in is hard to avoid. - OpenTelemetry helps, but homegrown S3 + custom annotation interfaces are valid. - No robust standards exist for LLM-specific logging yet.

📚 Reference: - Phoenix Tracing OSS - OpenTelemetry Tracing

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: Multiple SMEs & Sampling
docs.text:
Is it OK to have many SMEs across regions/products? What sampling strategy is best?

A: - Yes, as long as scopes are clear. - Appoint a "benevolent dictator" per dimension. - Start with random sampling, then move to stratified and exploratory methods.

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: Fine-Tuning Tradeoffs
docs.text:
When does fine-tuning stop being worth it? Can the LLM judge be fine-tuned for a recursive loop?

A: - Fine-tuning can help with specific structural/stylistic tasks. - But model updates (e.g., GPT-4.1) can make your fine-tune obsolete quickly. - Judge fine-tuning is valid—but you may need to tune both model and judge.

📚 Reference: - Anthropic on Model Evaluation

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: Prompt Iteration Challenges
docs.text:
How do you fix one part of a prompt without breaking others?

A: - Split into smaller sub-agents if needed. - If all else fails, try a more powerful model. - Fine-tuning is a last resort if prompts are already very clean.

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: Debugging Agent Traces
docs.text:
How do you debug long-agent workflows with long delays (e.g., 30 min execution)?

A: - Use analytics + test harnesses. - Gather a few failing examples and iterate. - Use guardrails to realign the agent mid-process. - Start with one agent; add more only if needed.

📚 Reference: - GitHub Copilot Eval Strategy – YouTube

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: Quick Fixes vs Evals
docs.text:
Should you immediately fix obvious issues or wait until axial coding is complete?

A: - Fix obvious and high-impact errors immediately. - Use evals for more complex, nuanced issues. - Not all problems need a full judge or eval cycle.

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: Markdown from PDFs
docs.text:
If using a library to convert documents to Markdown, when should LLMs be involved?

A: - For deterministic format conversion, don’t use LLMs. - For nuanced interpretation (e.g., scanned docs), LLMs may help. - Write evals + iterate prompts if using LLMs for this.

📚 Reference: - pdf2markdown Tools – GitHub

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: LLM Judge Time Saving
docs.text:
What gains come from using an LLM judge, even with imperfect alignment? Do prompt suggestions apply to task or judge prompts?

A: - Even “pretty good” judges save time and provide feedback loops. - Use disagreement as fuel for prompting improvements. - Prompt suggestions can improve either task or judge prompts.

📚 Reference: - AlignEval Project (GitHub) - Doc ETL – Evaluation Workflow

🔝 Back to Top

docs.title: Q: Eval Framework Origins
docs.text:
How was the evaluation framework developed? How do you build such frameworks for new domains like agentic systems?

A: - Frameworks are distilled from real-world consulting experiences and recurring failure points. - Combines dimensionality reduction + open coding. - The "3 gulfs" model was conceived by Shreya and refined through teaching and field work.

📚 Reference: - Evaluation-Driven Development for Agentic Systems (Arawjo et al., 2024)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Generative Pretrained Transformers (GPTs) represent the foundational architecture for modern large language models. In AI agents, GPTs serve as the core reasoning engine, enabling natural language understanding, generation, and complex task execution through their transformer-based architecture.

docs.title: Architecture Components
docs.text:
• Multi-Head Self-Attention: Enables the model to focus on different parts of the input sequence simultaneously
  • Feed-Forward Networks: Process information through dense layers for feature transformation
  • Layer Normalization: Stabilizes training and improves convergence
  • Positional Encoding: Provides sequence order information to the attention mechanism

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
The attention mechanism is computed as:

\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

Where: - \(Q\) = Query matrix - \(K\) = Key matrix - \(V\) = Value matrix - \(d_k\) = Dimension of key vectors

docs.title: AI Agent Applications
docs.text:
• Task Planning: Breaking down complex objectives into manageable subtasks
  • Natural Language Interface: Enabling human-like communication with users
  • Code Generation: Automating software development tasks
  • Decision Making: Evaluating options and selecting optimal actions

docs.title: Implementation Example
docs.text:
from transformers import GPT2LMHeadModel, GPT2Tokenizer

# Initialize GPT model for agent communication
tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained('gpt2')
model = GPT2LMHeadModel.from_pretrained('gpt2')

# Agent reasoning pipeline
def agent_reasoning(task_description):
    inputs = tokenizer.encode(task_description, return_tensors='pt')
    outputs = model.generate(inputs, max_length=150, num_return_sequences=1)
    return tokenizer.decode(outputs[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Mixture of Experts (MoE) models revolutionize AI agent efficiency by utilizing specialized expert networks. This architecture enables agents to scale computational capacity while maintaining inference speed through selective expert activation.

docs.title: Core Architecture
docs.text:
• Gating Network: Routes inputs to appropriate expert networks
  • Expert Networks: Specialized sub-models for different task domains
  • Sparse Activation: Only activates relevant experts per input
  • Load Balancing: Ensures even distribution across experts

docs.title: Gating Mechanism
docs.text:
The gating function determines expert selection:

\[G(x) = \text{softmax}(W_g \cdot x)\]

Expert output combination:

\[y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} G(x)_i \cdot E_i(x)\]

Where: - \(G(x)_i\) = Gate weight for expert \(i\) - \(E_i(x)\) = Output from expert \(i\) - \(n\) = Number of experts

docs.title: AI Agent Benefits
docs.text:
• Specialization: Different experts handle specific task types (reasoning, coding, creative writing)
  • Efficiency: Reduced computational overhead through sparse activation
  • Scalability: Easy addition of new experts for emerging capabilities
  • Performance: Enhanced accuracy through domain-specific optimization

docs.title: Expert Specialization Examples
docs.text:
• Coding Expert: Optimized for programming tasks and debugging
  • Reasoning Expert: Enhanced logical inference and mathematical problem-solving
  • Creative Expert: Specialized for content generation and creative writing
  • Factual Expert: Focused on knowledge retrieval and fact-checking

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) represent specialized architectures designed for complex logical inference and problem-solving. In AI agents, LRMs provide enhanced reasoning capabilities through structured thinking processes and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

docs.title: Reasoning Components
docs.text:
• Chain-of-Thought Processing: Step-by-step logical reasoning
  • Memory Integration: Access to long-term and working memory systems
  • RAG Integration: Real-time knowledge retrieval and synthesis
  • Verification Mechanisms: Self-checking and consistency validation

docs.title: RAG Architecture Integration
docs.text:
The RAG component enhances reasoning through:

\[\text{RAG}(q) = \text{LLM}(\text{concat}(q, \text{retrieve}(q, \mathcal{D})))\]

Where: - \(q\) = Input query - \(\mathcal{D}\) = Knowledge database - \(\text{retrieve}\) = Retrieval function - \(\text{concat}\) = Concatenation operation

docs.title: Reasoning Process Flow
docs.text:
• Problem Analysis: Decomposition of complex problems into sub-components
  • Knowledge Retrieval: Accessing relevant information from external sources
  • Logical Inference: Applying reasoning rules and logical operations
  • Solution Synthesis: Combining insights into coherent solutions
  • Verification: Checking solution validity and consistency

docs.title: AI Agent Applications
docs.text:
• Scientific Research: Hypothesis generation and experimental design
  • Legal Analysis: Case law research and argument construction
  • Medical Diagnosis: Symptom analysis and treatment recommendation
  • Financial Planning: Risk assessment and investment strategy

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable AI agents to process and understand multimodal information, combining visual perception with natural language understanding. These models are crucial for agents operating in real-world environments.

docs.title: Multimodal Architecture
docs.text:
• Vision Transformer (ViT): Processes visual input through attention mechanisms
  • Language Encoder: Handles textual information and instructions
  • Cross-Modal Attention: Aligns visual and textual representations
  • Fusion Layers: Combines multimodal features for unified understanding

docs.title: Cross-Modal Alignment
docs.text:
The alignment between vision and language is achieved through:

\[\text{Similarity}(v, t) = \frac{f_v(v) \cdot f_t(t)}{||f_v(v)|| \cdot ||f_t(t)||}\]

Where: - \(f_v(v)\) = Visual feature extractor - \(f_t(t)\) = Text feature extractor - \(v\) = Visual input - \(t\) = Text input

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• Image Understanding: Object detection, scene analysis, and visual reasoning
  • Visual Question Answering: Responding to queries about visual content
  • Image Captioning: Generating descriptive text for images
  • Visual Instruction Following: Executing tasks based on visual cues

docs.title: AI Agent Use Cases
docs.text:
• Robotics: Navigation and object manipulation in physical environments
  • Autonomous Vehicles: Scene understanding and decision making
  • Medical Imaging: Diagnostic assistance and report generation
  • Content Moderation: Automated detection of inappropriate visual content

docs.title: Implementation Framework
docs.text:
from transformers import VisionEncoderDecoderModel, ViTImageProcessor, GPT2TokenizerFast

# Initialize VLM components
processor = ViTImageProcessor.from_pretrained("nlpconnect/vit-gpt2-image-captioning")
tokenizer = GPT2TokenizerFast.from_pretrained("nlpconnect/vit-gpt2-image-captioning")
model = VisionEncoderDecoderModel.from_pretrained("nlpconnect/vit-gpt2-image-captioning")

def process_visual_input(image, instruction):
    # Process image and generate response
    pixel_values = processor(image, return_tensors="pt").pixel_values
    generated_ids = model.generate(pixel_values, max_length=50)
    return tokenizer.decode(generated_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Small Language Models (SLMs) provide efficient, lightweight solutions for AI agents operating under resource constraints. Models like Llama demonstrate that smaller architectures can achieve impressive performance while maintaining computational efficiency.

docs.title: Efficiency Optimizations
docs.text:
• Parameter Reduction: Fewer parameters while maintaining capability
  • Quantization: Reduced precision for faster inference
  • Pruning: Removal of unnecessary network connections
  • Knowledge Distillation: Learning from larger teacher models

docs.title: Architecture Optimizations
docs.text:
The efficiency gains are achieved through:

\[\text{Compression Ratio} = \frac{\text{Original Parameters}}{\text{Compressed Parameters}}\]

Inference speed improvement:

\[\text{Speedup} = \frac{T_{\text{large}}}{T_{\text{small}}}\]

docs.title: SLM Advantages
docs.text:
• Low Latency: Faster response times for real-time applications
  • Reduced Memory: Lower RAM and storage requirements
  • Edge Deployment: Suitable for mobile and IoT devices
  • Cost Efficiency: Lower computational and operational costs

docs.title: AI Agent Applications
docs.text:
• Mobile Assistants: Smartphone and tablet applications
  • IoT Devices: Smart home and industrial automation
  • Edge Computing: Local processing without cloud dependency
  • Embedded Systems: Resource-constrained hardware environments

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Large Action Models (LAMs) specialize in translating natural language instructions into executable actions. These models bridge the gap between language understanding and real-world task execution in AI agent systems.

docs.title: Action Planning Components
docs.text:
• Task Decomposition: Breaking complex goals into actionable steps
  • Action Space Mapping: Translating intentions to specific actions
  • Environment Modeling: Understanding action contexts and constraints
  • Execution Monitoring: Tracking progress and handling failures

docs.title: Action Planning Algorithm
docs.text:
The action planning process follows:

\[\pi(a_t|s_t, g) = \text{LAM}(\text{state}=s_t, \text{goal}=g, \text{history}=h_{t-1})\]

Where: - \(\pi\) = Policy function - \(a_t\) = Action at time \(t\) - \(s_t\) = Current state - \(g\) = Goal specification - \(h_{t-1}\) = Action history

docs.title: Action Categories
docs.text:
• Physical Actions: Movement, manipulation, and environmental interaction
  • Digital Actions: API calls, file operations, and system commands
  • Communication Actions: Message sending, notification, and reporting
  • Cognitive Actions: Analysis, planning, and decision making

docs.title: AI Agent Integration
docs.text:
• Robotic Control: Direct motor command generation for physical robots
  • Workflow Automation: Business process execution and optimization
  • Game Playing: Strategic action selection in competitive environments
  • Smart Home Control: Device management and automation

docs.title: Implementation Pipeline
docs.text:
class ActionPlanningAgent:
    def __init__(self, lam_model):
        self.lam = lam_model
        self.action_executor = ActionExecutor()

    def plan_and_execute(self, goal, current_state):
        # Generate action sequence
        action_plan = self.lam.generate_plan(goal, current_state)

        # Execute actions sequentially
        for action in action_plan:
            result = self.action_executor.execute(action)
            if not result.success:
                # Replan if action fails
                return self.plan_and_execute(goal, result.new_state)

        return "Goal achieved successfully"

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Hierarchical Language Models (HLMs) implement multi-level processing architectures that mirror human cognitive hierarchies. These models enable AI agents to handle complex tasks through structured, layered reasoning approaches.

docs.title: Hierarchical Structure
docs.text:
• High-Level Planning: Strategic goal setting and major milestone definition
  • Mid-Level Coordination: Task orchestration and resource allocation
  • Low-Level Execution: Detailed action implementation and monitoring
  • Cross-Level Communication: Information flow between hierarchical layers

docs.title: Mathematical Framework
docs.text:
The hierarchical processing is modeled as:

\[H_l(x) = \text{LLM}_l(\text{concat}(x, H_{l-1}(x), C_l))\]

Where: - \(H_l\) = Hierarchical layer \(l\) - \(\text{LLM}_l\) = Language model at layer \(l\) - \(C_l\) = Context from peer layers - \(l \in \{1, 2, ..., L\}\) for \(L\) layers

docs.title: Layer Responsibilities
docs.text:
Executive Layer (Top) - Strategic planning and goal prioritization - Resource allocation and high-level decision making - Performance monitoring and strategy adjustment

Coordination Layer (Middle) - Task scheduling and dependency management - Inter-agent communication and collaboration - Quality control and validation

Execution Layer (Bottom) - Detailed action implementation - Error handling and recovery - Real-time monitoring and feedback

docs.title: AI Agent Benefits
docs.text:
• Scalability: Handle increasingly complex multi-step tasks
  • Modularity: Independent development and optimization of layers
  • Robustness: Fault tolerance through hierarchical redundancy
  • Interpretability: Clear separation of reasoning levels

docs.title: Use Case Examples
docs.text:
• Project Management: Multi-level task breakdown and execution
  • Research Coordination: Literature review, hypothesis generation, and experiment design
  • Software Development: Architecture design, implementation, and testing
  • Supply Chain Management: Strategic planning, operational coordination, and execution monitoring

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Large Concept Models (LCMs) focus on learning and manipulating abstract concepts, enabling AI agents to perform high-level reasoning about ideas, relationships, and conceptual frameworks. These models excel at knowledge representation and conceptual understanding.

docs.title: Concept Learning Architecture
docs.text:
• Concept Extraction: Identifying abstract concepts from input data
  • Relationship Modeling: Understanding connections between concepts
  • Conceptual Reasoning: Performing inference at the concept level
  • Knowledge Integration: Combining concepts from multiple domains

docs.title: Conceptual Representation
docs.text:
Concepts are represented in a semantic space:

\[\text{Concept}(c) = \{e_1, e_2, ..., e_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\]

Concept relationships are modeled through:

\[\text{Relation}(c_1, c_2) = f(W_r \cdot [\text{Concept}(c_1); \text{Concept}(c_2)])\]

Where: - \(e_i\) = Embedding dimensions - \(W_r\) = Relation weight matrix - \(f\) = Activation function

docs.title: Concept Operations
docs.text:
• Concept Composition: Combining multiple concepts into new abstractions
  • Concept Abstraction: Generalizing from specific instances to broader categories
  • Concept Analogy: Finding similarities across different domains
  • Concept Transfer: Applying knowledge from one domain to another

docs.title: AI Agent Applications
docs.text:
• Scientific Discovery: Hypothesis generation and theory development
  • Creative Problem Solving: Novel solution generation through concept combination
  • Educational Systems: Adaptive learning based on conceptual understanding
  • Knowledge Management: Organizing and retrieving information by concepts

docs.title: Implementation Framework
docs.text:
class ConceptualAgent:
    def __init__(self, lcm_model):
        self.lcm = lcm_model
        self.concept_graph = ConceptGraph()

    def analyze_concepts(self, input_text):
        # Extract concepts from input
        concepts = self.lcm.extract_concepts(input_text)

        # Build concept relationships
        for concept in concepts:
            related = self.lcm.find_related_concepts(concept)
            self.concept_graph.add_relationships(concept, related)

        return self.concept_graph.get_insights()

    def conceptual_reasoning(self, query):
        # Perform reasoning at concept level
        relevant_concepts = self.concept_graph.query(query)
        reasoning_chain = self.lcm.reason_with_concepts(relevant_concepts)
        return reasoning_chain

docs.title: 🧭 Introduction
docs.text:
This transcript captures a detailed conversation between Hamel Husain and Charles Frye, highlighting the development and iterative improvement of a project centered around generating visually appealing and scannable QR codes using diffusion models.

Charles, representing Modal, shares deep insights into overcoming technical challenges in QR code generation—emphasizing the strategic role of evaluations (evals) and serverless compute scaling. This project stands as a practical case study in applying machine learning principles, evaluation frameworks, and cloud resources to deliver reliable generative model outputs.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: 📌 Key Points
docs.text:
• 🌀 Diffusion Models were used to generate QR codes that are both aesthetically pleasing and scannable.
  • 🔍 Early issues: QR codes looked good visually but failed to scan reliably.
  • 🎯 Operationalization of fuzzy terms like "looks good" and "scans" became a priority.
  • 🧠 A control net was added to the diffusion model to guide generation via brightness patterns.
  • 🌈 An aesthetic predictor model was used to rank the visual quality of QR codes.
  • 🤖 A QR code reader package automated the scanning evaluation process.
  • ⚖️ Trade-off prioritization: Scanning reliability > Aesthetics.
  • 🖼️ Manual labeling of QR code images was performed to train/validate eval models.
  • 🐞 A critical bug in evaluation code was found and fixed—it had been misclassifying non-scannable codes.
  • ☁️ Inference-time compute scaling boosted success rates during generation.
  • ⚙️ Modal’s serverless platform enabled efficient compute scaling for dev and deployment.
  • 🔁 Iterative process included multiple rounds of parameter tuning and evaluation.
  • ✅ Final system achieved 95% QR code scanning success, satisfying the SLO.
  • 🧪 Evaluation timing tip: Implement evals during the second iteration, not the first.
  • 💸 Charles elaborates on trade-offs between cost, latency, and quality during scaling.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: 🧵 Detailed Summary
docs.text:
This case study dives into a project led by Charles Frye from Modal, which aimed to generate QR codes that are both visually appealing and functionally scannable using diffusion models. The project originally suffered from the common issue of aesthetic success without practical reliability, as the QR codes looked impressive but frequently failed to scan.

To address this, Charles’s team operationalized the goals of “looks good” and “scans.” They incorporated a control net into the diffusion process to guide image generation based on brightness patterns, preserving the QR code’s structure while still allowing for visual customization.

The team also implemented an aesthetic predictor model to rank visual outputs, and a QR reader tool to automate the scan-check process. Prioritization became a key engineering decision: they chose to optimize scanning reliability over subjective aesthetics, ensuring end-user functionality.

During iterative development, a bug in the evaluation pipeline was discovered that had been misclassifying unscannable QR codes. Fixing this improved the quality of the evaluation system and helped the model generate reliably scannable outputs.

To scale performance, they used inference-time compute scaling—allocating more resources dynamically to boost the QR code success rate. This process was made seamless through Modal’s serverless platform, which allowed rapid scaling without infrastructure overhead.

The team conducted manual labeling of QR outputs to create high-quality evaluation datasets and fine-tuned model parameters across multiple rounds. As a result, they reached a 95% scan success rate, aligning with their defined Service Level Objective (SLO).

Charles also shared strategic advice: introduce evaluation frameworks in the second iteration of a project, once core functionality is stable. He emphasized that early evaluations can be a distraction, whereas well-timed evals lead to actionable insights and performance improvements.

He also outlined how to balance trade-offs: - 💰 Cost: High compute = better outputs but higher billing. - ⏱️ Latency: Real-time applications must minimize delay. - 📈 Quality: Optimal outputs may require aggressive tuning and inference resources.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: 🧠 Lessons Learned
docs.text:
• Define evaluation criteria early, but implement evals iteratively.
  • Use automation for reliability checks (like QR readers).
  • Don't neglect manual labeling—it adds crucial ground truth.
  • Use serverless compute platforms like Modal to avoid DevOps bottlenecks.
  • Always prioritize end-user functionality over subjective output quality when needed.

🔝 Back to top

docs.title: 📌 Quick Navigation
docs.text:
• 1. Core Message

docs.title: 1. Core Message
docs.text: 🔥 "Evaluate everything you can—all the time—independently if possible. And most importantly: look at your data." – Skylar Payne

docs.title: 2. Key Principle: Look at Your Data
docs.text: AI and RAG systems often fail silently—issues accumulate as technical debt. The only way to address these failures is to: - Build systematic evaluation into each RAG pipeline component - Avoid being blind to where problems originate - Empower debugging via component-level visibility

docs.title: 4.1 Corpus Coverage
docs.text:
• Problem: You can't retrieve what's not documented.
  • Fix:
  • Maintain a representative query set.
  • Measure % of queries returning relevant chunks.
  • Audit your corpus for coverage gaps.

💡 Example: A dev support bot failed to answer "Salesforce integration" because no documentation existed, despite the feature being supported.

docs.title: 4.2 Information Extraction
docs.text:
• Problem: Poor extraction from PDFs, code blocks, tables, or complex formats.
  • Fix:
  • Manually verify text extracted into chunks.
  • Validate semantic structure: tables, headers, Markdown formats.
  • Be cautious with OCR models or third-party converters.

docs.title: 4.3 Chunk Quality
docs.text:
• Problem: Over-chunked or under-chunked content harms retrieval and generation.
  • Fix:
  • Sample and review very large and very small chunks.
  • Track retrieval frequency of chunks:
    • High frequency? → Consider putting in prompt directly.
    • Never retrieved? → Irrelevant or corrupted.

💡 Tip: You might not need chunking if pages are small—feed entire documents.

docs.title: 4.4 Query Rejection & Elicitation
docs.text:
• Problem: Garbage-in = garbage-out. Many queries are vague or malformed.
  • Fix:
  • Reject ambiguous queries (e.g., “thing broken”).
  • Use elicitation: prompt users to clarify.
  • Track rejection/clarification rates in evaluation.

docs.title: 4.5 Retrieval Sufficiency
docs.text:
• Problem: Classic IR metrics (e.g., NDCG, precision@10) don’t assess if enough info is retrieved.
  • Fix:
  • Manually label if retrieved docs are sufficient to answer the query.
  • Think like SAT reading tests: Answer only using the provided passage.
  • Train an “AI judge” to scale this later.

docs.title: 4.6 Hallucination & Citation Verification
docs.text:
• Problem: LLMs fill in gaps with hallucinated content.
  • Fix:
  • Enforce in-text citations in generation outputs.
  • Validate:
    • Citation exists
    • Citation supports the claim via semantic matching
  • Reference: Jason Liu on Semantic Validation

docs.title: 4.7 Data Volatility & Reproducibility
docs.text:
• Problem: Indexes or external APIs silently change over time (e.g., Google Search limits).
  • Fix:
  • Add timestamps or versioning to indexed data.
  • Support time travel to reproduce eval results.
  • Ensure evaluation consistency over time.

docs.title: 5. Indexing Evaluation Tips
docs.text:
Evaluate each step of the document → index pipeline:

Step What to Evaluate Extraction Ensure parsing correctness from PDF, JSON, etc. Chunking Chunks should preserve context and be meaningful Embedding Confirm vectors map semantically to document intent Retrieval Retrieval should bring back expected content for key queries

Best Practice: Start with end-to-end error analysis, then drill down.

docs.title: 6. Late Interaction (e.g., ColBERT)
docs.text: Skylar’s opinion: - Too complex for most use cases - BM25 + embedding search often performs well enough - When retrieval fails, it’s often due to: - Poor chunking - Missing query terms - Not because of scoring method

docs.title: 7. Final Thoughts
docs.text:
• AI engineers already have 80% of the skills—just need guidance to cross the finish line.
  • Treat evaluation like software QA:
  • Add observability, logging, unit-like evals
  • Focus on data quality and visibility over clever model tweaks

  • 📘 ColBERT Late Interaction (Not recommended unless justified)

docs.title: Evaluation Driven Development for Agentic Systems
docs.text: The development process for Agentic Systems, particularly those based on Large Language Models (LLMs), is a continuous, iterative loop that prioritizes evaluation and feedback for successful evolution . This system aims to avoid common pitfalls by structuring the entire lifecycle from idea to production .

docs.title: 📌 Quick Navigation
docs.text:
• 1. Defining The Problem
  • 2. Building a Prototype
  • 3. Defining Performance Metrics
  • 4. Defining Evaluation Rules
  • 5. Building a Proof of Concept (PoC)
  • 6. Instrumenting the Application (Observability)
  • 7. Integrating with an Observability Platform
  • 8. Evaluating Traced Data
  • 9. Evolving the Application
  • 10. Exposing New Versions of the Application
  • 11. Continuous Development and Evolution of the Application
  • 12. Monitoring and Alerting

docs.title: 1. Defining The Problem
docs.text:
This is the initial and vital step for any Agentic System development . * Goal: Ensure the problem is clearly defined, bounded, and aligned with business goals . Agentic Systems use LLMs or other GenAI models to solve complex, real-world problems, often involving automation . * Key Questions: * Is the problem best solved by AI or traditional software? * Who is the end user? * What are the edge cases? * What are the boundaries of acceptable behavior? * Important: Many AI projects fail not due to bad models, but due to solving the wrong problem . * Roles Involved: AI Product Managers, Domain Experts, AI Engineers .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 2. Building a Prototype
docs.text:
After confirming AI is a good fit, the next step is rapid prototyping . * Goal: Primarily a learning phase to assess technical feasibility and de-risk the idea . * Key Considerations: * Use Notebooks or no-code tools, small datasets, and off-the-shelf models . * Focus on learning, not initial performance . * Document everything to avoid repeating mistakes . * Involve prompt engineering and market research for potential tools (e.g., Voice to Text platforms) . * Roles Involved: AI Product Managers, AI Engineers .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 3. Defining Performance Metrics
docs.text:
Every application should solve a real business problem, which needs to be grounded in specific metrics . * Goal: Optimizing for a "north star output metric" (e.g., reduce headcount, improve user satisfaction, increase development velocity) and breaking it down into "input metrics" that the application will directly target (e.g., reduce average customer support ticket resolution time) . * Important: Without properly setting this stage, the project risks being deprioritized for not demonstrating enough business value . Alignment with business stakeholders is crucial before implementation . * Roles Involved: AI Product Managers, AI Engineers, Business Stakeholders .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 4. Defining Evaluation Rules
docs.text:
Given the complexities of metrics for LLMs (e.g., human alignment, coherence, factuality), defining exact evaluation rules is highly beneficial . * Goal: Establish clear criteria for judging system responses, especially for chained LLM calls within an Agentic System topology . * Key Considerations: * Prepare an evaluation dataset (Inputs → Expected Outputs) for each node in your Agentic System topology . * Define unacceptable responses (e.g., toxicity, hallucinations, unsafe suggestions) . * Roles Involved: AI Product Managers, AI Engineers .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 5. Building a Proof of Concept (PoC)
docs.text:
This stage emphasizes getting the system into users' hands as quickly as possible . * Goal: Rapidly push out a user-facing application to gather crucial "unknown unknowns" from user feedback [9, 10]. * Key Considerations: * Use LLM APIs from providers like OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, etc., for quick development . * The PoC can be as simple as an Excel Spreadsheet with input/output pairs, as long as it helps move metrics forward and is exposed . * User feedback is key to shifting perspectives on application improvement . * Important: If you can't push it out quickly, there's an issue with the process . A successful LLM PoC may look like an Excel Spreadsheet . * Roles Involved: AI Engineers .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 6. Instrumenting the Application (Observability)
docs.text:
This is a key element in implementing Evaluation Driven Development . * Goal: Implement observability best practices by logging an extensive set of metadata about everything happening within the LLM-based system . * Key Considerations: * Log everything: prompts, completions, embeddings, latency, token counts, and user feedback . * Add additional metadata: prompt versions, user inputs, model versions used . * Ensure proper connection and ordering of operations within chains, as outputs of one LLM call often become inputs to the next . * Log multimodal data (PDFs, images, audio, video) . * Crucially, attach user feedback to the traces representing the user interaction when feedback was provided . * Roles Involved: AI Engineers .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 7. Integrating with an Observability Platform
docs.text:
Beyond just tracking data, efficient visualization and analysis are crucial . * Goal: Utilize an observability platform for efficient search, visualization, prompt versioning, and automated evaluation capabilities . * Key Considerations: * Store evaluation rules within the platform to apply them to traces . * Use platforms as Prompt Registries to analyze and group evaluation results by Prompt Groups, as your application is a chain of prompts . * Benefit from smart sampling algorithms for cost-effective storage of traces at scale, as storing all traces can become too expensive . * Utilize platform-specific tracing SDKs for seamless instrumentation . * Important: Set this up early as it brings visibility to the "black box" of LLM applications . * Roles Involved: AI Engineers .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 8. Evaluating Traced Data
docs.text:
With instrumentation and platform integration, you can now measure your application effectively . * Goal: Automatically run evaluations on the collected trace data, especially focusing on identifying failures . * Key Considerations: * Assumption: Evaluation rules are stored in the Observability platform, and traces with human feedback are connected . * Automatically run evaluations on traces hitting the Observability Platform . * Filter out traces with failing evaluations or negative human feedback; this "failing" data will be the primary focus for improvement . * Important: Running evaluations can be expensive (especially LLM-as-a-judge tactics), so sampling traces might be necessary . * Roles Involved: AI Engineers .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 9. Evolving the Application
docs.text:
This is where the application is improved based on data-driven insights . * Goal: Enhance the application by focusing on failing evaluations and human feedback . * Key Considerations: * Start with better prompt engineering, data preprocessing, and tool integration before increasing system complexity . * Increase complexity (e.g., Simple Prompts → RAG → Agentic RAG → Agents → Multi-agent systems) only if there's a hard requirement and the current topology is not up to the task . * Maintain a "failing eval dataset" that is continuously fed with new failing samples and is never 100% "solved" . Your goal is to achieve 100% but by adding more failing samples, you never get there . * Important: Always involve Domain Experts at this stage for their insider knowledge and potential prompt suggestions . * Roles Involved: AI Engineers, Domain Experts .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 10. Exposing New Versions of the Application
docs.text:
Rapid deployment of new versions is crucial for continuous improvement . * Goal: Quickly release updates to incorporate fixes and improvements, leveraging invaluable feedback . * Key Considerations: * Fast deployment improves user experience by fixing present problems, and some fixes can generalize to unknown problems . * Implement strict release tests and integrate evaluation datasets into CI/CD pipelines to ensure new releases do not degrade performance compared to previous versions . * Roles Involved: AI Engineers, Domain Experts .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 11. Continuous Development and Evolution of the Application
docs.text:
This represents the core iterative loop of the Evaluation Driven Development process . * Cycle: Build → Trace, collect feedback → Evaluate → Focus on Failing Evals and Negative Feedback → Improve the application → Iterate . * Goal: Continuously evolve the application, adding new functionalities (often as new routes in the Agentic System Topology) by following the same process of prototyping, defining metrics, and new evaluations [19, 20]. For example, a simple chatbot can evolve into a system that manages a shopping cart . * Roles Involved: AI Engineers, Domain Experts, AI Product Managers .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 12. Monitoring and Alerting
docs.text:
After implementing tracing and evaluation for development, monitoring almost comes out of the box . * Goal: Reuse implemented evaluations and traces for production monitoring and configure specific alerting thresholds . * Key Considerations: * Most relevant data for LLM-specific production monitoring is already available if application instrumentation was properly implemented . * Consider tracing and logging additional advanced metrics like TTFT (Time To First Token) and inter-token latency . * You will need to figure out the threshold for alerting . * Important: Try to avoid Alert Fatigue by carefully configuring thresholds that trigger alerts and avoid False Positives as much as possible . * Roles Involved: AI Engineers .

⬆️ Back to Top

docs.title: 📝 Description
docs.text: ChatGPT represents OpenAI's flagship conversational AI platform, designed as a versatile generative AI tool supporting text, images, video, and code generation with web browsing capabilities. Built for both productivity enhancement and creative applications, it serves as a comprehensive AI assistant for diverse professional and personal tasks.

docs.title: ⚡ When to Use ChatGPT
docs.text:
• Diverse Multimodal Requirements: When projects require seamless switching between text, image, audio, and video processing
  • Memory Enhancement Tasks: For applications requiring conversation history and context retention across sessions
  • Plugin Integration Needs: When workflow optimization requires third-party tool integration
  • Creative Work Support: Perfect for content creation, brainstorming, and iterative creative processes
  • Workflow Optimization: When building custom automation and productivity enhancement systems

docs.title: 🎯 Primary Use Cases
docs.text:
• Content Creation: Generate reports, marketing campaigns, presentations, and multimedia content
  • Custom GPT Development: Build specialized AI assistants tailored for specific business processes or personal workflows
  • Communication Automation: Automate email responses, meeting summaries, and customer support interactions
  • Educational Support: Create learning materials, explanations, and interactive educational content
  • Code Development: Full-stack development support with debugging, optimization, and documentation

docs.title: 💪 Key Strengths
docs.text:
• Comprehensive Plugin Ecosystem: Built-in access to web browsing, image generation, audio processing, and video capabilities
  • Cross-Platform Compatibility: Robust performance across different browsers and integration points
  • Domain Adaptability: Exceptional flexibility across diverse industries and use cases
  • Active Development: Continuous feature updates and capability expansions
  • Community Support: Large user base with extensive documentation and community resources

docs.title: ⚠️ Notable Weaknesses
docs.text:
• Premium Feature Limitations: Most advanced capabilities require paid subscription tiers
  • Accuracy Validation Needs: Generated content may require human verification for factual accuracy
  • Cost Considerations: Higher operational costs for intensive use cases
  • Information Currency: Knowledge cutoffs may affect real-time information accuracy

docs.title: 💡 Pro Tip
docs.text: Create custom GPTs tailored to your specific workflow needs. Define clear instructions, upload relevant documents, and configure specific behaviors to transform ChatGPT into a specialized assistant for your industry or role.

docs.title: 📝 Description
docs.text: Google's Gemini represents a deeply integrated AI solution built specifically for the Google ecosystem, encompassing Gmail, Google Docs, Sheets, and Search. Designed with multimodal collaboration at its core, Gemini excels in productivity workflows that leverage Google's comprehensive suite of tools and services.

docs.title: ⚡ When to Use Gemini
docs.text:
• Google Ecosystem Workflows: When your organization primarily operates within Google Workspace
  • Multimodal Input/Output Needs: For projects requiring seamless handling of text, images, and data formats
  • Collaborative Presentations: When creating visually rich content requiring real-time team collaboration
  • Data Integration Tasks: For workflows involving Google Sheets analysis and Google Drive document processing

docs.title: 🎯 Primary Use Cases
docs.text:
• Email and Document Analysis: Process email threads with attachments and extract insights from Google Docs
  • Visual Content Creation: Generate slides, charts, and visually rich presentations directly within Google tools
  • Team Collaboration: Enable seamless AI-assisted collaboration across distributed teams using Google Workspace
  • Data Visualization: Transform Google Sheets data into compelling visual narratives and insights
  • Research Integration: Combine Google Search capabilities with document analysis and synthesis

docs.title: 💪 Key Strengths
docs.text:
• Native Google Integration: Seamless operation across Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Drive, and other Google services
  • Multimodal Excellence: Strong performance in handling mixed content types within collaborative environments
  • Asynchronous Teamwork: Optimized for distributed team collaboration and document sharing workflows
  • Real-time Collaboration: Live editing and AI assistance during team meetings and document creation
  • Search Integration: Leverages Google's search capabilities for enhanced information retrieval

docs.title: ⚠️ Notable Weaknesses
docs.text:
• Experimental Feature Limitations: Some advanced capabilities remain in beta or limited release
  • Ecosystem Dependency: Performance and feature availability limited outside Google's platform
  • User Experience Variability: Interface polish and consistency may vary across different Google services
  • Third-party Integration: Limited connectivity with non-Google platforms and services

docs.title: 💡 Pro Tip
docs.text: Maximize Gemini's potential by creating integrated workflows that span Gmail, Google Docs, and Sheets. Use it to automatically analyze email data, generate reports in Docs, and create visualizations in Sheets within a single, streamlined process.

docs.title: 📝 Description
docs.text: Anthropic's Claude stands out as an AI model specifically engineered for deep analytical thinking, safety-first conversations, and processing extensive contexts. Designed with a focus on responsible AI principles, Claude excels in scenarios requiring nuanced reasoning, lengthy document analysis, and careful, defensible conclusions.

docs.title: ⚡ When to Use Claude
docs.text:
• Academic and Legal Research: When processing complex research papers, legal documents, or policy analysis
  • Long-form Content Analysis: For tasks involving extensive documentation review and synthesis
  • Safety-Critical Applications: When AI decisions require careful reasoning and risk assessment
  • Technical Documentation: For processing complex technical materials requiring precise understanding

docs.title: 🎯 Primary Use Cases
docs.text:
• Document Analysis: Summarize lengthy agreements, contracts, and complex legal documentation
  • Research Synthesis: Transform dense research papers into clear, actionable insights and summaries
  • Technical Review: Analyze complex technical documentation, code reviews, and system specifications
  • Policy Analysis: Process government documents, regulations, and policy papers for strategic insights
  • Academic Writing: Support scholarly writing, literature reviews, and research methodology development

docs.title: 💪 Key Strengths
docs.text:
• Long-form Text Processing: Exceptional capability for handling extensive documents and maintaining context
  • Logical Reasoning: Strong analytical and logical reasoning capabilities for complex problem-solving
  • Safety-Conscious Design: Built-in considerations for responsible AI use and ethical decision-making
  • Natural Writing Style: Produces human-like, nuanced writing that maintains professional tone
  • Deep Context Understanding: Maintains coherence across lengthy conversations and complex topics

docs.title: ⚠️ Notable Weaknesses
docs.text:
• Limited Multimodal Capabilities: Lacks native support for image, audio, or video generation
  • Conservative Approach: May be overly cautious in certain creative or experimental scenarios
  • Speed Limitations: Slower processing for quick, iterative creative tasks compared to other models
  • Feature Scope: Fewer integrated tools and plugins compared to more comprehensive platforms

docs.title: 💡 Pro Tip
docs.text: Leverage Claude's exceptional long-context capabilities by feeding it complete documents, research papers, or legal texts for comprehensive analysis. Structure your queries to request specific analytical frameworks or comparison criteria for optimal results.

docs.title: 📝 Description
docs.text: X's Grok represents a unique AI chatbot powered by real-time social media content and designed for conversational engagement with wit and contemporary relevance. Built specifically for the X platform ecosystem, Grok excels in real-time information processing, trend analysis, and generating engaging social content.

docs.title: ⚡ When to Use Grok
docs.text:
• Active X Platform Engagement: When social media presence and engagement are primary objectives
  • Real-time Trend Monitoring: For tracking live events, breaking news, and social media trends
  • Quick Conversational AI: When seeking rapid, witty responses and casual conversational interaction
  • Social Content Creation: For generating engaging, shareable content optimized for social platforms

docs.title: 🎯 Primary Use Cases
docs.text:
• Social Media Monitoring: Track live events, trending topics, and real-time social media conversations
  • Content Creation: Generate engaging, shareable social media posts with appropriate tone and timing
  • Real-time Q&A: Provide immediate responses with humor and contemporary references
  • Trend Analysis: Analyze social media patterns and emerging topics for marketing or research purposes
  • Community Engagement: Facilitate interactive conversations and community building on social platforms

docs.title: 💪 Key Strengths
docs.text:
• Real-time Data Access: Direct access to current X platform data and trending information
  • Conversational Engagement: Fast, engaging responses with humor and contemporary cultural references
  • Social Media Optimization: Content specifically optimized for social media engagement and virality
  • Speed and Responsiveness: Quick processing for immediate social media interactions
  • Platform Integration: Seamless operation within the X ecosystem and social workflows

docs.title: ⚠️ Notable Weaknesses
docs.text:
• Ecosystem Limitations: Functionality primarily limited to X platform and social media contexts
  • Research Limitations: Not optimized for technical rigor, academic research, or complex analysis
  • Professional Applications: May lack the depth and precision required for professional or technical tasks
  • Content Appropriateness: Potential for generating content that may not align with professional communication standards

docs.title: 💡 Pro Tip
docs.text: Use Grok strategically for real-time social media management by monitoring trending topics and generating timely, relevant content that capitalizes on current events and social media conversations.

docs.title: 📝 Description
docs.text: DeepSeek represents a Chinese-developed AI model optimized for high-performance computing, cost-effectiveness, and technical workloads. Designed as an affordable alternative to Western AI platforms, DeepSeek excels in technical programming, multilingual content generation, and resource-intensive analytical tasks.

docs.title: ⚡ When to Use DeepSeek
docs.text:
• Budget-Conscious Projects: When cost-effectiveness is a primary consideration for AI implementation
  • Technical Programming Tasks: For intensive coding, debugging, and software development projects
  • Multilingual Content Needs: When working with diverse language requirements and international content
  • Large-scale Processing: For analytical workloads requiring extensive computational resources
  • Alternative Platform Needs: When seeking independence from Western AI platform dependencies

docs.title: 🎯 Primary Use Cases
docs.text:
• Code Generation and Debugging: Develop, optimize, and debug code across multiple programming languages
  • Data Analysis and Research: Process large datasets and perform complex analytical computations
  • Multilingual Content Creation: Generate content in various languages for international audiences
  • Technical Documentation: Create comprehensive technical documentation and system specifications
  • Cost-Optimized AI Integration: Implement AI capabilities with minimal operational expenses

docs.title: 💪 Key Strengths
docs.text:
• Cost-Effectiveness: Significantly lower operational costs compared to premium AI platforms
  • Technical Proficiency: Strong performance in coding, debugging, and technical problem-solving
  • Processing Speed: Fast execution for computational tasks and code generation
  • Multilingual Capabilities: Effective handling of diverse languages and international content requirements
  • Resource Efficiency: Optimized for large-scale workloads without proportional cost increases

docs.title: ⚠️ Notable Weaknesses
docs.text:
• Ecosystem Development: Smaller ecosystem and community compared to established Western platforms
  • Integration Limitations: Fewer third-party integrations and platform connections available
  • Global Recognition: Lower international recognition and support infrastructure
  • Feature Maturity: Some advanced features may be less mature compared to established competitors
  • Documentation Availability: Limited English-language documentation and community resources

docs.title: 💡 Pro Tip
docs.text:
Leverage DeepSeek for large-scale technical projects where cost efficiency is crucial. Combine it with other specialized tools for comprehensive workflows while maintaining budget control.

docs.title: 📄 Summary of "Distributional Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge"
docs.text:
Source: Distributional Bias — Verdict Documentation

Language models (LLMs) used as automated evaluators (LLM-as-a-judge) can suffer from distributional biases introduced by: - Model selection - Prompt design - Ordering of answer choices - Using the same model for generation and judgment

This guide outlines two major bias types and mitigation strategies.

docs.title: 1. Positional Bias
docs.text:
• Issue: The order of presented options can influence model scoring.
  • Mitigation Techniques:
  • Multiple Evidence Calibration (MEC): Ask for reasoning before assigning scores.
  • Balanced Prediction Calibration (BPC): Average results across all answer-order permutations.
  • Max-Voting: Aggregate scores from multiple random shuffles.
  • Prompt-Level Randomization: Shuffle options before each evaluation.

docs.title: 2. Self-Preference Bias
docs.text:
• Issue: LLMs tend to give higher scores to outputs they generated themselves.
  • Mitigation: Use different models for generation and evaluation.

docs.title: 🧠 Jina AI: Late Chunking in Long‑Context Embedding Models
📌 Table of Contents
docs.text:
• 1. Overview
  • 2. Problem Statement
  • 3. Methodology
  • 4. Python Implementation
  • 5. Quantitative Evaluation
  • 6. Use Case Impact
  • 7. Colab & Data
  • 8. References & Further Reading

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text: In this case study, we examine Late Chunking, a novel embedding technique introduced by Jina AI to improve retrieval accuracy in long‑document contexts. Late Chunking applies chunking after embedding processing—leveraging long‑context embedding models to retain broader document information in chunk embeddings. Back to Top

docs.title: 2. Problem Statement
docs.text: Traditional pipelines chunk text before embedding, often severing long‑range context. Consider a document referring to “Berlin” only once—subsequent sentences like “the city” lose connection without context. Late Chunking addresses this by embedding entire text, then pooling over logical segments, preserving semantic information. Back to Top

docs.title: 3. Methodology
docs.text:
1. Use a long‑context model (e.g., jina‑embeddings‑v2‑base‑en) to embed the entire document (up to 8K tokens).
  2. After obtaining token‑level embeddings, apply mean pooling on contiguous segments (chunks).
  3. This preserves cross‑chunk references and improves downstream retrieval tasks.
Step Naive Chunking Late Chunking Split Before embed After embedding Context Local only Full‑document embed context Embedding i.i.d. chunks Context‑aware chunks

Back to Top

docs.title: 4. Python Implementation
docs.text:
from jina import Client

client = Client()  # initialize your Jina embedding client

doc = "Berlin is the capital ... the city is also ..."
embeddings = client.embed_long_context(doc)  # pseudo-API

# Naive vs Late
chunks = ["Berlin is ...", "Its more than...", "The city is..."]
naive_embeds = [client.embed(c) for c in chunks]
late_embeds = embeddings.chunk(mean_pool=True)

print("Naive:", [e.cosine_sim("Berlin") for e in naive_embeds])
print("Late:", [e.cosine_sim("Berlin") for e in late_embeds])

👉 Open in Colab

Back to Top

docs.title: 5. Quantitative Evaluation
docs.text:
On BeIR retrieval benchmarks, Late Chunking outperforms naive chunking across multiple datasets using nDCG@10 metrics (higher is better):

Dataset Naive Chunking Late Chunking SciFact 64.2% 68.7% FiQA 27.5% 31.4% TREC-COVID 77.8% 81.1%

Back to Top

docs.text:
• Improved semantic recall for cross-referenced entities in long documents.
  • Better performance in legal, scientific, and technical document retrieval.
  • Reduced context fragmentation when handling large datasets.
